equation: EHCP(x*_obs) = E_{x*_miss}[F(x*_obs, x*_miss)] ≈ (1/M) Σ_m F(x*_obs, x*_miss^(m))
claim: Expected Hypothetical Completion Probability (EHCP), introduced by Deshpande & Evans (arXiv:1910.12337v1), is the expected completion probability for a receiver on an NFL passing play had the ball been thrown to him, defined as the expectation of the completion-probability function F over hypothetical unobserved covariates and approximated by averaging over M draws from the marginal empirical distribution of all observed passes.

On the NFL Big Data Bowl 2019 completion-probability task (N=4,913 passes from 91 games of the 2017 season's first 6 weeks), Bayesian Additive Regression Trees beat Bayesian logistic regression on all three metrics across 10 random 75/25 splits: MSE 0.086 vs 0.099, misclassification 0.113 vs 0.138, log-loss 0.289 vs 0.332.

BART posterior splitting-probability variable importance ranked receiver speed at catch attempt (20.74%), receiver-ball distance at catch (17.29%), and total distance traveled from snap to catch (10.92%) as the top three predictors of NFL pass completion; speed from snap to throw (0.27%), separation at throw (0.08%), and distance run snap-to-throw (0.01%) were negligible.

In Week 1 of the 2017 NFL season, Cooper Kupp's touchdown had a 47% forecasted completion probability and 65.1% EHCP at arrival, but his EHCP was 85.1% about 2 seconds earlier; Sammy Watkins held the play's highest EHCP (92.2%) 1.5 seconds after snap. Tolzien's interception: T.Y. Hilton's arrival-time EHCP was 59.0% vs ~89% about 2 seconds earlier. EHCP thus grades QB decision timing, not just outcome.

Bruce (arXiv:1511.04351v2) defines the Statistical Diversity Index (SDI) for NBA player similarity as the squared Euclidean distance between players in a 4-principal-component space derived from 66 standardized tracking stats; lower SDI means more similar. The first four PCs retained 68% of variance (PC1 42%, PC2 12%, PC3 9%, PC4 4%).

Team style is aggregated as a minutes-weighted average of player component scores. In an OLS of 2013-14 NBA team win percentage on the four team PC scores, R² was 0.59 (in-sample, no holdout); PC2 (0.17, p=0.005), PC3 (-0.20, p<0.001), and PC4 (0.09, p=0.013) were significant while PC1 (raw usage) was not — interpreted as ball movement, rebounding, and rim protection associating with winning rather than raw usage.

Tracking-data similarity identified J.J. Barea (SDI 0.7) as the closest player to Tony Parker, while traditional-stats-only similarity picked DeMar DeRozan — whose tracking SDI to Parker was 75 with 89 players closer — used in the paper as a value-play example ($12.5M vs $4,687,000 salaries).

Everett et al. (arXiv:2402.04898v1) model expected points from a chosen squad C as 3 times win probability plus draw probability, and optimize squad selection as an MDP via the Bellman equation V(s) = max_a (R(s,a) + γ Σ_{s'} Pr(s'|s,a) V(s')), solved with MCTS (UCB1 + progressive widening); rollouts simulate the first three transitions with injuries, then assume none.

On English Premier League 2017/18–2018/19 data (760 games), an XGBoost injury classifier from workload features achieved log loss 0.1676 ± 0.0005 vs a heuristic baseline 0.1700 ± 0.0002 (injury base rate ~4%); the full-season MCTS squad-optimization simulation found an expected-points difference vs greedy strongest-eleven of -0.1% ± 0.3 (null), while squad injuries fell ~5%, top-11 injuries ~13%, and expected-points variance fell 17%.

Broatch & Karl (arXiv:1710.05284v1) jointly estimate team strength by modeling binary win/loss outcomes together with game-level responses (YPP, sacks, fumbles, scores) via correlated team-level offense/defense/win-propensity random effects with unstructured 3×3 covariance, with game sub-model E[y_ih] = f_1(b^o_h − b^d_a), E[y_ia] = f_1(b^o_a − b^d_h), P(r_i=1) = f_2(b^w_h − b^w_a).

The joint likelihood integrates over the correlated random effects, enforcing conditional independence of the continuous and binary outcomes given b. On NCAA football 2005–2013, the joint model beat the binary-only model on win log-loss significantly in all years for the YPP, sacks, and scores sub-models; fumbles gave no significant improvement in any season (deliberately chosen irrelevant-response control). The joint scores+win model beat binary-only in all years and the NCAA tournament in 17 of 19 tournaments (p=0.0002).

As a demonstration, the joint scores+win model gave Notre Dame a 22.2% win probability in the 2012 Alabama–Notre Dame title game (correct direction), while the binary-only model said 62.5% and was wrong (Alabama won).

The sixth annual SoccerNet challenge-results report (arXiv:2607.07320v1, 427 teams, 1,129 entries across 5 tasks) records winners: ball-action anticipation FAANTRA-WS mAP_avg 24.08 vs baseline 16.76; player-centric action spotting PAVE macro-F1@0.15 58.94 vs 46.41; novel view synthesis DENSER PSNR 29.89/SSIM 0.791/LPIPS 0.388 vs 3DGS baseline 26.74/0.751/0.410; athlete localization SELabSoccer mAP-LocSim 97.67 vs 77.30; VQA vitomeme 98.0% accuracy vs 25.0% random. The ledger's verdict was REJECT for quantitative NFL engine transfer (no transferable method or metric).

Cucuringu (2015) Sync-Rank maps pairwise rank offsets to angles Θ_ij and builds the Hermitian matrix H_ij = e^{iΘ_ij}, recovering the ranking from the top eigenvector's phases. For rank aggregation across k rating systems, H̄ = Σ_{u=1..k} H^(u) (EIG-AGG/SDP-AGG). The recovery phase transition is 1−η > 1/√n (Eq. 21), with an ER-graph variant 1−η > √(n⁵/(8m³)).

On EPL 2013–14, Sync-Rank matched least squares (44 upsets, Kendall 0.87) and beat SVD (66 upsets, Kendall 0.69); on NCAA basketball 1985–2014, SYNC-SUP was 'twice as good as any of the other methods' on upsets. Documented failure mode: on ordinal ERO dense graphs, Serial-Rank averaging beats sync methods by 2–3 orders of magnitude at η ≤ 0.2.

SPRINT (arXiv:2608.05560v1) is a benchmark testing whether multimodal LLMs can proactively warn of imminent physical danger in sports videos, evaluated on three hierarchical binary dimensions (D1 hazard detection, D2 factor coverage, D3 cause identification, where D_i requires all D_j for j<i), under 3 prompt explicitness levels and temporal-window truncation (Window A: start→T1 earliest cue, B: start→midpoint(T1,T2), C: start→T2 obvious moment). The best model exceeded 95% on D1 but stayed below 50% on D3 — detection without understanding.

Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with LoRA (r=16, α=32, dropout 0.05, 2 epochs on 71,249 GPT-5-generated samples) lifted full-video D1 0.48→0.99 and D3 0.16→0.52; in the hardest case (Window A, neutral prompt) D1 went 0.09→0.84 and D3 0.02→0.32, with first-frame false-positive rate dropping 0.18→0.00. Explicit prompting increased false alarms: GPT-5's FPR went 0.28→0.59 and Doubao's 0.13→0.88 on safe videos, with even a static first frame triggering warnings.

Penn, Michael & Bhatt (2025) forecast bookmaker odds by imputing bookmaker probabilities p = d/‖d‖₁, assuming Elo-form odds P(a beats b) = 1/(1+10^{r_b − r_a}), and log-transforming odds so they are additive: x_{ab} = log((1−p_{ab})/p_{ab}) = r_a − r_b with x_{ab} = x_{ac} + x_{cb}. Ratings are fit via convex least squares f(r) = Σ_{a,b} W_{ab}((r_a − r_b) − E_{ab})² on a weighted directed graph with geometric temporal decay ρ and Markovian recursive updates W'_{ab} = ρ^t W_{ab} + w_{ab}(M); E'_{ab} = (W_{ab}ρ^t E_{ab} + w_{ab}(M)x_{ab}(M))/W'_{ab}. Theorem 1 proves geometric decay is the necessary weight function for Markovian updates.

On 7 Grand Slams 2024–2025 (1,684 matches), the odds-distillation model won 1,237 (73.5%) vs bookmakers 1,249 (74.1%) — not significant (p=0.40) — and beat rankings-based prediction (69.7%) significantly (p=0.0006), winning all 7 tournaments against rankings and beating bookmakers in 4 of 7. Model-vs-bookmaker probability correlation was ≈0.88 with best-fit line y = 0.88x + 0.08. The paper states explicitly that the model can never systematically beat the bookmaker — it is a distillation, not an edge generator.

equation: λ_it = Σ_{k∈V} γ_k(m_it) x_itk + Σ_{k∉V} β_k x_itk with γ_k(m_it) = α_k + β_k m_it
claim: Tsokos et al. (2018) compare Bradley–Terry extensions where the time-varying-coefficient (TVC) model lets feature weights change linearly with games played m_it: λ_it = Σ_{k∈V} γ_k(m_it) x_itk + Σ_{k∉V} β_k x_itk with γ_k(m_it) = α_k + β_k m_it (equivalently the linear-feature model plus {m_it x_itk} interactions). Scoring uses the ranked probability score RPS = (1/(r−1)) Σ_{i=1}^{r−1} Σ_{j=1}^{i} (p_j − a_j).

On >200,000 matches across 52 leagues, validation/challenge-test RPS was: BL 0.2242/0.2261, CS 0.2112/0.2128, LF 0.2088/0.2080, TVC 0.2081/0.2080, AFD 0.2079/0.2061, hierarchical Poisson log-linear (HPL, attack/defense + AR(1) across seasons fit with INLA) 0.2073/0.2047 (best). Validation-test correlation was 0.973 excluding BL, validating the temporal framework. Only goal difference and last-season points tally had time-varying coefficients significantly nonzero (Wald p < 0.001).

Diniz et al. (2017) compare two Bayesian multinomial-Dirichlet models using only each team's win/draw/loss counts (Mn-Dir1: w=1/2 mixture of two Dirichlet posteriors combined by linear opinion pooling with uniform D(1,1,1) prior; Mn-Dir2: grid search over 400 (w,α) pairs minimizing first-half Brier) against bivariate-Poisson and Bradley–Terry–Davidson baselines on 1,710 Brazilian championship matches. The BT–Davidson outcome probabilities are p^W_ij = γπ_i/(γπ_i + π_j + ν√(π_iπ_j)), p^D_ij = ν√(π_iπ_j)/(γπ_i + π_j + ν√(π_iπ_j)).

Total Brier scores (n=1,710): BT 1085.9 (SE 14.9), Arruda 1053.2 (12.6), Lee 1075.5 (14.9), Mn-Dir1 1067.59 (10.4), Mn-Dir2 1073.5 (8.8). Mn-Dir1 beat BT on Brier (estimate −0.01, p=0.04) and log score (p=0.01); Arruda was best on all three scoring rules but not significantly different from Mn-Dir1. Goodness-of-fit χ² (40 df): BT 112.8 (p=0.001, rejected), Mn-Dir1 61.5 (p=0.91, best). Calibration curves showed Arruda and both Mn-Dir models track the 45° line while BT and Lee over-estimate probabilities of frequent events.

Thulasidasan et al. (2019) propose the Deep Abstaining Classifier (DAC): an extra abstention output trained with loss ℒ(x_j) = (1−p_{k+1})(−Σ_i t_i log(p_i/(1−p_{k+1}))) + α·log(1/(1−p_{k+1})) — cross-entropy over real classes with abstention mass normalized out, plus an abstention penalty. Lemma 1: ∂ℒ/∂a_j ≤ 0 for the true-class pre-activation, so learning on true classes persists while abstaining. Lemma 2: with fixed α, abstention rate γ→0 or γ→1 as t→∞, so α must be auto-tuned (Algorithm 1: L warmup epochs, set α = β̃/ρ with ρ=64, μ=0.05).

DAC CIFAR-10 ResNet-34 test accuracy at uniform label noise 0.2/0.4/0.6/0.8: Baseline 88.94/85.35/79.74/67.17 vs DAC 92.91/90.71/86.30/74.84 (fraction removed / remaining noise: 0.24/0.01, 0.41/0.03, 0.56/0.07, 0.75/0.16); DAC beats the oracle cleaner at 0.2 noise. Caveat: DAC removes up to 75% of training data at 0.8 noise — dangerous for small sports samples.

equation: Δ̂(c) ≤ ε_Bayes(c) + ε_approx(c) + ε_rank(c) + ε_stat(c) + ε_misc(c)
claim: Rabanser's (2025) thesis gives a finite-sample gap decomposition Δ̂(c) ≤ ε_Bayes(c) + ε_approx(c) + ε_rank(c) + ε_stat(c) + ε_misc(c) with the key theorem that monotone post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling) cannot reduce the ranking term ε_rank — only non-monotone or feature-aware calibrators shrink it. Selective rule: (f,g)(x) = f(x) if g(x) ≤ τ else ⊥; SPTD is a free abstention signal from training-checkpoint disagreement with weighting v_t = (t/T)^k, best k ∈ [1,3], 10 checkpoints sufficing for the high-coverage regime at O(1) training cost.

On CIFAR-10 at coverage 50, SPTD reached 99.8±0.0 accuracy vs Deep Ensembles 99.7±0.1 and softmax response 98.6±0.2; at coverage 90 SPTD 96.5 vs DE 96.8. On StanfordCars at coverage 70, SPTD 93.6 vs DE 92.4. The Mirage adversarial-confidence attack manipulated CIFAR-100 ECE 0.0662→0.1821 while accuracy stayed 83.98→83.92 — confidence manipulated with accuracy unchanged.

Ziel (2018) won 2nd of ~100 teams in the GEFCom2017 open track with a framework decomposing log-load as L_t = trend_t + Y_t, fitting trend by OLS on hour-of-week dummies + Fourier-2 annual basis + periodic B-splines + cubic temperature polynomials, and the remainder by 24 hourly quantile regressions (46 parameters each: 7 day-of-week dummies + 28 annual Fourier-2 × day-of-week interactions + 11 annual B-splines), evaluated by pinball score S_τ(y,q) = (y−q)(τ − 𝜙{y−q<0}). Final quantiles: q̂_τ(L) = q̂_τ(Y) + q̂_τ(trend).

The GEFCom2017 winner beat the Vanilla benchmark in 90% of zone×task cases; Task 1 TOTAL pinball 358.44 MW vs benchmark 402.68 MW (+10.99%), Task 6 TOTAL +11.19%. In-sample 10–90% quantile range was ≈0.1 (log scale) vs trend-component range <0.008 — uncertainty driven by the quantile-regression component. Admitted weaknesses: holidays ignored, non-linear effects, structural changes (Massachusetts solar boom); quantile summation only valid under comonotonicity.

Bransen & Van Haaren (arXiv:2003.01712v1) define Joint Offensive Impact JOI_m(p,q) = Σ_k V(I^k_m(p,q)) + Σ_l V(I^l_m(q,p)) over consecutive-action interactions (V = VAEP value of on-ball actions), with JOI90 = 90·Σ_m JOI_m / Σ_m MINS_m(p,q), and Joint Defensive Impact JDI_m(p,q) = Σ_o (E[OI_m(o)] − OI_m(o))·RESP_m(p,q,o)·MINS_m(p,q,o)/90 where RESP comes from inverse Euclidean distance of default positions on a 5×5 pitch grid. E[OI_m(p)] uses Bayesian shrinkage to a position-specific prior below 700 minutes.

CatBoost prediction of unseen-pair chemistry on Wyscout data (355,671 training pairs): JOI RMSE 0.04464 vs mean baseline 0.05448 (~18% reduction, real signal); JDI RMSE 0.88906 vs baseline 0.89075 — essentially null, so predicted JDI is unproven. Top JOI90: Salah–Firmino 2017/18 UCL 0.7077 (highest in dataset); Suárez–Messi 2015/16 0.6497. Player Role scores dominated feature importance; matches-played-together mattered most early, diminishing after ~50 matches; same-nationality/language cultural features had limited predictive power.

equation: μ_t = Σ_k w_k p_k / Σ_k w_k with w_k = π/((μ_t−p_k)β_k√3)·tanh((μ_t−p_k)π/(β_k√12))
claim: Ebtekar & Liu's Elo-MMR (arXiv:2101.00400) Phase 1 estimates each round performance as the unique zero of Q_i(p) = Σ_{j≻i} l_j(p) + Σ_{j∼i} d_j(p) + Σ_{j≺i} v_j(p) (Theorem 3.3); Phase 2 minimizes L(s) = L_2((s−p_0)/β_0) + Σ_k L_R((s−p_k)/β_k) with L_R(x)=2 ln(cosh(πx/√12)), yielding the robust weighted average above. Uncertainty: 1/σ_t² = Σ_k 1/β_k². Skill evolution uses pseudodiffusion Elo-MMR(ρ) with κ = (1 + γ_t²/σ_{t−1}²)^{-1}; ρ∈(0,∞) provably satisfies six properties (Theorem 4.1). Theorem 5.7: robustness bounds Δ+ = lim_{p_t→+∞} μ_t−μ_{t−1} is bounded — extreme performances cannot move ratings arbitrarily.

Elo-MMR predictive accuracy (pair-inversion / rank-deviation): Codeforces ρ-variant 78.6%/14.7% (best; TrueSkill collapsed to 61.7%/25.4%), TopCoder 73.1%/18.2% (best). Runtime for the whole Codeforces dataset: Elo-MMR(ρ) 35.4s vs Codeforces production 212.9s and TrueSkill 67.2s (~6× faster; the abstract's 'order of magnitude' slightly overstates). TrueSkill ≈ Elo-MMR when distinct ranks are < ~60, explaining its collapse on large ranked fields. The paper documents the Glicko-2/TopCoder volatility-farming exploit (intentional underperformance to amplify future gains) — a caution against volatility-weighted updates.

Metulini (arXiv:1805.02501) segments basketball games into phases by k-means over time instants (objects = milliseconds, similarity = vector of pairwise player-dyad distances), choosing k by the between-deviance/total-deviance (BD/TD) elbow (5→6 increment ≈ 11–12%, 6→7 ≈ 6–7%, so k=6 consistently across five lineups). Clusters switch every ~2 s (309 switches in 8:21 of game time) — micro-configurations, not tactics. The 62.5% FG 'best configuration' claim rests on 15 shots with no test (Wilson interval on 5/8 ≈ (30%, 87%)) — anecdotal.

equation: AABRP(i) = Σ_j BR(i,j)/n; BR(i,j) = +1 if (payout=1, loss=0); −1 if (payout=0, loss=−1); 0 otherwise
claim: Gao, Yang & Liu (arXiv:2409.16599v1) run a Monte Carlo study of weather parametric-insurance basis risk: individual AABRP ∈ [−0.201, 0.203] with portfolio AABRP' = 0.005 (→0, hedging effect); individual σ ∈ [0.118, 0.589] vs portfolio σ' = 0.041 (~3–14× volatility cut). Fit: σ(m) = a/(m − b) + c with a=0.482, b=2.126, c=0.003, R²=0.993. Spatial-ratio thresholds: AABRP threshold γ=0.85 (R²=0.821 below, 0.388 above, p<0.01); σ threshold γ=1.93. Severity findings: below trigger → risk 0; above trigger → no significant correlation between severity and basis-risk level or volatility — the trigger, not the magnitude, matters.

Dinsdale & Gallagher (arXiv:2201.11533) forecast a soccer transfer's per-90 output change with four grouped multi-head TensorFlow NNs (windows N=1000 player, M=3000 team-position, 1,000-minute target horizon, 13 KPIs in 4 groups; hyperparameters tuned with HyperOpt), a hierarchical ability system (Team ability = E_continent + E_country + E_league + E_team, Elo components rescaled 0–100 daily), and the prior blend X'_{i,j,g} = (1−w_{j,g})P_{i,j} + w_{j,g}R_{i,j,g} with w_{j,g} = min(1, (Σ minutes)/c), c=1000, nested prior order ability → team/team-position → player.

The transfer model achieved 49% average MSE improvement over the naive carry-forward baseline on transfers (21% on transfers+non-transfers combined); xG/90 improved 54%. Per-target improvement ranged 37% (crosses) to 61% (short passes) — team-style-sensitive metrics gain most. Case study: Gakpo's shots/90 dropped from the 59th to the 27th percentile moving PSV→Rennes. Caveat: 49% is against a deliberately weak strawman baseline, and evaluation is retrospective on completed transfers (selection bias).

equation: ℒ(f,x,y) = −log p_y(x) + λ·ℓ(f,x̃,y) + η‖∇_x(z_y − max_{i≠y} z_i)‖_1
claim: Laidlaw & Feizi (arXiv:1911.11253v1) propose CARL (Combined Abstention Robustness Learning): a single network with an extra abstain class trained with loss ℒ(f,x,y) = −log p_y(x) + λ·ℓ(f,x̃,y) + η‖∇_x(z_y − max_{i≠y} z_i)‖_1, where x̃ is an adversarial example generated to fool the classifier WITHOUT abstaining (six new attack losses); λ dials the natural/adversarial tradeoff. The baseline abstains when geometric margin γ(x) ≤ γ*, and Theorem 1 gives exact natural error plus an adversarial-error upper bound via the signed-margin CDF F_Γ.

On CIFAR-10 (L∞ ε=8/255), baseline γ*=0 gave 77.1% correct / 0.0% abstain / 22.9% incorrect with union-attack adversarial error 50.9%; γ*=4/255 gave 62.9/30.1/7.0 with adv err 29.2%; γ*=8/255 gave 49.7/47.7/2.6 with adv err 11.7%. CARL ℓ⁽¹⁾ λ=1 gave 68.1/30.0/1.8 with adv err 35.8% (baseline wins on the union attack at similar abstention); CARL ℓ⁽¹⁾ λ=4 gave 54.3/45.3/0.4 with adv err 13.9%. On MNIST, CARL reduces baseline adversarial error by more than half at equal natural error. Key safety stat: CARL λ=1 is 68.1% correct, abstains 30%, and outright WRONG only 1.8% on natural inputs.

Liu et al. (arXiv:2404.19383) propose CFSC, a plug-and-play module cascading shallow-block features into deeper GCN blocks: F_v = TC_v(f_v ⊕ λ·F_{v−1}) with ⊕ = element-wise addition (beat avg/max/concat/multiply), TC_v = temporal convolution kernel (K_t,1) with stride aligning temporal dims; then F'_M = (F_M − F_mean)/F_std → ReLU → auxiliary feature F_dis; F_dis ⊕ f_10 (final block output) → global average pooling → softmax. Block selection: cover ≥2 of {shallow, medium, deep}; avoid adjacent blocks; moderate M.

CFSC deltas on the new FD-7 fencing dataset: HD-GCN joint 93.6→95.7 (+2.1), bone 98.2→99.6 (+1.4); CTR-GCN joint 79.3→91.1 (+11.8); 2S-AGCN joint 61.8→78.2 (+16.4). On FSD-10 figure skating: HD-GCN joint 85.9→88.2 (+2.3), bone 88.2→90.1 (+1.9). λ sweep: joint peaks at λ=0.3, bone at λ=0.5; auto-learned λ FAILED (joint 89.3, bone 94.6) — fixed λ required. K_t: joint best K_t=7 → 98.2%; bone best K_t=3 → 99.6% (degrades to 96.4 at K_t=11) — short kernels for fast sports motion.

Karl (arXiv:1806.08059v2) shows that mixed/random-effects models of team strength absorb scheduling bias into home-field estimates: in the score-differential model y_{ijt} = μ_t + α_i − α_j + ε_{ijt}, the mixed-effects variant (α_i ~ N(0, σ²)) is biased when E[α_i | schedule_i] ≠ 0 (home-game assignment depends on team strength), while the fixed-effects variant (α_i as free parameters) stays unbiased under nonrandom scheduling. In simulation with true HFA = 3, mixed-effects estimates came out at 3.37 (FBS football), 3.26 (men's college basketball), 3.13 (women's college basketball); fixed-effects recovered 3.00 exactly.

Brill, Wyner & Barnett (arXiv:2308.14339v3) develop entropy-based multi-entry portfolio theory for bracket pools/DFS: optimize objectives E[max_k score_k], P(win), E[profit] over K entries via entropy-controlled strategy families, trading off expected score against outcome-space coverage rather than submitting N copies of the best single entry. Central rule: optimal portfolio entropy increases in (number of entries K, opponent-field entropy). N best single entries by EV is suboptimal; the paper assumes true outcome probabilities and opponent strategy are known — both must be estimated in practice.

Graziani et al. (arXiv:1904.02855) recalibrate miscalibrated forecast densities by fitting a Gaussian-process density (GPME) to historical PIT values: p₁(x;J,C) = π(F=F̃(x;J,C)|ℱ,C)·p(x;J,C). Theorem 1: E[KL[Π‖p] − KL[Π‖p₁]] = ∫ π(F|ℱ,C) log₂ π(F|ℱ,C) ≥ 0. Predicted entropy-game winnings: ΔS̄ = KL[π(F|ℱ,C)‖U] ≥ 0; Forecast Advantage Measure FAM = ΔS̄/√Var(ΔS) ~ O(N^{1/2}); Kelly link: ignorance-score difference −ΔIgn = expected log₂ wealth growth per bet for a Kelly bettor.

GP-PIT recalibration results: nonlinear-circuit case ≈0.6 bits/turn entropy-game winnings → wealth multiplier ×1.5/turn; ENSO NINO 3.4 case 0.2–0.6 bits/turn vs raw BMA, with predicted ΔS̄ matching actuals; PIT autocorrelation to 15-month lags required ×5 thinning (64 training points); FAM in that case was only 1–2. Caveats: no code released; no sports data; autocorrelated PITs must be thinned (discarding most data); assumes stationarity of the miscalibration itself.

equation: max Σ_p proj_p · x_p, x_p ∈ {0,1}, Σ salary_p · x_p ≤ cap
claim: Grody, Bansal & Ashqar (arXiv:2411.11012) on MLB DFS lineup optimization: the naive maximize-projected-points binary integer program (PuLP, subject to salary/position constraints, crude exposure-cap iteration loop, no covariance/ownership/variance modeling) was REJECTED by the ledger — generated lineups averaged 144.6 projected vs hindsight-optimal 251.9 (107.3 gap dominated by projection error), the paper reports '10.510' as 'mean squared error' while describing an average actual-minus-projection difference (apparently MAE, misnamed), and reports '0.19' as 'R-mean-squared,' a nonstandard undefined metric; maximizing mean projection is documented as known-suboptimal for GPPs.

equation: LR = P(observed signal sequence | cheating model with signal probability p) / P(same sequence | honest base-rate model)
claim: Boonstra & Meester (arXiv:2409.08172) build a Bayesian competing-hypotheses likelihood-ratio framework for testing alleged cheating via hidden signaling codes: LR = P(observed signal sequence | cheating model with signal probability p) / P(same sequence | honest base-rate model), updating prior odds to posterior odds via Bayes factor; trials assumed conditionally independent given the hypothesis.

The LR framework found bridge bidding-code case LR ≈ 4 × 10^19; Astros trash-can case LR ≈ 3.4 × 10^30 (n=267, m=201, b=85, p=0.8); Astros vs Minnesota order 10^9, vs Toronto 10^23, vs White Sox 10^12. Limitations: retrospective selection bias (scandals selected because suspicion existed; no multiple-comparison control), extreme sensitivity to assumed p, trials treated as independent though game contexts have dependence, no code/data released.

Raheman et al. (arXiv:2204.10185) build per-channel Twitter/Reddit sentiment metrics for crypto prediction (~100,000 items, 77 feeds/subreddits, July–December 2021) including a 'contradictive' compound: contradictive = SQRT(positive × ABS(negative)). Pearson correlation with ground-truth labels: Aigents 0.33, fine-tuned Aigents 0.57, finBERT 0.32 (best of 22 models). The selectively weighted compound indicator reached 0.55 correlation at lag −1 day, but channel/metric selection was optimized on the same six-month series used to report the 0.55 — serious snooping risk with no held-out predictive backtest.

equation: L = L_CE(treatment | representation) + L_recon + λ·‖mean-difference‖_{2,1} + L_RMSE(outcome)
claim: Damera (arXiv:2008.09858) Hi-CI does deep causal inference with high-dimensional correlated covariates and continuous treatments via L = L_CE(treatment | representation) + L_recon + λ·‖mean-difference‖_{2,1} + L_RMSE(outcome) (treatment-distribution cross-entropy + reconstruction + mixed L_{2,1} decorrelation penalty + outcome loss), evaluated by PEHE, MAPE over ATE, MISE (dosage), dosage-effect MAPE. On semi-synthetic NEWS100: PEHE 8.1432 ± 0.0476 vs PM 48.3878 ± 0.5620 vs MultiMBNN 49.6386 ± 0.8520 (~6× better); MAPE-ATE 0.507 ± 0.0171 vs 1.9850/2.2014. Caveat: ~6× margins partly reflect known-weak baselines (no X-learner/R-learner/causal-forest); ground-truth ITE exists only because the DGP was invented.

panispani's Chain-Reaction Causal Discovery (arXiv:2603.22620) recovers a causal graph via blocking interventions: under do(Xᵢ=0), Xⱼ = 0 for all descendants j of i, so pᵢⱼ := P(Xⱼ=1 | do(Xᵢ=0)) = 0 ⟺ j ∈ descendants(i); decision rule Â(i,j)=1 iff p̂ᵢⱼ = 0. False-positive bound: Pr(Â(i,j)=1) ≤ exp(−q_min · nᵢ); full-matrix recovery guarantee ≥ 1 − N(N−1)·exp(−q_min · n_min). On synthetic Pymunk physics environments: exact graph recovery ≥95% (100 seeds each), only 1–2 interventions per object; F1 = 0.963–0.999 vs best observational baseline F1 = 0.686–0.825. NFL/engine systems violate all four assumptions (directed tree, monotone binary activation, noiseless labels, perfectly blocking interventions) — use the descendant-recovery idea, not the exact tree algorithm.

Van Arem, Goes-Smit & Söhl (arXiv:2502.07528) on one-year-ahead forecasting of soccer player quality (SciSkill) and transfer value (ETV): XGBoost had the lowest loss of all models on quality (both RMSE and MAE, full test set), tree-based beat linear, RF similar to XGBoost below age 22, all models best at ages 24–28, kNN-time-series worst. On value: RF lowest RMSE and MAE overall, distinctly lower on high-value (≥€10M) — the only model capturing the peak-then-decline pattern via the 'etv' feature. Top quality features: age_years, age_years², years_diff_peak_age, current sciskill, sciskill_diff_mean_team, previous_zero_months (injury-layoff penalty). Exact RMSE/MAE numbers are figures-only, not quoted in text; UQ intervals never empirically validated for coverage.

Jabbour et al. (arXiv:2508.07617) behavioral experiment (259 clinicians diagnosing acute respiratory failure): treatment accuracy on the inaccurate subset was 62% (47–75) Clinician Alone → 50% (36–65) with AI (automation bias, p<0.001) → 55% (40–69) with Selective Prediction (partial, non-significant recovery). False positive rate: 40% → 55% (p<0.05) → 41% (back to baseline). False negative rate: 31% → 41% (p<0.05) → 42% (31–53), p<0.05 — stays elevated: people undertreat when told the AI abstains. Perceived difficulty rose 1.17 → 1.20 → 1.27. Operational finding: announcing abstention is not behaviorally neutral — it shifts the audience's error pattern toward false negatives (missed plays).

equation: F^Logit(p) = sigmoid(|N|/α · Σ w_j logit(p_{i,j})), α = 2
claim: Wang, Liu & Chen (arXiv:1910.03779) aggregate probabilistic forecasts by first ranking forecasters with peer-prediction scores (no ground truth needed), selecting the top max(10%|N|, 10) per event by peer-assessment score, then applying F^Mean(p) = Σ w_j p_{i,j} or F^Logit(p) = sigmoid(|N|/α · Σ w_j logit(p_{i,j})), α = 2. Example mechanism: CA: R^{CA}_j = Σ_{u,v∈{0,1}} |δ̂^{j,k}_{u,v} − δ̂^j_u · δ̂^k_v|. On 14 real-world binary-event human forecast datasets, 9 of 10 PAS-aided aggregators beat the best benchmark on ≥5 of 14 datasets; DMI-aided mean Brier 0.221 (std 0.150) vs Mean 0.290 (0.130), Logit 0.317 (0.224), VI 0.315 (0.267) cross-dataset; PAS selection peaks at top 5–20% and 'perfectly recovers' oracle Brier-aided performance on G2, but fails when forecasters make <40 predictions.

Frazier et al. (arXiv:2308.05263) theoretically explain the 'forecast combination puzzle' (optimally weighted combinations failing to beat equal weighting) as an artifact of two-step estimation (fit models, then fit weights): Theorem 4.1 gives weight-distance δ_T ≍ δ/T^ξ, and for ξ∈(1/4,∞] the rejection probability of standard accuracy tests → 0 for all α (no local power). Corollary 4.1: the null distribution of the two-step loss-difference statistic is generalized chi-squared (no closed form) — standard normal critical values are wrong. Theorem 4.2: one-step combination asymptotically always (weakly) beats two-step, including equal weights, for ANY strictly proper scoring rule or consistent scoring function. The two-step-aware test is W_P^{2s}(α) = {P·Δ_P > cv_{(1−α)H}} with cv simulated from B=10,000 draws of ½‖X + (P/R)^{1/2}M̂_{ηγ}Z‖²_{M̂_{ηη}^{-1}}.

Empirics for the two-step combination puzzle: standard test size under the null 0.0000–0.0004 (MSFE and log-loss, all T) vs two-step-aware test size 0.020–0.053 (MSFE) / 0.044–0.053 (log-loss) — near nominal. Power under a small deviation: standard 0.010–0.012 (MSFE) / 0.0000 (log-loss) vs two-step-aware 0.154/0.304/0.655 (MSFE) and 0.196/0.367/0.687 (log-loss) at T=1000/2000/5000. Even with optimal weight far from equal (η*=0.25), standard-test rejection stays below 50% for all sample sizes <1000. S&P500 out-of-sample p-values: equal vs optimal two-step 0.8251 (the puzzle); equal-two-step vs one-step 5.675e-05; optimal-two-step vs one-step 6.935e-12.

Nuthanakaluva & Gaddam (arXiv:2608.28116v1) propose an online ensemble-weighting scheme computing Gibbs weights w_i ∝ exp(−η · normalized_loss_i) from normalized predictive losses, with directional/symmetric diversity corrections rewarding complementary models and Local-UCB bandit adaptation of hyperparameters (grids η ∈ {.01,.05,.1,.2}, λ ∈ {.01,.05,.1,.5}); simplex updates via exponentiated gradient, squared-error point-forecast setting only. Findings: Gibbs-family wins several M4 regimes but not universally — gains over plain exponential weighting are regime-dependent; diversity corrections sometimes hurt. Monash aggregate leaders: Traffic Hourly Stable Gibbs-NCL 421.1985; Electricity Hourly Stable Gibbs 19,561,022,006; Solar Weekly Stable Gibbs 17,890,727,069.

Greenhough et al. (arXiv:cond-mat/0110605v2) fit Poisson, negative-binomial, and extreme-value families to soccer goal counts: pooled worldwide (>135,000 matches, 169 countries, 1999–2001), Poisson/NBD fail over the full range; tails fit Fréchet with a=1.04 (home), a=1.10 (away); total goals fit Gumbel (a=1). Tail departure points: home beyond ≈ μ+3σ (~6 goals), away beyond ≈ μ+4σ (~6 goals), total beyond ≈ μ+3σ (9 goals). English-only data (1970/71–2000/01) are adequately fit by Poisson/NBD with no extremal signature — the pooling of 169 heterogeneous leagues plausibly manufactures the heavy tail (mixture effect). Ledger verdict: REJECT — no predictive model, no out-of-sample test.

Pendergrass (arXiv:0907.2196v1) analyzes a two-player zero-sum path-guessing game with wagering on directed graphs: for fans (Theorem 1), the Chooser's optimal strategy is p(j) = v_j^{−1}/Σ_k v_k^{−1} with game value = harmonic mean n/Σv_j^{−1}; for trees, value propagation v_i = n_i^{−1}Σ_{i→j}v_j^{−1}; for terminating graphs, limiting reciprocal values u = (I−A)^{−1}Bu_t. Fairness conditions: terminating graphs fair ⟺ all terminal values 1 and all out-degrees ≥ 2; strongly connected fair ⟺ every vertex out-degree ≥ 2. Ledger verdict: REJECT — theorems with proofs only, no empirical results, no mapping to fixed-odds sizing (the game is against an adversary who observes your wager).

Byrnes & Barnett (arXiv:1806.05293) derive the exact multivariate Kelly first-order condition for portfolios of multiple simultaneous investments with arbitrary return distributions and correlations: ∫ k_l(x_l)·p(x)/(1 + Σ_{l'} f_{l'}·k_{l'}(x_{l'})) dx = 0, l=1..L. Small-parameter approximation: M·f = b with M_{ll'} = E[k_l·k_{l'}], b_l = E[k_l]; Gaussian closed form f = μ/(μ² + σ²). Key qualitative result: positive correlation between investments reduces optimal fractions; negative correlation increases them. Single-investment form: ∫ k(x)·p(x)/(1 + f·k(x)) dx = 0.

Brockwell (arXiv:2109.10814v1) derives growth-optimal (Kelly) and fractional-Kelly portfolio rules under geometric Brownian motion: k⋆ = (μ−r)/σ²; multivariate k⋆ = Σ⁻¹(μ−r); fractional k_α = αΣ⁻¹(μ−r), α∈(0,1). Expected log-growth L(k_α) = r + (α − α²/2)S² with S² = (μ−r)ᵀΣ⁻¹(μ−r) (squared Sharpe); variance of log-growth V(k_α) = α²S² — growth quadratic-concave in α (max at α=1), risk falls quadratically as α↓.

On 2001–2021 Vanguard funds VFIAX/VUSUX: Fractional Kelly — growth 0.089, annualized SD 0.176, max drawdown 41.9%, final wealth $576,464; Full Kelly — growth 0.172, annualized SD 0.594, max drawdown 89.8%, final wealth $3,002,829. Fractional trades roughly half the growth for ~1/3 the volatility and ~1/2 the drawdown — the classic growth-vs-security frontier in one table.

Sharma (arXiv:2607.09505v1) proves that any portfolio's suboptimality vs the growth-optimal (Kelly) portfolio is measured exactly by KL-divergence quantities: objective identity E_P[log(X_T^{π⋆}/X_T^π)] = D_KL(P‖P^π); subjective mirror E_{P^π}[log(X_T^π/X_T^{π⋆})] = D_KL(P^π‖P). The Kelly condition is σ_tᵀπ_t⋆ = θ_t; growth-optimal growth g_t⋆ = r_t + ½‖θ_t‖²; instantaneous growth gap g_t⋆ − g_t^π = ½‖θ_t − σ_tᵀπ_t‖² (half the squared tracking error to Kelly in volatility units). Conceptual result: every portfolio is growth-optimal under some belief P^π; suboptimality under the true P is exactly D_KL(P‖P^π).

Tondapu (arXiv:2402.02623) studies Betfair UK horse-racing tick data (1,056,766 price-change signals, 73 markets, one month): returns R_t = ln(P_t) − ln(P_{t−1}) with 5% commission deducted; unconditional distribution fit vs generalized Gaussian f(x,β) with β=1.19 best (β=1 Laplace, β=2 Gaussian); log returns over 41,588 intervals: mean −0.0018, SD 4.0323, skewness +0.0241, kurtosis 1.0994 (platykurtic — opposite pattern vs finance). Hill tail index −0.348 to −0.877 for k 1–10% (light tails). Two-sample KS test for gain-loss asymmetry: D=0.0068 < D_c=0.0080, p=0.1347 — no asymmetry.

Betfair findings: ADF rejects unit root in all 73 markets (statistics −5.02 to −8.52, p≈0). Autocorrelation: large negative first lag, then rapidly negligible — no exploitable linear structure. Absolute-return power-law decay exponent α: mean 0.62435, SD 0.3052, range 0.1645–1.9755 — faster decay than financial 0.1–0.4, i.e., quicker information absorption. Review finding: favorite-longshot bias is strong on exchanges; exchanges are more informationally efficient than dealer markets. Limitations: one-month sample; Hurst exponent claimed in abstract but deferred to future work.

Zaborowski, Lipiecki, Petropoulos & Weron (arXiv:2608.10620) post-process prediction errors to beat traditional Gaussian predictive distributions with four post-processors: HS (signed-error empirical quantiles: q̂^p = ŷ + Q_p({ε_t})); CP (absolute-error symmetric intervals: q̂^p = ŷ ∓ Q_{2p/2(1−p)}({|ε_t|})); QR/QRM (quantile ~ linear in point forecast, sorted to fix crossing); GARCH(1,1) with variance targeting (σ̂²=ω+αε²+βσ̂²; multi-step σ̂²=ω+(α+β)σ̂²; Gaussian quantiles). Metric: CRPSS_h = [1−exp(mean ln rCRPS)]×100%, geometric mean over series; CRPS via 99 pinball quantiles.

On 14,407 monthly M4 series (2,074,608 forecast–observation evaluations per method), all 8 post-processing variants beat the benchmark, gains up to 4.6%: Theta QR_in 4.59%, ARIMA QR_in 4.53%, ETS HS_in 3.25% / CP_in 3.14%. In-sample beats out-of-sample in 11/12 model–method combos (largest gaps: HS on ETS +1.49pp, CP on ETS +1.35pp); sole exception QR on ETS (−1.78pp, out-of-sample better). Compute: rolling-origin out-of-sample calibration costs 180–215× more (Theta 8.4ms→1.8s, ETS 0.45s→83s, ARIMA 1.1s→3.3m); post-processing itself trivial (CP/HS 0.20ms, GARCH 2.2ms, QR 0.12s). No single method dominates: best method depends on base model and horizon.

equation: p_ij,1 = Φ̄(d − Ds_ij − h); p_ij,3 = Φ̄(d + Ds_ij + h); p_ij,2 = 1 − p_ij,1 − p_ij,3
claim: Foulley (arXiv:1501.05831) builds a hierarchical Bayesian cumulative-probit (Glenn–David) model for Champions League win/draw/loss outcomes with latent Z_ij ~ N(m_ij, 1), m_ij = Ds_ij + h: p_ij,1 = Φ̄(d − Ds_ij − h); p_ij,3 = Φ̄(d + Ds_ij + h); p_ij,2 = 1 − p_ij,1 − p_ij,3 (Φ̄ = survival function). Hierarchy: X_ij|θ ~ Cat(Π_ij); s_i|η_i,σ_s² ~ N(η_i, σ_s²); η_i = βx_i, x_i = standardized external rating; priors for d, h, β, γ_s refreshed each season from previous season's posteriors (recursive Bayesian learning). Expert (odds-setter) views blend as implicit Dirichlet-multinomial data: l(m) = Σ_k a_{m,k} log p_{m,k}, a_{m,k} = w_m p^ex_{m,k} − 1.

Foulley's Champions League results (2013–14, Brier/accuracy, overall group+knockout): Zero (all teams equal) 0.685/38.3%; UEFACR 0.595/43.3% (+13.1% accuracy); FCWR 0.530/47.4% (+23.8% accuracy, +22.6% Brier). Group stage FCWR +27.0% accuracy; Round of 16 +24.0%; QF/SF/F — advantage vanishes (FCWR 0.635/38.7% vs Zero 0.667/38.7%). Key decay finding: once ~10+ matches are observed the likelihood dominates and external info adds nothing — priors matter early, vanish later. External ratings UEFA Club Ranking vs Football Club World Ranking correlated r = 0.807 [0.628, 0.905].

equation: f ⪰ f† iff I_f(t) ≥ I_f†(t) ∀ t, where I_f(t) = E[(t − p)_+]
claim: Tang & Zhang (arXiv:2607.08744) on algorithmic expert aggregation: a pure-theory paper on constructing calibrated output experts that Blackwell-dominate input experts (f ⪰ f† iff I_f(t) ≥ I_f†(t) ∀ t, I_f(t) = E[(t − p)_+] is the integrated CDF), with polynomial-time LP algorithms (Search-Aggregation via extreme-ray decomposition + Stern–Brocot search; OPT-Aggregation additive FPTAS) and NP-hardness for the deterministic case (SubsetSum reduction); no multiplicative PTAS for Brier optimization unless P = NP. Zero empirical forecasting application: no datasets, no experiments, no numbers. Ledger verdict: REJECT.

Ziel (arXiv:2107.06268) won 3rd place (top 3 not significantly different) in the IEEE DataPort Post-COVID day-ahead load-forecasting competition with Bernstein Online Aggregation with P-spline smoothing of combiner weights across forecast horizons: ŵ = B(B′B+λD′D)⁻¹B′w, λ tuned by exponentially-discounted (ρ=0.01, ~100-day effective) past MAE; fully adaptive BOA with gradient trick on absolute-deviation loss; updates for r, E, η (min(E/2, √(log K/Σr²))), R (second-order + indicator correction), w (w₀=1/K). Fronted by a holiday-adjustment procedure: high-dim lasso on log-load with lagged log-loads ±168…510h, p-quantile ReLU-transformed weather, all weather interactions, daily/weekly dummies, annual periodic cubic B-splines, and impact-adjusted holiday dummies scaled by the (Q90−Q37 rolling quantile gap) to handle the COVID level shift.

Smoothed-BOA competition results: forward stepwise expert selection (30-day burn-in, 60-day calibration) picked 5 of 40 candidates; the 5-model BOA combination achieved ≈10% lower validation MAE than the best individual model (~11.4 vs ~12.4). Selected 5 diverse: 3 lasso (two ≈3yr windows, one ≈3mo window), 1 GAM (7mo window), 1 STL+ETS — window-diversity in a few linear models beat model-class diversity; GAM underestimates and STL+ETS overestimates, acting as bias correctors. Short-window models (lasso D=76, GAM D=209) get more weight at far horizons (h=40). GBM/neural nets tested and dropped (linear effects dominate). No comparison against plain unsmoothed BOA; MAE objective transfers to point forecasts, not probability calibration.

Rosito et al. (arXiv:2604.14534) propose an unsupervised athlete-monitoring framework using Ward hierarchical clustering on multivariate blood-biomarker data (22 male amateur soccer players, 8 biomarkers × 3 windows, Z-score normalization z_ij = (x_ij − μ_j)/σ_j; GMM augmentation p(x) = Σ_m w_m N(x|μ_m, Σ_m) with diagonal Σ_m for scalability). Findings: k=3 silhouette 0.185, k=5 silhouette 0.162 (both weak — near the 0.2 boundary of 'no substantial structure'). The 'silent-risk' detection is circular: the pattern was embedded in the synthetic seed by the authors, then recovered by clustering. No predictive validation by design. Ledger verdict: REJECT — n=22 amateurs, no injury ground truth, blood panels unavailable to GSE.

equation: R_k = max(1, min(⌊N_p·|B_k|/N_o⌋ + s_k·⌊N_p·|B_k|/N_o⌋, |B_k|)), s_k = Var(f_t|t∈B_k)/max_j Var
claim: TimeSoccer (arXiv:2504.17365) is an end-to-end multimodal LLM that jointly predicts timestamps and generates soccer commentary over full 45-minute matches in a single forward pass, built on TimeChat with MoFA-Select, a training-free motion-aware frame compressor: (a) time-constrained K-Means of N_o frame features into U=6 segments minimizing Σ_k Σ_{t∈k}(1−sim(f_t,c_k)); (b) motion-aware budget per cluster R_k = max(1, min(⌊N_p·|B_k|/N_o⌋ + s_k·⌊N_p·|B_k|/N_o⌋, |B_k|)) with s_k = Var(f_t|t∈B_k)/max_j Var; (c) iterative fine-grained merging of max-similarity adjacent pairs, skipping merge when Δ_motion(i)=Var({f_i,f_{i+1}}) > δ=0.3. Training uses a progressive schedule (3→15→45-min videos) plus position-embedding extrapolation by periodic replication (beats interpolation).

TimeSoccer 45-min end-to-end: P@0.3 17.0, P@0.5 11.0, P@0.7 6.0, P@0.9 3.4 (vs SN-Caption 12.5/7.2/3.0/1.1); CIDEr 8.3, METEOR 6.2, SODA_c 2.7; LLM-judge M-S 5.03, C-S 5.14 (vs SN-Caption 3.41/4.30). The 3-min×15 chunked variant scores higher (P@0.3 22.5, F1 12.0, CIDEr 13.8, C-S 6.18) but needs 15 forward passes, not end-to-end. MoFA-Select beats G-Prune; removing motion-awareness hurts captions most in ablations. Absolute temporal precision remains modest (P@0.9 = 3.4%). No public code release.

A 2026 theory paper (arXiv:2605.09599) makes prediction-market liquidity itself adaptive by mixing a family of LMSR cost-function markets via online learning: C^mix(q;w) = (1/β)log(Σ_k w(k)e^{βC_k(q)}), β>0 (small β → near-averaging, large β → soft maximum), preserving no-arbitrage and bounded worst-case loss with only a (1/β)log M overhead. Prices: ∇C^mix(q;w) = Σ_k π_k(q;w)∇C_k(q) with posterior weights π_k(q;w) = w(k)e^{βC_k(q)}/Σ_j w(j)e^{βC_j(q)}. Hessian decomposition: ∇²C^mix = Σ_k π_k∇²C_k + β·Cov_{k~π}(∇C_k(q)) — curvature = expected expert curvature + β × expert disagreement variance. Hybrid signal: Γ^hyb_{k,t} = a(S_{k,t} − (1/M)Σ_j S_{j,t}) + bL_k(q_t); slippage S_{k,t} = D_{C_k}(q_t,q_{t−1}); liability L_k(q) = max_o ρ(o)·q − (C_k(q)−C_k(0)). Worst-case loss: sup_{T,(r_t),o} Loss_T(o) ≤ max_k B_k + (1/β)log M + C^mix(q_0;w_1) − min_o ρ(o)·q_0. Regret: O(√(T log T)) vs best ≤J-switch regime sequence.

In the adaptive-liquidity paper's stylized 2-outcome/2-LMSR-expert simulation over four regimes: in R1 (sustained directional flow) effective liquidity drops sharply to low as inventory accumulates; in R2 (oscillatory, neutral inventory) it jumps up and plateaus high; in R3 (large alternating trades) the adaptive curve sits between fixed benchmarks with damped slippage spikes; in R4 liability dominates and liquidity collapses. Key qualitative result: the learner switches regimes state-dependently rather than smoothing — liquidity aligns with whichever risk (price impact or inventory) dominates; slippage governs short-term responses, liability governs long-term regime positioning. Guarantees are on the hybrid surrogate signal, not on trader surplus, price accuracy, or information aggregation; strategic traders could exploit predictable switches.

A 2016 paper (arXiv:1611.09130) generalizes Kelly along three axes — finite horizon, wealth held outside the betting account, general concave utility — with a recombining-binomial implementation cutting complexity from exponential to O(f²). One-step log-utility closed form: f* = (2p−1)(1 + w/g), where w = outside wealth, g = current gambling bankroll. Worked example: p=.6 coin-flip, w=1000, horizon 25 flips → first-bet fraction ≈.659 of gambling bankroll (vs .2 for plain Kelly without outside wealth). The paper flags that this is dangerous if w is not truly available to cover losses. Binary-outcome only; assumes w constant over horizon; no miscalibrated-p analysis.

equation: α_{t+1} = α_t + γ(α − err_t), err_t = 1{Y_t ∉ C_{α_t}(X_t)}
claim: Gibbs & Candès (2021, arXiv:2106.00170, NeurIPS 2021) introduce Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI): an online α_t feedback controller, α_{t+1} = α_t + γ(α − err_t) with err_t = 1{Y_t ∉ C_{α_t}(X_t)} — a miss pushes α_t down (wider intervals); a cover pushes it up (narrower); online gradient descent on the pinball/quantile loss. Theorem 2 gives a distribution-free long-run guarantee with NO distributional assumptions, holding for ANY sequence: |(1/T) Σ err_t − α| ≤ (max(α_1, 1−α_1) + γ)/(Tγ) — converges at O(1/(Tγ)). Experiments use γ = 0.005 as the empirical sweet spot (larger γ adapts faster but intervals oscillate; smaller γ is sluggish).

ACI applications: stock volatility (12 S&P-500 stocks, GARCH(1,1) on rolling 1,250-trading-day window, next-day absolute return, nominal 90%) — fixed-α conformal's local coverage oscillates and sags well below 90% during volatility regimes while ACI tracks ~90% throughout, widening exactly when volatility spikes; 2020 US election (~3,000 counties ordered by timezone to simulate reporting-order shift) — fixed conformal coverage troughs at timezone transitions while ACI maintains ≈90%. Limitations: the guarantee is LONG-RUN average only — any finite window can undercover; with γ=0.005 adaptation takes hundreds of steps (an NFL season is ~272 games); local coverage has NO guarantee; requires Y_t revealed each step (mid-week props/futures with delayed feedback are unresolved); no comparison to rolling-window recalibration.

Gupta, Kuchibhotla & Ramdas (2022, arXiv:1910.10562) present a nested-set framework unifying split, cross-conformal, jackknife+, and OOB conformal methods: F_t(x) = {y : s(x,y) ≤ t}, nested in t; calibrating t on held-out scores ≡ standard conformal; any nonconformity score induces nested sets; framework extends to K-fold cross-conformal, CV+, jackknife+ as nested-set operations. QOOB = quantile-regression-forest nested quantile sets + OOB predictions as calibration scores (no split) + cross-conformal aggregation, including an EFFICIENT cross-conformal algorithm (naive is O(n²)-ish per test point). Theoretical results: score-based ⟺ nested equivalence proofs; finite-sample coverage for C^LOO; Conv(C^LOO) can be strictly SMALLER than the jackknife+ interval.

QOOB significantly outperforms split-CQR at small sample sizes on ALL 6 UCI regression datasets (narrower intervals at valid coverage); nominal quantile selection has a significant effect on QOOB width (needs tuning); QOOB intervals get SHORTER as T (trees) increases — no plateau in tested range. Cross-conformal outperforms jackknife+ (tighter, still valid). QOOB shows empirical conditional coverage on a contaminated simulation (Y ~ Pois(sin²(X)+0.1) + 0.03Xε₁ + 25·1{u<0.01}ε₂) at n ≤ 300, matching split-CQR's behavior at n=2000. Costs: QOOB ≈ n× the prediction compute of split-CQR; exchangeability assumed throughout, no drift handling; MATLAB reference.

Zhang et al. (2020, arXiv:2004.03019) fix the sticky HDP-HMM by disentangling three confounded quantities — transition-row similarity, mean self-persistence, and state-specific persistence variation — into DS-HDP-HMM: HDP prior β ~ GEM(γ); π_j ~ DP(α, β) (shared transition sparsity); self-transition probability κ_j ~ Beta(a, b) per state j, separate from DP-distributed off-diagonal transitions; full row = mixture of sticky self-component and shared π_j. Complexity O(TK²) per Gibbs sweep vs O(T²K + TK²) for general HSMM — explicit-duration-like flexibility at HMM cost. Two Gibbs samplers (direct-assignment and weak-limit truncated at L).

DS-HDP-HMM results: synthetic multinomial/Gaussian emissions — beats both HDP-HMM and sticky HDP-HMM on held-out NLL and Hamming distance consistently; rat hippocampal data (100 neurons, 10 Hz, ~36k frames) — test NLL advantage over sticky HDP-HMM significant at p < 0.05, cleaner spatial/temporal state structure; mouse decision-making (1,126 trials × 189 frames) — infers 22 states vs 16 for parametric ARHMM baseline, with lower test NLL. Limitations: Gibbs with 7 chains × 10–15k iterations is expensive; truncation L is a tuning choice; very long regimes may still be mis-split.

Eckert, Hyndman & Panagiotelis (2023, arXiv:2207.07318) build GLOBAL forecast combination: per-task combination weights shrunk toward a shared weight vector via a task-coupling penalty — soft global objective min_{w^{(1)}…w^{(m)}∈𝒯, w̄} Σₖ₌₁ᵐ (w^{(k)ᵀ}Σ^{(k)}w^{(k)} + λ‖w^{(k)}‖_q^q + γ‖w̄−w^{(k)}‖_q^q), q∈{1,2}. γ→0 ⟹ local combination; γ→∞ ⟹ hard global; finite γ ⟹ soft global. Closed form for q=2: Ω_{γ,2} = (γ/m)Σ_{k,l}‖w^{(l)}−w^{(k)}‖₂² — explicitly penalizes mutual distances between task weight vectors. γ=0 ⟹ Bates–Granger weights shrunk toward equal by λ; γ tuned over 10 log-spaced values (0.001–1000) per task by LOO-CV; extensions: task grouping, task scaling by per-task difficulty, tandem shrinkage λ‖w‖_q^q.

Soft-global combination results: synthetic — hard global improves roughly linearly with task relatedness but HURTS when tasks are unrelated (worse with more tasks); soft global with CV'd γ nearly matches hard global when tasks identical and ameliorates the unrelated case ('best of both worlds'); more tasks ⟹ more upside; q=1 vs q=2 makes no material difference. ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters pre-COVID (2017–2019): soft global MSFE/EW ≈ 0.921 average, beating local, hard global, AND equal weights. Post-COVID (2019Q4+): mixed (~half cases beat EW) — structural break (F-tests: forecast-error variance differs post-COVID at 1% level for growth/inflation) with too little post-break data; authors recommend EW 'until more data is available' — an operational answer to the forecast-combination puzzle.

equation: log λi = β0 + β^B·Zi^B + β^P·Zi^P + Σ_s Ss·Xi,s^S + Σ_p (βp^LL·Xi^LHB·Xi^LHP + βp^LR·Xi^LHB·Xi^RHP + βp^RL·Xi^RHB·Xi^LHP + βp^RR·Xi^RHB·Xi^RHP)·Xi^p
claim: Osborne & Levine (2025, arXiv:2506.22350) estimate personnel-adjusted MLB home-run park factors with a Poisson GLMM, log link: log λi = β0 + β^B·Zi^B + β^P·Zi^P + Σ_s Ss·Xi,s^S + Σ_p (βp^LL·Xi^LHB·Xi^LHP + βp^LR·Xi^LHB·Xi^RHP + βp^RL·Xi^RHB·Xi^LHP + βp^RR·Xi^RHB·Xi^RHP)·Xi^p — 120 park-by-matchup parameters of interest; season random effects Ss ~ N(0, σS²); unit = game × handedness-matchup (LL, LR, RL, RR), N = 123,886 observations over 2,451,105 PAs, 2010–2023 excl. 2020. The 'elsewhere' (leave-one-park-out) covariates break the circularity of measuring player quality with the same data used to rate parks: batter quality q^B = HR rate in all OTHER parks (e.g., Trevor Story 25/562 = 0.044 vs LHP away from Coors); pitcher quality q^P likewise (e.g., Kershaw 150/7105 = 0.021 vs RHB away from Coors); aggregated per game-matchup as Zi^B = Σq^B, Zi^P = Σq^P.

Adjusted park rankings differ substantially from raw: Cleveland Progressive Field LR 1.025 HR/g (rank 1) → adjusted 0.657 (rank 15); Minnesota Target Field LR 0.771 (rank 11) → adjusted rank 24; White Sox Rate Field LR 0.722 (rank 18) → 0.767 (rank 7); Toronto Rogers Centre RR 1.179 (rank 1) → 0.776 (rank 12); Phillies/Milwaukee/Cincinnati RL move ranks 20/15/21 → 5/3/2 after adjustment. Variance decomposition: full model s² = 2.42 (AIC 220,189); park-only 2.50; personnel-only 2.58; batter-only 2.60; pitcher-only 4.07 — batter personnel matters more than pitcher; park effects add modestly beyond personnel. League HR intensity: 1.72 HR/g (2014) → 2.78 HR/g (2019), +62%. Caveats: elsewhere measures still home-park-contaminated (acknowledged, uncorrected); no CIs on ranks; 2020 excluded.

equation: Y_{i,j,e} = α_{i,e} + Σ_d β_{d,e} φ_d(age) + Σ_{m=1}^{e−1} γ_{m,e} Y_{i,j,m} + ε_{i,j,e}
claim: Nguyen et al. (2026, arXiv:2602.17043) model elite decathlon careers with Bayesian hierarchical models: Eq. 1 (baseline) P_{i,j} = α̃_i + Σ_d β̃_d φ_d(age_{i,j}) + ε; Eq. 2 (simple) Y_{i,j,e} = α_{i,e} + Σ_d β_{d,e} φ_d(age) + ε_{i,j,e}; Eq. 3 (compositional) Y_{i,j,e} = α_{i,e} + Σ_d β_{d,e} φ_d(age) + Σ_{m=1}^{e−1} γ_{m,e} Y_{i,j,m} + ε_{i,j,e} — performance in each event depends on preceding events + nonlinear age curves + athlete random effects. World Athletics scoring: Points = a(b−y)^c (track), a(y−b)^c (field). Fit in rstan: 4 chains × 2,000 iterations, 1,000 burn-in; weakly informative N(0,1)/Inv-Gamma(2,1) priors; φ_d = cubic polynomial or cubic spline with knots at age deciles.

Decathlon CV standardized MSE: general framework baseline 0.234 vs simple/compositional 0.235 (cubic) — essentially tied; tail CV (hold out each athlete's last decathlon) baseline 0.358 vs compositional 0.362 — baseline marginally better on pure prediction. Parameter recovery: near-nominal 95% coverage (exceptions: JT and PV columns at 90.5%). Inter-event antagonism: 0.1 s improvement in 100m ↔ +0.45 min worse 1500m (age- and sequence-adjusted); empirical correlations: 100m–LJ −0.54, 100m–400m +0.66, SP–DT +0.73. 9,200-point probabilities: Mayer 7.7%, Eaton 5.65%, Šebrle 10.3%, Warner 1.8%, Dvořák 0.6%. Observed correlations fall inside the compositional model's posterior predictive intervals but outside the simple model's.

Mureika (2005, arXiv:physics/0505118) simulates how air temperature, barometric pressure, and humidity alter 100 m sprint times through aerodynamic drag F_drag ∝ ρ(T, P, RH)·(v−w)², air density from ideal-gas + humidity correction, numerically integrated per condition. Parameter sweep: T = 15–35°C, RH = 0–100%, P = 85–105 kPa, wind −3…+3 m/s vs a standard race (no wind, sea-level, 25°C). Core concept: density altitude — hot/humid air simulates higher physical altitude (less drag → faster times). Temperature alone: 0.02 s differential over the 15–35°C range (within timing noise); humidity × temperature combined matters more; combined extremes: 0.1+ s variation between 85 kPa/100% RH/35°C and 105 kPa/0%/15°C after wind correction. Direction: heat/humidity → higher density altitude → less drag → faster times. Caution: assumes drag is the only T/P/RH pathway; ignores physiology.

Setlur, Li & Smith (2020, arXiv:2011.14048v2) argue meta-training episode samplers should use a FIXED canonical support pool per task ('fix-ml') instead of random support sampling: standard objective [A] min_w E_C E_{(S,Q)|C} ℓ(w,S,Q) rewritten as [B] min_w E_{S_p~Unif(𝒫)} E_C E_{Q|C} ℓ(w;S_p^C,Q); fix-ml objective (Eq. 2) min_w E_C E_{Q|C} ℓ(w;S_{p,0}^C,Q) with a single fixed support pool S_{p,0}. Diagnostic: approximate Takeuchi Information Criterion tr(C)/tr(F) (C = uncentered gradient covariance, F = Fisher information), correlating with the generalization gap.

fix-ml results: miniImageNet 5-way 5-shot, Prototypical Networks ResNet-12: fix-ml 78.19% vs ml 77.43% (+0.76pp), competitive with MetaOptNet-SVM 77.40% and TADAM 76.70%. On all mini and CIFAR 5w1s and 5w5s evaluations, fix-ml-trained Protonets beat ml; SVM and Ridge-Regression last-layer solvers also improve. WRN-16-10 (over-parameterized): fix-ml still beats ml; Conv64 (shallow): fix-ml hinders performance — the effect requires over-parameterized models. Run variance: 5 fix-ml runs with different random pools have standard deviation 'not only not worse but actually better than ml'. Mechanism: fix-ml ends with higher ml-training loss but lower ml-test loss (smaller generalization gap); approx-TIC ratio tr(C)/tr(F) is higher for ml than fix-ml on all three datasets. Sharpness visualization inconclusive (fix-ml sits at a sharper minimum yet generalizes better).

Li Jiang et al. (2023, arXiv:2307.02752) prove uniform-penalty CQL degrades under Zipf/power-law imbalanced state coverage: CQL's penalty is 'a constant for every state-action pair,' so under imbalance it over-penalizes rare states and amplifies distributional shift. The fix, RB-CQL (retrieval-augmented CQL), builds an auxiliary dataset D_aux of related experiences; retrieval similarity Sim(s_ori^i, s_aux^i) via MIPS (exp inner product over Enc(s)) or Euclidean distance; CQL Bellman updates are augmented with retrieved (s,a,r,s') tuples. On D4RL AntMaze-medium Easy→Hard: RB-CQL robust ('especially from Easy to Medium without any performance drop'); CQL decreases from 60 to 20; TD3+BC decreases from 20 to 0. MuJoCo locomotion: RB-CQL outperforms others at 95% and 97% random dataset ratios. Failure boundary: all algorithms including RB-CQL fail on the extremely hard AntMaze Hard+ task. Authors' limitations: retrieval 'requires huge computation sources from the CPU'; high-dimensional inputs needing embedding networks not studied.

Diffuser (Janner, Du, Tenenbaum, Levine 2022, arXiv:2205.09991) plans by running a diffusion model over full trajectories tau = (s_0, a_0, ..., s_T, a_T) with a 1D-temporal-conv U-Net, trained with the denoising objective L(theta) = E[||eps - eps_theta(tau^i, i)||^2]; it generates jointly-coherent long-horizon plans non-autoregressively.

In Diffuser, guided sampling follows control-as-inference: p_tilde_theta(tau) = p(tau | O_{1:T}=1) proportional to p(tau) * p(O_{1:T}=1 | tau) with p(O_t=1) = exp(r(s_t,a_t)); guide gradients equal the gradient of a return predictor J_phi trained on noisy trajectories.

Diffuser enables planning as inpainting: clamping observed states (e.g., s_0, s_T or any timesteps) during denoising yields goal-conditioned plans from undirected data, and warm-starting (forward-diffusing the previous plan a few steps then re-denoising) makes replanning roughly 10x faster with minimal performance loss.

Diffuser achieved D4RL Maze2D scores of 113.9±3.1 (U-Maze), 121.5±2.7 (Medium), and 123.0±6.4 (Large), exceeding the reference expert (100) in all sizes, while the best baseline on Large maze scored 58.6; on block stacking it scored 58.7±2.5 unconditional and 45.6±3.1 conditional versus BCQ 0.0 and CQL 24.4/0.0.

MPPI with ground-truth dynamics performed poorly on the long-horizon Maze2D multi-goal task, which the Diffuser paper presents as evidence that long-horizon planning is hard even with zero prediction error, and that model-free baseline IQL+HER drops substantially in the multi-goal setting where Diffuser matches its single-task performance with no retraining.

PCMCI+ (Runge 2020, arXiv:2003.03685) is a three-phase constraint-based causal discovery algorithm for autocorrelated nonlinear time series: (1) lagged skeleton via PC-style edge removal with conditioning sets of increasing size, ranking survivors by I^min; (2) contemporaneous skeleton using Momentary Conditional Independence (MCI) tests; (3) orientation of lagged links by time-order and contemporaneous links via collider phase plus Meek rules R1-R3 adapted to time series.
equation: X_t^j = a_j X^j_{t-1} + Σ_i c_i f_i(X^i_{t−τ_i}) + η_t^j

claim: PCMCI+ is sound under causal sufficiency, Causal Markov, Adjacency Faithfulness, oracle CI tests, stationarity, time-order, and correct tau_max (Theorems 1-4), supports ParCorr (linear) and GPDC (Gaussian-process + distance correlation, nonlinear additive noise) CI tests, and keeps false-positive rates well-controlled at high autocorrelation where PC and LiNGAM show strong lagged-FPR increases.

In Runge's simulations (N=5, T=500, a=0.95, tau_max=5, alpha=0.01, 500 realizations), PCMCI+ achieved more than twice the contemporaneous orientation recall of competitors at larger N with almost no conflicts, while PC's conflicts increased with autocorrelation; GPDC runtime was orders of magnitude longer than ParCorr and failed in high-dimensional highly-autocorrelated settings.

DAG-NoCurl (Yu, Gao, Yin, Ji 2021, ICML, arXiv:2106.07197) learns DAGs via a two-step procedure: unconstrained L-BFGS on the cyclic solution with the NOTEARS loss, then a Hodge decomposition projecting onto the curl-free gradient of a potential function; its theorem states DAG weighted-adjacency matrices are exactly the weighted gradients of graph potentials, making it 10-100x faster than NOTEARS while reaching the same global minimizer.

DAG-NoCurl runtime matches FGS and MMPC (over one to two orders of magnitude faster than NOTEARS) with comparable accuracy: lowest SHD on ER-Gaussian (NoCurl-2) and SF4-Gumbel (NoCurl-1); on nonlinear SEMs it matches DAG-GNN accuracy at 3-4x speed and beats NOTEARS-MLP and GraN-DAG by over an order of magnitude; the paper finds L1 regularization adds little and thresholding suffices.

Holzmuller, Grinsztajn, Steinwart (2024, arXiv:2407.04491) argue that meta-tuned default hyperparameters (RealMLP-TD with one-hot encoding, robust scaling, smooth clipping, plus tuned XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost defaults using row subsampling, 1000 fixed estimators, hist method for XGBoost) combined with algorithm selection over defaults beats per-dataset HPO on the time-accuracy tradeoff.

On a meta-generalization protocol of 118 meta-train datasets to 90 deliberately more extreme meta-test datasets, RealMLP showed a favorable time-accuracy tradeoff versus other neural baselines and was competitive with GBDTs; tuned defaults cannot match HPO on average but outperform library defaults on the meta-test benchmark.

Stochastic batch acquisition (Kirsch et al. 2021, arXiv:2106.12059) proves the Gumbel-top-K equivalence: taking top-K of (s_i + eps_i) with eps_i ~ Gumbel(0, beta^-1) is exactly an ordered sample without replacement from Categorical(exp(beta s_i)/sum_j exp(beta s_j)); three variants are Softmax p(i) prop exp(beta s_i), Power p(i) prop s_i^beta, and Soft-rank p(i) prop r_i^{-beta}, with beta=1 default, beta->inf giving top-K and beta->0 uniform.
equation: arg top_k{s_i + ε_i}, ε_i ~ Gumbel(0,β⁻¹) ≡ ordered sample without replacement from Categorical(exp(βs_i)/Σ_j exp(βs_j))

claim: The BatchBALD decomposition I[Y_1:K;Omega|x_1:K,D] = sum_j E[I[Y_j;Omega|x_j,prev,D]] is not equal to the sum of per-point BALD scores, exposing the top-K fallacy: top-K BALD selection is suboptimal versus joint batch acquisition because it ignores dependence between selected points.

Stochastic batch acquisition runs at O(M log K) with the same wall-clock cost as top-K (0.2s at K=10/100/500) versus BatchBALD (566s/5,364s/29,984s) and BADGE (9.2s/82.1s/409.3s), while matching or beating them: PowerBALD (K=10) beat top-K BALD, BADGE, and approximately matched BatchBALD (K=5) on Repeated-MNISTx4, and BatchBALD took over 12 days for 115 acquisitions on EMNIST ByMerge before being halted.

Pathway (Bartoszkiewicz et al., arXiv:2307.13116v1) is a unified batch/streaming engine with a Python layer building the computation graph and a Rust incremental-dataflow layer (modified differential dataflow plus custom operators on a modified LSM tree); the same code runs batch and streaming, with inserts/deletes/modifications propagating as deltas and consistency stronger than eventual via injected COMMIT control messages instead of approximate watermarking.

On streaming PageRank over the LiveJournal graph (4,847,571 nodes, 68,993,773 edges), Pathway beat Flink by roughly 40-48x (e.g., 5M edges: Pathway 61.0/36.1/21.4/17.3s vs Flink 3350/3190/1286/830s), and on full-graph backfill Flink did not finish (OOM or >2h) while Pathway finished in 150/90/58/49s single-edge stream; Spark variants cannot express the backfill workload at all. The ledger flags these as upper bounds because all authors are Pathway.com staff.

AutoAlpha (arXiv:2002.08245) mines formulaic alpha factors with a hierarchical evolutionary algorithm using an 'effective root gene' hierarchy, PCA-similarity Quality-Diversity search with PCA-similarity(i,j) = Pearson(PC1(A^(i)), PC1(A^(j))) penalizing alphas above 0.9 similarity, and warm-start/parent-offspring replacement to prevent premature convergence.

AutoAlpha fitness uses mining IC (information coefficient) with AR = exp(365/T' * log(S_T/S_0)) - 1 and SR = (R_p - R_f)/sigma_p; on CSI 300 (train 2010-2017, test 2017-2019, 0.3% transaction cost) it found 434 diverse alphas with IC > 0.05 (h=1) versus gplearn 35 and Alpha101 0, with backtest AR/SR of 90.0%/3.39 versus gplearn 61.8%/2.34 and SFM deep learning -60.0%/-2.05.

TabDDPM (arXiv:2209.15421) models mixed-type tabular data with parallel Gaussian diffusion (numerical) and multinomial diffusion (categorical) on one joint representation, trained with the loss L_t^TabDDPM = L_t^simple + (sum_i L_t^i)/C (MSE for the Gaussian term, KL terms for multinomial terms averaged over C categorical features), using a shared MLP reverse model with 128-dim sinusoidal time embeddings and Optuna tuning (50 trials) guided by ML efficiency versus CatBoost.

TabDDPM ranked best on categorical JS divergence (1.62) and correlation-matrix L2 (1.73) across 15 UCI/OpenML benchmarks, and best-or-tied-best on ML efficiency (train on synthetic, test on real) for a majority of datasets, while black-box membership-inference attack ROCAUC stayed near random (0.51-0.57) versus SMOTE's 0.610-0.999, and DCR privacy beat SMOTE on all 16 sets.

Diff-MTS (arXiv:2407.11501) generates multivariate time series with a conditional diffusion model regularized by classifier-free Ada-MMD condition-consistency: L_diff = (1-w)L_{theta,xc} + w*L_MMD(eps, eps_theta(x_t,t|x_c)) (Eq. 11) with learnable w, a cosine noise schedule (s=0.008), and a TDR-UNet denoiser where X_Trend = AvgPool(Pad(X)), X_Peak = MaxPool(Pad(X)) with conv-attention between UNet encoder/decoder.

On NASA C-MAPSS FD001-96, Diff-MTS achieved discriminative score 0.611 (2-layer LSTM real-vs-synthetic accuracy, lower better) versus DiffWave 0.904, TimeGAN 0.935, and TTS-GAN 0.987, and predictive score 15.554 on FD003-96 versus DiffWave 28.433 (-45.2%); removing Ada-MMD degraded predictive scores on all 4 FD sets, and TDR-UNet beat the original UNet by 7.5% on average discriminative score.

SHARP (arXiv:2605.06822) is a neuro-symbolic policy where reasoning is confined to a bounded human-readable rubric of condition-action rules, evolved via a tri-agent loop: Attribution agent (backtests rubric, examines K_attr=20 worst days, maps failures to rule IDs), Evolution agent (atomic mutations: threshold changes, signal-weight tweaks, rule add/remove; |R| <= M_max), Validation agent (accept R* iff validation excess return e(R*) > e(R_best) + eps).

SHARP evolved from a Static rubric at +0.6% / +0.09 SR to +20.9% / +1.83 SR (3-sector average, GPT-4o-mini, 2025-2026 walk-forward with three 4-month train + OOS windows and J=5 evolution rounds), beating FinCon-4o's +15.9%; the killer ablation A2 showed free-form reflection instead of structured edits dropped Sharpe from +2.45 to -0.84 and return from +33.2% to -12.1%, worse than the no-adaptation static baseline.

The unified invasion-games taxonomy (arXiv:2108.11149) uses three mutually-exclusive paths: game-status-changing events (referee decisions vs static-ball actions), ball possession changes, and individual ball events (reception to release; intentional pass/shot vs unintentional interference/self-induced); evaluation uses tIoU for duration events, Nearest Neighbor Matching (many-to-one, positive bias) versus Sequence Consistent Matching (penalizes count mismatches), and temporal Average Precision over tolerance areas.

The EIGD-S/EIGD-H gold datasets (github.com/mm4spa/eigd, 125 min per sport, 1280x720 @ 30fps video + audio + 20Hz positional data) counted expert events EIGD-S: possession change 171, reception 923, release 1531, pass 1346 (83 intercepted), shot 31; human annotator agreement was high at top hierarchy levels and decreased with depth, while a commercial data provider showed low agreement with precise expert annotation attributed to imprecise real-time manual annotation.

Lag-Llama (arXiv:2310.08278v1) is a 2,449,299-parameter decoder-only transformer foundation model for probabilistic time-series forecasting whose input is x_t = [y_{t-l_1}, ..., y_{t-l_k}, dtf_t] (lags per frequency plus date-time features), with a Student-t output head (nu_t, mu_t, sigma_t) = head(h_t) and likelihood p(y_t) = StudentT(y_t; nu_t, mu_t, sigma_t), trained to minimize sum_t -log StudentT over the prediction horizon and evaluated with CRPS.

Lag-Llama pretrained on 27 datasets across 6 domains (7,965 univariate series, ~352M windows) ranked 6.714 zero-shot (competitive but not leading) and 2.786 fine-tuned (best on average, SOTA on 3 individual datasets) against baselines DeepAR, PatchTST, TFT, N-BEATS, and ETS-family models; the ledger prescribes using the lag-covariate recipe and Student-t head inside a sports-native model, never frozen zero-shot.

Conformal risk-averse decision making (arXiv:2606.05551) defines action-conditional safety: for all actions a, P(u(a(X),Y) >= nu(X) | a(X)=a) >= 1-alpha, with max-min rule a^C_RA(x) = argmax_a min_{y in C(x)} u(a,y); the finite-sample AC-RAC algorithm uses the action-specific nonconformity score lambda*_a(x,y) = inf{lambda_a >= 0: y in QuantileSet_{1-t_hat(x,lambda_a)}[u(a,Y)|Y~f_x]} (Eq. 14) with pinball loss l_alpha(u,v) = (v-u)(1{u<=v}-alpha) optimized via projected subgradient descent, with a distribution-free lower bound (Thm 4.3) under exchangeability.

On a medical benchmark (COVID-19 Radiography Database, 4 treatment actions, 40 random seeds), AC-RAC was the only method with valid conditional coverage across ALL actions at alpha=0.05 while baselines never selected action 2 (Quarantine), and its critical error rate was 0.21-0.35% versus RAC's 3.35-4.70% with average utility within 5% of RAC at a ~3.7% mean set-size increase.

Halpern & Leung (arXiv:1302.5681) define weighted sets of probabilities P+ = {(Pr, alpha_Pr)} with alpha_Pr in [0,1], likelihood update alpha_Pr <- Pr(E)/sup_{Pr' in P} Pr'(E), and the minimax weighted expected regret rule reg_{M,P+}(f) = sup_{Pr in P}(alpha_Pr * sum_s Pr(s)*reg_M(f,s)), preferring the act with the smallest maximum weighted expected regret, which is strictly less conservative than maximin expected utility.

The convergence theorem of weighted sets of probabilities states that under a stable data-generating measure, weights of the closest measures converge to 1 and all others to 0 almost surely (unlike measure-by-measure updating, which does not concentrate on the truth); MWER can be dynamically inconsistent (ex-ante optimal plans not followed ex-post), with the paper discussing resolute choice and sophisticated planning as remedies without resolving which to use. No numerical results (pure decision theory).

Vercel Pro bills $20/mo platform fee including a $20 usage credit (no rollover); function invocations $0.60/1M; Active CPU (Fluid) iad1/cle1/pdx1 $0.128/CPU-hr vs sfo1 $0.177 vs gru1 $0.221; Provisioned Memory iad1 $0.0106/GB-hr vs sfo1 $0.0147; builds $0.0035/CPU-min; edge middleware 1M included then $0.65/1M; log drains $0.50/GB; Observability Plus $1.20/1M events. Region price spread is ~73%: moving sfo1 to iad1 cuts compute ~28-38%.

Vercel AI Gateway offers 360+ models via one OpenAI-compatible endpoint with 0% inference markup (provider list price), per-request cost/latency/routing logging, budgets at 4 scopes (team/project/API key/user), ordered provider+model fallbacks, OIDC auth, and per-request ZDR free; free tier carries a $5/mo credit forfeited permanently on first top-up; default training-data posture assumes providers train on data unless disallow-prompt-training/ZDR is set.

The Vercel audit identifies cost/infrastructure levers: ISR-cached function responses cost zero invocations and zero GB-hrs; Vercel cron endpoints are publicly invokable (require a CRON_SECRET check); long-running I/O-heavy functions with high memory (e.g., signals-writer cron, Neon queries) are the #1 compute waste shape since memory bills through I/O waits even when CPU billing pauses; new teams default to a $200/billing-cycle on-demand budget with 50/75/100% alerts.

FantasyPoints claims '#1 DFS Fantasy Projections' on DraftKings citing a 0.71 weekly correlation across 18 regular-season main slates (self-reported, competitors anonymized as 'Comp. 1-3', methodology unpublished, not tracked by any independent benchmark); the ledger judges this a different measurement than FantasyPros ranking accuracy or FFA projection MAE and not independently verifiable from public data.

FantasyPros accuracy leaderboards (150+ analysts scored): 2025 in-season winner Justin Boone (Yahoo); 2024 winner Tyler Orginski; Nathan Jahnke (PFF) was the most accurate in-season ranker in six straight seasons; draft rankings leader Jody Smith (Draft Sharks) on a 3-year rolling window; the Fantasy Football Analytics 2019-2023 MAE study (startable pool top-20 QB/TE, top-50 RB/WR) found the simple average/consensus consistently near the top across positions and seasons while per-position leaders rotate year to year.

The GSE rankings program hard rule: rankings never maintain a separate projection fork — a divergence between the engine's pick and the published ranking for the same player/week is a bug, not a feature; rankings products (rest-of-season, week-by-week, positional, weeks 4 through fantasy playoffs) are gated behind a locked projection source, adjustment layer + player signals, and off-field intake, with internal accuracy measured as MAE/RMSE/Spearman vs actuals per position per week.

The Sportvision/FOX telestration family (6 patents, expired 2017-2019 on normal 20-year term) covered human-drawn telestration smoothed into 3D field coords, auto-reveal via separate sensor + barrier geometry, two-camera triangulation, six-radar Doppler, and color-sampling compositing so the line passes under players; the claims do NOT cover automatic drawing generation without a human hand, neural-segmentation/non-color compositing, radar-free CV speed measurement, or all-at-the-venue processing — so an automatic, no-stadium-hardware, segmentation-based pipeline does not read on them. SMT acquired 100% of Sportvision on Oct 4 2016 (reported >$25M); PVI's sensorless L-VIS approach was never blocked.

The Sharp Labs football-video family (7 patents, all expired fee-related 2022-2026, deliberately unpaid) claimed vanishing-point start detection, a 70% voting sliding window (US7639275), 5-6 sigma histogram scene-change end detection (US7474331), full-speed vs slow-motion classification (US8018491), and logo-transition replay detection (US7474698/US7653131); claims were locked to handcrafted color/frame-difference heuristics and do NOT cover learned/classifier boundaries, scoreboard/clock OCR, audio cues (whistle/crowd), broadcast metadata, or league data feeds. Sharp's own engineers concluded deterministic rules were too difficult and moved to probabilistic (HMM) methods; Object Prediction Technologies US7609855B2 (filed by Sada/Tsai/Meijome, granted Oct 27 2009, expired fee-related 2027) covers vanishing-point moving-object analysis.

The expert-partner signal playbook states sources are rights-gated before display, storage, redistribution, training, or expert-signal conversion; candidate scale is modeled for 500,000+ URLs with paginated review and triage; records are kept distinct as active/open, activation/license, reference, and candidate-only; the next step is replacing generated fixtures with authorized production feeds.

The sliding-window OGD calibration analysis fits the map g = sigma(a * logit p + b) by online gradient descent under log-loss, re-fit on a trailing chronological window (default window = 120 samples); diagnostic fields are full.a (OGD a on entire chrono series), window.a (a on last window samples), deltaA = window.a - full.a, deltaVarCal = Var[P_cal] window minus full, and expansionPreferred in {full, window, neither}; durable fields slidingWindowA/slidingDeltaA/slidingExpansionPreferred are wired into the map bake-off.

The OGD sliding-window read table states: window.a > 1 + beats-raw-Brier + deltaVarCal > 0 means the recent sample is underconfident (RES-cal candidate offline); window.a approximately 1 means the identity map is fine and maps won't invent RES; unstable/flipping window.a means non-stationary (shadow diagnostics only); if neither beats raw Brier, raise independent ranking first. Laws: live eligibility stays map-free; never free-stretch p' = 0.5 + k(p - 0.5) without outcomes; CALIBRATION_ADJUSTMENTS_ENABLED stays OFF until live RES floors clear; the sliding window is tracking, not a publish policy.
