Dutta, Yurko & Ventura (arXiv:1906.11373v3, 2020) classify man vs zone pass coverage for cornerbacks from NFL tracking data using unsupervised Gaussian mixture models plus hierarchical clustering; the per-cornerback-play feature vector (snap to forward pass) includes VAR_X, VAR_Y, SPEED_VAR, OFF_VAR, DEF_VAR, OFF_MEAN, DEF_MEAN, OFF_DIR_VAR, OFF_DIR_MEAN, RAT-MEAN, RAT-VAR plus distance-ratio summaries at snap, throw, and midpoint; GMM posteriors serve as probabilistic man/zone assignments.

The paper reports NO accuracy/AUC or supervised metric — no ground truth exists at scale, so evaluation is qualitative cluster inspection only; it covered 6,712 pass plays and 16,316 cornerback-play observations from the inaugural Big Data Bowl release (first six weeks of the 2017 NFL season, all 22 players + ball at 10 Hz, x in 0-120, y in 0-58, no orientation data).

The coverage paper's limitations: cornerbacks only (no safeties/nickel/linebackers, so no team-level scheme); the snap-to-throw window ignores pre-snap alignment, which the ledger calls the strongest signal of coverage intent; six weeks of 2017 data is stale; unsupervised solutions are sensitive to undocumented normalization/K choices; acceptance gate pre-registered by the ledger is bootstrap ARI >= 0.70 over >= 100 resamples plus >=90% qualitative audit agreement on 100 sampled plays.

Winkelmann et al. (arXiv:2605.30209, 2026) model live-betting stake dynamics in Serie B with a hurdle state-space model: Pr(y_t=0) = pi_t (pi_t = 1 when market closed); log(y_t)|y_t>0 ~ N(mu_t, sigma); mu_t = nu_t + s_t; s_t = phi s_{t-1} + x_t^{(2)'}omega + sigma_s eps_t with |phi|<1; the exact likelihood is intractable so a Kitagawa-style fine discretization (~m=100 intervals) approximates the SSM as a large HMM with likelihood via the forward algorithm and BFGS maximization.

The hurdle SSM baseline estimates are phi-hat = 0.986, sigma_s-hat = 0.215, sigma-hat = 0.924, pi-hat = 0.094 (matches the empirical 0.094), with DeltaAIC = 160,747 versus the hurdle model without a state process — overwhelming support for latent dynamics; full-model effects: opponent red card beta_4 = 1.075 [1.004;1.146], own red card beta_3 = -0.414, score diff 0.420, halftime 0.210 (~23.7% elevated halftime stakes), surprising goal omega_1 = 0.285 [0.257;0.313], unsurprising goal omega_3 = -0.379, xg_diff omega_4 = 0.001 (not significant — differs from Bundesliga).
equation: π_t = logit⁻¹(α_0 + α_1·gini + α_2·gini² + α_3·minute + interactions)

claim: The Serie B stake-dynamics paper defines goal-surprise tiers: surprising = scorer's pre-match win probability <= 0.25, slightly 0.25-0.5, unsurprising > 0.5; descriptively, stakes peak in the first 10 minutes, rise at halftime and late in the second half, favorites average 1.98 stakes vs 1.34 for underdogs, and zero-stake minutes correlate with Gini (0.41) and minute (0.23); the paper produces NO detection results (no precision/recall, no flagged matches) and ignores draws on an asserted-but-untested 'less prone to fraud' assumption.

The engine's entire labelled dataset is ~2,641 settled picks (NFL stratum has ~70 settled picks ever — thin strata must borrow via partial pooling); nflverse provides millions of unlabelled plays back to 1999 and closing-line/line-movement ticks serve as dense labels; any deep model at the 2,641-label scale is over-parameterised — more parameters is the wrong answer (Chinchilla discipline).

Two contaminations were already measured in the repo: backfill-independent-trueprob.ts rewrites independentEdge.trueProb on settled rows (answer-fit), and walk-forward.ts cuts folds by row index with fixture triplication (boundary leakage); 'ten months of work has not compounded because the loop was never closed' — walk-forward, trials-registry, placebo, logit-pool, logistic, calibration-blend, evidence-readiness-matrix (13 factor keys, called by nothing at runtime), and feature-store (point-in-time validated, zero registered features) were none wired/run; BAEE_NUM_MODELS is pinned at 1 with an empty endpoint list (Bayesian model averaging never had a second model).

Yao et al. (2025, arXiv:2509.25858) model NBA aging curves in two stages: an autoencoder (336-dim input = 48 features x 7 years, dense 128 with batch norm and dropout 0.1, then 64 with ReLU) with K-means career-trend clustering on the 64-dim embeddings (optimal K=2 by Silhouette: K=2 -> 0.16, K=3 -> 0.15, K=4 -> 0.12, declining to 0.09 at K=8), trained with reconstruction loss L = (1/N) sum_i ||x_i - decoder(encoder(x_i))||_2^2; Stage 2 is an LSTM(64) over the 7-year sequence concatenated with a one-hot cluster vector, dense 32 -> 16 (ReLU), Adam with early stopping, outputting 3 values = predicted BPM at ages 29, 30, 31.

On 177 NBA players with complete career trends (141 train / 36 test, Kaggle 'NBA history | seasonal data 1995-2023'), the proposed cluster-conditioned model achieved test MAE 1.42 / R^2 0.55 (best on both) versus Random Forest 1.48/0.49, standard LSTM 1.84/0.19, GRU 1.82/0.23, BiLSTM 1.84/0.21, SVR 1.81/0.17, MLP 1.93/-0.01; the unclustered LSTM collapses to near-zero predictions for everyone (LeBron ages 29/30/31: actual 8.80/7.10/9.00 vs standard LSTM 0.30/0.24/-0.29 vs proposed 7.00/5.89/5.55).

Star players (n=23) versus regular players (n=199) showed structurally different career-trend curves: standard LSTM MAE 4.83 / R^2 -4.15 on stars vs proposed 1.78 / 0.23 (63.1% MAE reduction), and 1.96 / -0.07 vs 1.45 / 0.39 on regulars (26.0% reduction); the ledger's caveats are a 36-player test set, silhouette 0.16 (very weak clustering, authors concede), unstated whether Stage 1 clustering was fit on train only (leakage risk), a 177-vs-222 sample denominator inconsistency, and that NBA aging structure (peak ~27) does not transfer to NFL positions.

Brown, Scott & Kilduff (2025, arXiv:2504.19612) axiomatic framework for relative metrics uses the measurement model X_A = mu_A + eps_A + eta, X_B = mu_B + eps_B + eta with eps_i ~ N(0, sigma_i^2) and shared eta ~ N(0, sigma_eta^2); the relative transformation R = X_A - X_B cancels the environment to R = (mu_A - mu_B) + (eps_A - eps_B); SNR_single_abs = (mu_A-mu_B)^2/(sigma_A^2 + sigma_eta^2) and SNR_rel = (mu_A-mu_B)^2/(sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2), giving improvement ratio SNR_rel/SNR_abs = (sigma_A^2 + sigma_eta^2)/(sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2) which approaches 1 + sigma_eta^2/(sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2) when shared noise dominates.

The paper's ML insight: a two-feature absolute predictor given both X_A and X_B implicitly learns relativization — optimal linear weights converge to w_A = 1, w_B = -1 — and SNR_twoabs approx 4*SNR_rel (pure scaling, same boundary); its four axioms for valid relative metrics are invariance to shared effects, ordinal consistency, scaling proportionality, and optimality (X_A - X_B minimizes expected squared error in estimating mu_A - mu_B); linked metrics are separability S = Phi(d/2), information content I = 1 - H(S), Mahalanobis distance D_M = |mu_A-mu_B|/sqrt(sigma_A^2 + sigma_B^2), d = 2*D_M, with metric-selection guidance: focus on S when d < 1, on I when d > 3 (S saturates, I keeps improving).

In high-noise simulations, accuracy was single absolute 0.735 +/- 0.014, two-feature absolute 0.941 +/- 0.009, relative 0.943 +/- 0.009; relative beat two-feature in only 51% of accuracy trials / 61% of AUC trials (a statistical tie, predicted by theory); headline gains up to ~28-28.3% classification-accuracy improvement under high noise, with the largest gains at moderate |delta mu| (5-20) and moderate sigma_indiv (2-5).

The rugby validation (127 matches, 2021-2022 United Rugby Championship) gave AUC-ROC for carries over gain line 0.619 (home) / 0.738 (both) / 0.782 (relative), defenders beaten 0.642/0.744/0.771, tackle completion 0.584/0.723/0.738 — average +21.3% over single absolute but +5.2% over two-feature absolute; inferred rugby noise ratio sigma_eta/sigma_indiv approx 0.46 average (0.51 carries, 0.45 defenders beaten, 0.39 tackle %), estimated SNR gain ~8.3-fold, effect sizes d approx 1.0-1.5; the ledger's adversarial caveat: single-team-absolute is a straw man (the fair two-feature comparison is tied), so the honest rugby delta is +5.2%, not the headline +21.3%, and NFL is already difference-dominated (scores are differences) so marginal gain over current practice is smaller.

Scholtes & Karakus (2023, arXiv:2311.13707) fit Bayesian hierarchical logistic regression (bambi/PyMC, 1500 draws, 250 burn-in, 4 chains = 6000 samples, 95% target acceptance) for expected goals on 63,309 open-play shots from StatsBomb (EPL ~10,000+, La Liga ~19,000 shots Barcelona/Messi-heavy, Bundesliga ~7,500); likelihood is Bernoulli with logistic logit(p_i) = beta_0 + sum_j beta_j X_ji; baseline (Eq. 8): logit(p_i) = beta_0 + beta_1*distance + beta_2*angle + beta_3*(distance*angle); hierarchical (Eq. 10): logit(p_ik) = beta_0k + sum_j beta_jk*X_ji + beta_{N+1,k}*X_{N+1,i} with group-specific intercepts beta_0k and slopes beta_jk.

BayesxG priors use directional skew-normal (SN) distributions where sign is predictable: distance SN(mu=-1,sigma=5,alpha=-1), angle SN(mu=1,sigma=5,alpha=1), one-on-one alpha=2, open goal alpha=4, under pressure alpha=-2, GK in triangle alpha=-2, positions alpha={ST:2, AM:1, M:0, D:-2} with sigma~HN(gamma=5), players alpha in {2,0} by reputation (2 = good finisher); neutral coefficients N(mu=0,sigma=5); the prior-sensitivity battery (§4.5, 6 prior setups) found the paper's priors win, wide normal comparable, wide uniform poor (non-convergence at fixed budget), tight uniform/normal systematically underestimate (mass <= 0.8), and ill-suited narrow flipped-skew priors give few predictions above 0.5.

BayesxG1 positional adjustments: ST 0.009/0.010, AM 0.019/0.020, M -0.006/-0.005, D -0.042/-0.044 (attacking midfielders got larger positive adjustments than strikers); BayesxG2 with extended situational features collapsed positional adjustments ('few adjustments now exceed 0.01') — richer features absorbed what looked like position effects, with the ordering AM > ST > M > D and shrinkage replicating in La Liga and Bundesliga; BayesxG3 player effects persisted even with extended features (Pires up to +0.3 above baseline, Aguero consistently positive, Shelvey substantially negative), while Aubameyang was anomalous (high conversion 20.6% but negative adjustments — his goals come from already-high-xG chances).

BayesxG Table 4 (frequentist): baseline RMSE 0.095 / MAE 0.058 / R^2 0.428 / Brier 0.086; extended model RMSE 0.055 / MAE 0.029 / R^2 0.826 / Brier 0.076 vs StatsBomb benchmark 0.075 ('nearly identical', comparable to industry-leading xG); the ledger's adversarial caveats: player priors use subjective reputation, BayesxG3 player selection is post-hoc by observed conversion rate (circularity risk), and team effects confound player effects (Vardy/Leicester vs Aguero/City); sampler validation via the Bayes-theorem adjustment P(goal|position_i) = P(position_i|goal)*P(goal)/P(position_i) (Eq. 11) reproduced the hierarchical adjustments.

Passi & Pandey (2018, arXiv:1804.04226) predict cricket ODI batsman run-bands and bowler wicket-bands with a Consistency/Form/Opposition/Venue four-way feature decomposition weighted by the Analytic Hierarchy Process (Saaty): Batting Consistency (whole career) = 0.4262*average + 0.2566*innings + 0.1510*SR + 0.0787*centuries + 0.0556*fifties - 0.0328*zeros; raw measures are binned to 1-5 ratings before weighting; targets are classification (runs in 5 classes: 1-24 / 25-49 / 50-74 / 75-99 / >=100; wickets in 3 classes: 0-1 / 2-3 / >=4) with Naïve Bayes, C4.5/CART decision trees, Random Forest, and multiclass SVM (LIBSVM) plus SMOTE oversampling.

The cricket paper reports Random Forest 90.74% accuracy (precision/recall/F1 0.908, AUROC 0.987, RMSE 0.1604) on 5-class runs prediction and 92.25% on 3-class wickets (Table 1-2, 90% train), but the ledger's adversarial caveats invalidate these as generalization claims: random (not time-ordered) train/test splits on time-series data, SMOTE applied before splitting (leaking synthetic samples across train/test), 90.74% on 5-class runs prediction not credible as generalization, subjective AHP weights, author-chosen 1-5 binning thresholds, zero Opposition/Venue history replaced with class averages, and no calibration, no betting-market comparison, no profit metric.

LAPIS (arXiv:2602.18541v1, Daniel García García) is a token-efficient API description format as a deterministic conversion target from OpenAPI 3.x for LLM consumers; it achieves mean 85.5% token reduction vs OpenAPI YAML across 5 production specs (cl100k_base), 88.6% claimed vs OpenAPI JSON, 79.8-90.9% vs minified JSON; attribution: metadata elimination ~25-30%, signature syntax ~25%, type-system compaction ~15%, error centralization ~10-20%; tokenizer consistency within 0.5-1.9% across cl100k_base/o200k_base.

LAPIS conversion uses deterministic rules (§5): resolve $ref, flatten allOf, oneOf/anyOf -> most common variant (complex unions -> any), schemas referenced more than once become named types, 4xx/5xx deduplicated by code+schema; sections are [meta], [types], [ops] (required), [webhooks], [errors], [limits], [flows]; [limits]/[webhooks]/[flows] are NOT produced by the converter — they must be hand-authored; per-spec reductions: GitHub 82.7% (1,811,843 -> 313,101 tokens), DigitalOcean 90.8%, Twilio 92.1%, HTTPBin 71.9%, Petstore 82.7%; the cost example is the GitHub spec in context at $3/M input tokens: $5.44/call -> $0.94/call.

LAPIS quantified GitHub API error duplication: 1,594 error definitions vs 14 unique codes (404 repeated 531 times); LLM reasoning quality on LAPIS vs OpenAPI is explicitly untested — the paper admits no comprehension experiment — and the lossy conversions (oneOf -> most common variant, complex unions -> any) are exactly where an agent could pick the wrong variant.

The 7-page narrative literature review of web communication protocols (REST, SOAP, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, SSE, HTTP/2/3, MQTT) has no dataset, no experiments, no equations, no quantitative comparison, and no code — narrative review only; the deep-read verdict is REJECT with no actionable content.

Gao & Kowalczyk (2019, arXiv:1910.03203v1) compared SVM, logistic regression, and random forest on 49,188 ATP entries (2000-2016), reporting random forest 83.18% accuracy vs betting odds 69.04%; the deep-read verdict is REJECT because the decisive serve features (FirstWonFirstIn, SecondWonSecondIn) have no stated pre-match aggregation window and appear sourced from per-match charting — probable target leakage — and the train/test split was random (not chronological), so the 83.18% is not credible evidence; SVM scored 62.06% and logistic regression 61.60%.
equation: score = (p − 0.5)·w, w = +1 win / −1 loss [UNCERTAIN — extraction-garbled reconstruction]

claim: The tennis paper's TRUST-SIGNAL cautionary patterns: random (non-chronological) split means future matches inform past predictions, no walk-forward validation, no calibration metrics, no betting simulation/ROI despite the betting framing; implied probability from decimal odds is computed as P = 1/ODDS; the first author affiliation is Darlington School (a high school) — noted in the read, not disqualifying.

SVI-Bench (arXiv:2605.31529v2, Pan et al. 2026) is a 9-task, four-pillar benchmark for strategic video intelligence in basketball, soccer, and hockey (no American football) built from ~35K hours broadcast video, ~15M timestamped play-by-play records, ~15K hours of commentary (Whisper ASR), ~23K postgame recaps, and ~103K box scores across 64 leagues 2018-2025, temporally aligned via shared game/player identifiers with a three-stage QC (auto consistency, task filters, expert review); code at github.com/texaser/svi-bench (MIT), data at huggingface.co/datasets/mvpgroup/svi-bench under a gated-access agreement.

On the T5 Outcome Forecasting task (114K MCQs, 3-15 min observation windows, targets beyond the window, metric = accuracy + calibration error with CE = 0 perfect), a finetuned Qwen3-VL 8B reached 44.8% accuracy with CE 0.01 (zero-shot 36.9%, CE 0.23) versus GPT-5.2 zero-shot 38.2% with CE 0.28 and a 28-point confidence-accuracy gap, and humans at 58.9%; the oracle experiment (GPT-5.2 + play-by-play instead of video) scored 41.9% vs 38.1% video-only on T5 basketball (+4.2 points) — 'accurate perception alone is insufficient for strong forecasting'.

SVI-Bench's horizon-overconfidence finding: as temporal distance to the target event grows, model accuracy drops 91% -> 45% while model confidence barely moves (98% -> 94%) — an overconfidence gap widening with horizon, with the model not adjusting confidence for longer-horizon uncertainty; humans 'not only outperform models but also know when they are uncertain' (T2 human accuracy 30% at low confidence -> 90% at high; T5 50% -> 100%), while models show no such pattern; the capability cliff runs from T2 73.91% (finetuned LLaVA-Video-7B, normalized 0-100) to T9 ~5%.

The Bradley-Terry survey (Fang et al., 2026) states the core models: BT-S P(Y_ij = i>j) = gamma_i/(gamma_i+gamma_j) with gamma_i > 0; BT-U P = sigma(u_i - u_j) with sigma(x) = (1+exp(-x))^{-1}, identifiable only up to an additive constant with the recommended constraint sum u_i = 0 (variance-minimization property); BT-MLE u_hat = argmax_{sum u = 0} sum log sigma(Y_ij; u_i - u_j), which exists iff the comparison graph plus outcomes are strongly connected (Ford 1957) — otherwise u_hat_i -> infinity, with ridge regularization as fallback.

The survey's covariate-assisted PlusDC model is P(Y_ij = i>j) = sigma(u_i - u_j + (x_{i,j},i - x_{i,j},j))^Tv); the file states 'The BT model with home-field advantage in sports analytics is a special instance of PlusDC', with covariates split into static (player attributes) vs dynamic (home-field, positional bias — 'play a vital role in model identifiability and data fitting'); the Plackett-Luce form is P(Y_e = i_pi(1)>...>i_pi(k)) = product_{j=1}^{k-1} exp(u_{i_pi(j)})/sum_{l=j}^k exp(u_{i_pi(l)}) with latent form X_i = u_i + eps_i, eps_i i.i.d. Gumbel(0,1); the BT mixture is P = sum_{h=1}^H omega_h sigma(u_i^{(h)} - u_j^{(h)}) with omega_h > 0, sum_h omega_h = 1.

BT solvers surveyed: Zermelo FPI gamma_i <- sum_j w_ij / sum_j n_ij/(gamma_i+gamma_j) (slow, observed); Newman FPI gamma_i <- [sum_j w_ij gamma_j/(gamma_i+gamma_j)] / [sum_j w_ji/(gamma_i+gamma_j)] — 'observed to converge much faster than (Zermelo) in a number of scenarios'; RankCentrality (stationary distribution of an ergodic Markov chain with transitions proportional to defeat probabilities); LSR/I-LSR (MLE-via-global-balance of a continuous-time Markov chain); Accelerated Spectral Ranking; EM-MAP gamma_i <- (a-1+sum_j w_ij)/(b + sum_j n_ij/(gamma_i+gamma_j)) with Zermelo as the special case a=1, b=0.

Surveyed theorems: uniform (l_infinity) consistency of the MLE at the optimal ER-sparsity threshold p_n >~ (log n)/n (extension from the earlier suboptimal (log n)^3/n); PL mixture non-identifiable if H >= (n+1)/2 when each edge contains all n objects, generically identifiable if 1 <= H <= floor((n-2)/2)! and n >= 6; BT mixture with H=2 generically identifiable on a complete graph if n >= 5; sports datasets catalogued: ATP tennis 130K comparisons/1.8K objects, club football 230.6K/1.2K, NBA 72.6K/30, NFL 5.3K/32, Hong Kong horse racing 6.3K/2.8K, Pokémon battles 50K/800, StarCraft II 374.8K/10.8K, top-player chess 65K; sports datasets split into a dense regime (|E| = O(n^2), e.g., NFL/NBA round-robin) and sparse regime (|E| = O(n log n), e.g., tennis/chess/esports).

Ayana et al. (2025) test soccer goal timing against a uniform-rate null with the average goals-per-minute rate Gbar = (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N (G_i / T_i) (Eq. 1 — the paper's only equation), simulating 6,000,000 null games with goals at rate Gbar and average game length Tbar, each goal randomly assigned 50/50 to the two teams; comparisons vs null use goal-timing histograms (chi^2), inter-goal time distributions via exponential-decay fit and chi^2, same-team vs opposing-team next-goal splits, and time remaining when the last goal is scored.

On 3,433 StatsBomb matches (21 leagues/competitions), goal timing deviates from uniform: frequency increases as the match progresses (r approx 0.438, p approx 7.13e-6; chi^2 approx 288.62, p = 3.72e-21); fewer-than-expected goals in the early minutes of each half and a dip between minutes 45 and 50 (halftime restart); inter-goal times follow exponential decay in both observed and null (chi^2 approx 0.044, p = 1) — clustering of goals shortly after a previous goal is explained by time-dependent rate structure, not mentality/cadence shifts.

The same-team vs opposing-team finding: the same team scores the next goal more often than the opposing team across all intervals (bursty behavior), with a large observed-vs-null gap at short intervals (0 to ~30 minutes) — the same team is more likely than expected immediately after scoring and the opposing team less likely than expected; the paper's in-file caveat is that burstiness is partially confounded by team-strength heterogeneity (null assigns goals 50/50 ignoring skill).

Peters & Pacheco (2023) tested whether individual player lineups beat team-level aggregates for predicting soccer final scores on 680 chronological EPL matches (2020-2022, last 100 as test), fitting two independent regressions per match (home goals, away goals) and evaluating on a 4-part scorecard: (i) fitness (MAE, RMSE, R^2), (ii) real-world standings (Kendall tau rank correlation of reconstructed table, top-4 accuracy, relegation accuracy), (iii) flat-stake betting sim (£1 bet per predicted exact scoreline, winnings = stake x odds, starting pot £0); feature sets were Players (1 home / -1 away / 0 neither), Lineup Stats (52 per-position-group season-to-date averages for the starting XI), and Team Stats (same 52 features squad-averaged ignoring lineups).

Fitness-best did not equal betting-best: home goals best fitness was Lineup Stats SVR (MAE 0.89, RMSE 1.16, R^2 0.17) and away goals best was Team Stats SVR (MAE 0.87, RMSE 1.14, R^2 0.20), but the flat £1-betting sim over 100 test bets gave Team Stats KNN +£42.5 (42% ROI, best) while the best-fitness model (Lineup Stats SVR) lost -£30.9; Players models were all deeply negative (-£37 to -£90); heuristics were Home Win MAE 1.12/R^2 -0.23, Tradition 1.0/-0.30, Recency 1.41/-1.06; Players LR was degenerate (MAE <<1, R^2 -1.97 — encoding failure). The paper reported no significance tests on betting profits and no multiple-comparison correction across 18 models.

The chi^2 feature-importance ranking found goalkeeper stats ranked #1 and #2 for both models (away keeper clean sheets 420.0, away keeper goals against 80.5 for the home model; home keeper clean sheets 405.0, home keeper goals against 96.5 for the away model) with attacker goals conspicuously absent and goal-creating actions ranking 3-5; standings reconstruction gave Kendall tau of Players 0.232 (best), Team Stats 0.053, Lineup Stats -0.021; top-4 accuracy was 50% for all ML models; relegation was 100% for Lineup Stats and Team Stats, 67% for Players.

Vohra & Gordon (2021) model ODI cricket as a Markov Reward Process with Monte Carlo value learning (reward = fraction of total runs scored in the state) using a neural-network value-function approximator (5 input neurons first innings / 6 in second innings, hidden layers, 1 output = value = % scoring resources remaining); state spaces are first innings [51, 11, 50, 6, 2] and second innings [51, 11, 50, 50, 6, 2] (over, wickets lost, score band in 10-run intervals, ball-in-over, extra indicator; second innings adds target band); the scoring predictor is PredictedScore = ceil(CurrentScore / (1 - r)) where r = resources remaining (Eq. 1), with %Error = (Predicted - Actual)/Actual x 100 averaged per fold (Eq. 2).

The neural value model vs Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (10-fold CV, random interruption after over 20): first innings best net mean % error range -2.11% to -0.11% vs DLS 2.77% to 5.41% (model underestimates slightly, DLS overestimates with larger magnitude); second innings best -0.96% to 1.82% vs DLS 2.06% to 4.54%; the headline 'up to 10 times improved accuracy' is a ratio of small percentages (first innings -1.11% vs 4.27% approx 3.8x; second innings 0.43% vs 4.35% approx 10x) with absolute improvement ~3 points.

The cricket inverse-RL (first innings only) used an MDP with actions = {dot ball (0), 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 runs} and linear reward r(s,a) = x_1 s_1 + ... + x_5 s_5 (a=0, dot ball) and x_1 s_1 + ... + x_5 s_5 + y_a*1000*a otherwise (Eq. 3), with objective maximize sum_i p(V^{pi*}(s_0) - V^{pi_i}(s_0)) where p = squared Euclidean distance (Eq. 4, Ng & Russell 2000 form) and expert strategies = action sequences of WINNING teams; the inferred coefficients showed state features 1 (over), 3 (score band), 4, 5 hitting the upper bound 1.0 (constraint-bound, unidentified per the ledger's critique) with wickets lost the ONLY negative coefficient; action coefficients: 2 runs = 1.0 (highest), 4 runs second, 6 runs just above 0.5, 1 run low, 3 runs lowest.

The optimal batting policy inferred: win by losing fewer wickets and batting the full 50 overs; dot balls valuable early and after wicket clusters; singles valuable early; fours the highest-value action (declining as wickets fall); sixes valuable late with more than half the wickets in hand; linearity forces action rankings to be state-independent (flagged limitation); the game simulator with optimal actions won 82% of 100 simulations vs 50% using transition probabilities only, but was evaluated in-sample (optimistic).

Brown (2008, Annals of Applied Statistics) gives the canonical field test of empirical-Bayes shrinkage for in-season MLB batting-average prediction using the variance-stabilizing transform X_i = arcsin(sqrt((H_i+1/4)/(N_i+1/2))), theta_i = arcsin(sqrt(p_i)), giving X_i ~ N(theta_i, sigma_i^2) with sigma_i^2 = 1/(4N_i) (Eqs. 3.1-3.2), under the constant-ability assumption theta_ji = theta_i across halves (Eq. 3.3); validation used SSPE[delta] = sum_{i in S1 intersect S2} (X_2i - delta_i)^2 (Eq. 3.4) and normalized TSE*[delta] = TSE[delta]/TSE[delta_0] with the naive estimator delta_0(X_1i) = X_1i as the unit baseline (Eq. 3.5).

The parametric EB method-of-moments estimator has the Bayes form theta_i^Bayes = mu + tau^2/(tau^2 + sigma_1i^2)*(X_1i - mu) (Eqs. 4.3-4.4); on all batters, TSE* (naive=1): grand mean 0.852, EB(MM) 0.593, EB(ML) 0.902, NPEB 0.508, harmonic prior 0.884, James-Stein 0.525 (best order: NPEB, J-S, EB(MM)); under weighted TWSE James-Stein is best (0.502); within homogeneous subgroups the grand mean is nearly unbeatable (pitchers: mean 0.127 vs naive 1; nonpitchers: mean 0.378).

The batting-average study's assumption-violation checks: N-X correlation violates every estimator's motivating assumptions (R^2 = 0.25 overall, 0.19 for nonpitchers — pitchers have few at-bats and low averages); the {theta_i} is a two-component mixture rather than normal, which hurts EB(ML) and the harmonic prior most; simulations showed pairwise TSE* differences have SD 0.05-0.20, so fine-grained estimator rankings may not be stable across seasons; Section 7 found the binomial-model assumption empirically adequate and no hot-hand effect (conditional on the constant-ability framework); the ledger's verdict is REJECT (no NFL transfer) but keeps it as a citable shrinkage-estimator precedent.

Bonidia et al. (2018, arXiv:1810.12850v1) systematically reviewed 31 included papers on computational-intelligence techniques in sports (2010-2018 window): 1,582 titles retrieved from ACM (493), IEEE (517), ScienceDirect (72), Semantic Scholar (500); peak years 2014 and 2016 (6 papers each); technique shares: classification 51.28%, clustering 17.95%, heuristics 15.39%, association 12.82%, regression 2.56%; the only formula stated is Bayes' theorem P(H|E) = P(E|H)*P(H)/P(E); the reader's verdict is REJECT (dated, coarse, superseded by GSE's 2026 corpus).

Mlynczak & Krysztofiak (2018, arXiv:1807.03152) ran six off-the-shelf R causal-discovery algorithms (Generalized Correlations, CAM with selGAM pruning, FGES, GFCI, Hill-Climbing, Tabu Search) on resting ECG + breathing parameters of 100 elite Olympic athletes (National Centre for Sports Medicine, Warsaw; 6-min supine + 6-min standing); breathing regularity was defined as BR = (100 - 20*(tanh(sigma_iRR/iRRbar) + tanh(sigma_InsT/InsTbar) + tanh(sigma_ExpT/ExpTbar) + tanh(sigma_InsV/InsVbar) + tanh(sigma_ExpV/ExpVbar))) [%]; supine results: 5/6 methods agreed cInsT -> cExpT and cInsV -> cExpV, all agreed cExpV -> cExpT and cInsV -> cExpT, but cardiac direction was ambiguous; five candidate 3-node paths via Sobel mediation were all non-significant; the authors' own summary: cardiorespiratory path discovery 'appears ambiguous', effects 'mild'; verdict REJECT for the engine (no NFL-transferable data).

The reusable method note from the cardiorespiratory paper is its cross-method agreement protocol: report only edges supported by >=3 of the 6 discovery algorithms spanning constraint-based, score-based, and asymmetry families — a cheap robustness screen for any future DAG-based variable selection.
In sports betting economics, the implicit 'betting price' per euro wagered is defined as the overround-derived margin p = 1 minus the sum of reciprocal decimal odds.

Germany's July 2012 5%-on-turnover sports-betting tax was passed through to consumers at an average rate of 76% (difference-in-differences coefficient 0.038, SE 0.004); excluding cross-leagues 82%; near 100% with a restrictive foreign-domain control group.

Bookmakers that 'shrouded' the tax (surcharge added at checkout rather than in posted odds) passed 90% of the tax to consumers (posted prices fell ~10%), versus only 16% for non-shrouding agencies — an ~80 percentage point gap that is descriptive rather than strictly causal because shrouding is endogenous.
8 of 10 German-targeting agencies were shrouding the betting tax by end of sample, 6 of them within 6 months of the reform; average betting price was 0.0706 overall and 0.0734 for soccer.

The pass-through of Germany's 2012 betting tax rose over time: ~70% in the first four quarters, ~80% after one year, reaching ~0.045 absolute by end of sample, while German betting revenues grew similarly to other European countries — implying limited corrective effect of the tax.
Optimal-tax theory invoked in the paper (Farhi & Gabaix 2020): the optimal sin tax equals the average marginal mistake divided by the tax-salience parameter theta.
equation: optimal sin tax = average marginal mistake / θ

claim: The paper estimated pass-through with a difference-in-differences two-way fixed-effects regression of betting price on treatment-times-post (German-targeting agency times post-July-2012), with agency and time fixed effects and homogeneous treatment timing, plus an event-study parallel-trends check.

The study scraped oddsportal.com and Tipico to build an agency-by-time panel of effective margins covering 68 online agencies (55 unique brands), over 80,000 events, 16 leagues, 6 countries, 5 sports, 2008-2018, using pre-match closing odds plus a manual audit of betting slips to classify shrouding policies.

SAIL (Skill Abstraction with Interpretable Latents) learns persistent disentangled player-skill embeddings z_s in R^d from trajectory data by blending per-subskill novice-expert basis pairs: bar-B_bullet(z_s,c) = sum_j w_bullet^(j)(z_s,c) B_bullet^(j)(c) for bullet in {exp, nov}, and tau-hat_{z_s} = alpha elementwise-multiply bar-B_exp(z_s,c) + (1-alpha) elementwise-multiply bar-B_nov(z_s,c).
equation: B̄_•(z_s,c) = Σ_j w_•^(j)(z_s,c) B_•^(j)(c), • ∈ {exp, nov}; τ̂_{z_s} = α ⊙ B̄_exp(z_s,c) + (1−α) ⊙ B̄_nov(z_s,c)

claim: SAIL's training loss is a weighted sum of trajectory, metric, and mutual-information losses: L = lambda_traj L_traj + lambda_metric L_metric + lambda_MI L_MI, where L_MI = -E_{tau-hat ~ p_phi(tau-hat|z_s,c)}[log q_theta(z_s|tau-hat)] is a variational MI lower bound that guards against posterior collapse.
equation: ℒ = λ_traj ℒ_traj + λ_metric ℒ_metric + λ_MI ℒ_MI; ℒ_MI = −E_{τ̂∼p_φ(τ̂|z_s,c)}[log q_θ(z_s|τ̂)]

claim: SAIL on 95 racing participants (1,545 laps): silhouette 0.72 (0.08), test-retest reliability 0.995 (0.003), in-context RMSE 2.75 (0.12), out-of-context RMSE 6.37 (3.0); the without-basis ablation nearly doubled error (5.05/12.77).

SAIL disentanglement quality: AR 3.25 (0.79), TCI 0.93 (0.06), RIR 2.11 (0.46), interpretability 3.0 (best); removing counterfactual subskill swaps collapsed AR to 1.24 and interpretability to 1.37, while beta-VAE and AE baselines scored near 0 on several composites.

In SAIL's downstream AI-coaching task, conditioning on the learned skill embeddings gave weighted F1 0.595 vs 0.573 trial-time-conditioned vs 0.541 unconditioned — a 10.0% relative lift, paired t(14)=2.50, p=0.025 — and embedding quality correlated with a professional coach's ratings at Spearman rho = 0.81, p<0.001, 95% bootstrap CI [0.56, 0.94], n=22.
SAIL's supplemental baseball experiment (13 semi-pro players, 74 batting trials, optical motion capture, 3 subskills) achieved test-retest 1.000, in-context RMSE 0.161, and AR 0.758.

SAIL enforces disentanglement via counterfactual subskill swaps, where the k-th slice of an embedding is replaced by a donor's slice (z-tilde_orig^(k) = z_donor^(k), remaining slices fixed) and the metric loss is applied only for the swapped subskill.

Sathya Ramesh et al. (2019) estimate win probability empirically as P(Win | PS) = the historical win percentage of teams whose point spread was PS, a non-parametric mapping with no normality assumption that uses only games concluded before the game being priced.
equation: P(Win | PS) = Historical Win % of Teams with Point Spread = PS

claim: The paper's expected-value screen is Expected Value = [P(Winning) x Payout] - P(Losing) on a $1 bet, using the maximum moneyline payout across the 16-casino panel, with two hyperparameters: epsilon threshold (bet outside the 0.5-epsilon, 0.5+epsilon band = always take favorite) and EV threshold tau (bet only if EV > tau), chosen per sport to maximize Total Return = ROI x N.
Pure +EV bets with no thresholds (Simple strategy, 2009-2017 window) returned ROI: NFL 10.81% (742 bets, n=922 games), NBA 3.42%, NCAAF -2.49%, NCAAB -1.10%, WNBA 4.38%.

With optimally tuned epsilon and tau, Simple-strategy ROI rose to NFL 16.57% (tau=0.013, 567 bets), NBA 9.04%, NCAAF 7.29%, NCAAB 4.07%, WNBA 17.01%, but year-by-year variance was extreme (NFL 2011 +76.03% vs 2013 -15.16%; all-leagues peak 29.09% in 2015).

A 10,000-resample-per-sport bootstrap grid-searching epsilon (step 0.01) and tau (step 0.001) showed all ROI and epsilon 95% CIs excluding zero, including Bonferroni-corrected one-sided 99% CIs (e.g., NFL Simple ROI CI (8.11, 82.85)).

The deep-read ledger flags three hard limitations in 'Beating the House': epsilon/tau were tuned in-sample on the same 2009-2017 data used to report ROI (no true holdout), EV uses the unachievable panel-maximum payout, and stationarity of the 1990-2017 spread-outcome table is assumed — with thin WNBA (255 games) and NCAAB samples.

The study's data panel combined 16 Las Vegas casino sportsbooks via vegasinsider.com (spread + moneyline panels; older movements from archive.org snapshots) with historical spread-to-outcome data 1990-2017, restricting college games to Power-Five members and excluding preseason/exhibition.

Field Converter (Khan et al. 2026) is a two-stage pipeline for world-grounded player pose estimation from soccer broadcasts: Stage 1 initializes each player's root position by casting a ray from the camera center through the detected root keypoint and intersecting it with the pitch plane; Stage 2 (a TCN with 41-frame windows, stride 8, five residual blocks, dilations (1,2,4,8,16), 1.278M parameters) predicts only the residual correction on top of that geometric initialization, never absolute position.

On the test set, geometry-only initialization gave root error 48.58 cm, reduced by residual refinement to 13.63 cm (MLP), 10.12 cm (TCN), 11.04 cm (Transformer); world MPJPE fell 48.36 to 13.20 cm (TCN); reprojection error fell 5.39 to 3.43 px.

Direct absolute-root prediction without geometric initialization failed badly (MLP 256.00 cm, TCN 63.05 cm root error), demonstrating that the geometric initialization does most of the work and the network only refines.

Field Converter degrades on airborne frames: ~37 cm error in the highest foot-clearance interval versus grounded frames (~1 m for geometry-only), and depth (camera z-axis) remains the dominant error component after refinement; local MPJPE was identical 7.74 cm across all variants — the contribution is purely global localization, not pose quality.

The FIFA Skeletal Tracking Light 2026 dataset used for Field Converter contains 89 clips from 8 matches with ~2.41M valid player-frame observations (per-frame video, 2D keypoints, boxes, per-clip camera calibration; SAM 3D Body relative-pose reference), split match-disjoint: 62 clips/6 matches train, 12 clips (BRA_KOR) val, 15 clips (ENG_FRA) test.

Time-Aware Synthetic Control (TASC, Rho et al. 2026) replaces permutation-invariant synthetic control with a linear-Gaussian state-space model x_t = A x_{t-1} + q_{t-1}, q ~ N(0,Q); y_t = H x_t + r_t, r ~ N(0,R); x_0 ~ N(m_0, P_0), with hidden dim d << min(n,T), learned by EM (Kalman filter forward + RTS smoother backward E-step, closed-form M-step).

TASC's EM M-step has closed forms: A' = C Phi^{-1}, H' = B Sigma^{-1}, Q' = Diag(Sigma - 2CA^T + A Phi A^T), R' = Diag(D - 2BH^T + H Sigma H^T), m'_0 = m^s_0, P'_0 = P^s_0 + (m^s_0 - m_0)(m^s_0 - m_0)^T, with complexity O(N1 * T0 * N^3).
equation: A′ = CΦ⁻¹, H′ = BΣ⁻¹, Q′ = Diag(Σ − 2CA⊤ + AΦA⊤), R′ = Diag(D − 2BH⊤ + HΣH⊤), m′_0 = m^s_0, P′_0 = P^s_0 + (m^s_0 − m_0)(m^s_0 − m_0)⊤

claim: TASC theory (Prop. A.1): the Kalman filtered state and covariance are minimal sufficient statistics for forecasting, so by the data-processing inequality the Kalman-based predictor weakly MSE-dominates any permutation-invariant predictor (strict when A != 0).

TASC builds counterfactuals by setting the target's post-intervention observation variance r_1 to infinity (driving the Kalman gain for the target coordinate to zero) and predicting y-hat_{0,t} = h_1^T m^s_t for t > T0, with 95% CIs from the latent-state covariance that are narrower than CIM's MCMC intervals.

A permutation stress test confirmed TASC exploits temporal order: permuting time indices raised TASC post-intervention RMSE by mean +48.5% (std +25.7%), while classical SC/RSC were unchanged by design.

On IPL cricket ball-by-ball data (1,524 innings, T=120, placebo T0=72), TASC had the lowest median RMSE for donor pools n in {36,72,144}, best overall 7.88 at n=72; on NBA play-by-play (7,574 games Jan 2020-Jun 2023, T=192, placebo halftime), TASC was lowest across all donor sizes and best at n=192, with the gap widening late in Q4.

In the Prop 99 (California 1988 tobacco tax) placebo test, TASC had the lowest median RMSE and smallest variance with d=2 optimal; California's learned observation variance was 2.58 versus donor median 12.95 (std 36.17, max 170.79).

TASC limitations per the ledger: univariate only; linear time-invariant trend A (misspecification-prone); EM is slow and initialization-sensitive; no non-negativity/sum-to-one constraints so it can extrapolate outside the donor convex hull; the cricket/NBA 'interventions' are placebos that validate forecasting, not causal identification; underestimating latent dim d hurts more than overestimating.

UMEG-Net (Liu et al. 2025) encodes each video frame as a unified multi-entity graph G_t = (V_t, E_t) with nodes V_t = {Vpt (N persons x K joints), Vbt (ball keypoints), Vct (court-corner keypoints)}, |V_t| = N*K + |Vbt| + |Vct|, and edges E_t = E_t^intra union E_t^{p-b} union E_t^{p-c} union E_t^{c-c} (skeletal topology; court corners as rectangle; sport-specific player-to-ball links; feet-to-court-corners), all undirected.
equation: G_t = (V_t, E_t); |V_t| = N·K + |Vbt| + |Vct|; E_t = E_t^intra ∪ E_t^{p–b} ∪ E_t^{p–c} ∪ E_t^{c–c}

claim: UMEG-Net's encoder stacks UMEG Blocks = spatial GCN (H^(l+1) = ReLU(A^(l) H^(l) W^(l))) + a parameter-free temporal multi-scale shift (channels split static/forward/backward with alpha=1/8, bidirectional shift at deltas in {1,2,4} frames, fused via downscale-floor(d/|delta|), concat, ReLU, residual add, upscale-d).

With only 100 labeled clips (F1evt / Edit; 2.2M params, fewest of all compared methods), UMEG-Net was best in all 10 cells: Tennis 9.4/31.7, ShuttleSet 49.2/64.0, FineGym-BB 49.2/54.4, Figure Skating 39.2/49.6, SoccerNet-BAS 27.0/44.8 — best RGB baseline F3 ED managed only 3.9/15.3 on tennis, showing few-shot collapses RGB-only methods.

Distilling the frozen graph teacher (per-frame loss L_feat = (1/T) sum_t ||F_tch^(t) - F_stu^(t)||^2_2 on all unlabeled clips) into a VideoMAEv2-plus-bidirectional-GRU RGB student lifted scores by average +5.8% F1evt / +6.7% Edit over the teacher (67.8M params: tennis 12.5/40.7, ShuttleSet 59.1/69.0, FineGym-BB 58.4/61.2, FigSkating 45.9/56.2, SoccerNet-BAS 27.1/50.8) and decisively beat contrastive self-supervision (FineGym-BB 58.4/61.2 vs 54.5/56.8).

UMEG-Net ablations: adding entities pose-alone to plus-ball to plus-court to all raised tennis F1evt 5.6 -> 8.6 (ball) -> 6.6 (court) -> 9.4 (all), making the ball the highest-value entity; temporal scales {1,2,4} beat {1} on ShuttleSet (49.2/64.0 vs 46.5/61.2).

Under full supervision UMEG-Net was competitive with E2E-Spot — better on 3/5 datasets (tennis 47.5/71.2 vs 44.6/71.1; ShuttleSet 71.4/76.1 vs 71.2/76.1; FigSkating 61.8/71.8 vs 58.0/63.9) and led at every labeled-clip count k in {15,25,50,100}.

UMEG-Net's smallest gains were on the densest dataset (SoccerNet-BAS: 27.0 vs 22.7 F1evt over baseline), and its graph quality is bounded by off-the-shelf detectors (HRNet poses, YOLOv8 ball/player, court-corner detectors, TrackNetV3 shuttlecock); edge rules are sport-specific heuristics and weak/non-entity events like off-ball fouls are unhandled; no football data was tested.

The arXiv badminton smash-speed system (Diwen Huang, arXiv:2509.05334v1) was REJECTED in the deep read: on 20 smashes by a single player versus a Bushnell Speedster III radar gun, vision-vs-radar disagreement was MAE 66.41 km/h and RMSE 74.68 km/h — roughly 20-30% relative error on typical 200-400 km/h smashes — with manual trajectory correction allowed during validation.

The badminton system fused detection with a composite score S = 0.3*C_YOLO + 0.7*P_K, where the Kalman proximity score P_K = max(0, 1 - d/(W_frame/4)) rewards detections near the Kalman-expected region (d = distance, W_frame = frame width); detector ran YOLOv5 at confidence 0.1, IoU 0.45 on strictly perpendicular video.

The system's speed formula was v = (delta-pixels / delta-t) x S_f x 3.6 (km/h), with scale factor S_f = d_real / d_pixel supplied by the user (e.g., a measured court dimension on screen), so user measurement error propagates 1:1 into every speed estimate; implied speeds below 5 or above 375 km/h were rejected as invalid.
equation: v = (Δpixels / Δt) × S_f × 3.6; S_f = d_real / d_pixel

claim: At 30 fps a ~300 km/h shuttlecock moves ~2.8 m per frame, so the reported 'peak' speed is an aliased sample of the true peak; the validation had no train/test split for the speed estimator, no cross-player/cross-device/cross-venue validation, no confidence intervals, and no baseline comparison — though the detector itself scored 93% precision, 87% recall, 91% mAP@0.5 on the custom 15,000-image set.

The 'Light Future' future-frame-prediction paper (arXiv:2507.14809v2, fine-tuning InstructPix2Pix to predict 100 frames ahead on RoboTwin robot simulation) was REJECTED in the deep read: zero sports experiments, and its headline SOTA table compares every baseline on a different dataset (ConvLSTM on Moving MNIST, VDM on UCF-101, MAGVITv2 on BAIR, InstructPix2Pix-FT on RoboTwin) — a void comparison.

Light Future's training objective was theta* = argmin_theta E[L(f_theta(I_t, T), I_{t+delta-t})] with delta-t = 100 frames and composite loss L = lambda_1 L_diff + lambda_2 L_perc + lambda_3 L_adv with weights 1.0/0.1/0.01; inference used 100-step DDIM with classifier-free guidance epsilon_theta(z_t,c) = w*epsilon_theta(z_t,c) + (1-w)*epsilon_theta(z_t, empty).
equation: L = λ_1 L_diff + λ_2 L_perc + λ_3 L_adv; ε_θ(z_t,c) = w·ε_θ(z_t,c) + (1−w)·ε_θ(z_t,∅)

claim: Light Future's stage-2 training pairs were sampled every 10 frames from the same ~400-frame episodes (0->100, 10->110, ...), creating near-duplicate train/test frames, so the reported 0.9823 SSIM / 59.41 dB PSNR are consistent with memorized backgrounds rather than prediction skill; the paper claims motion-trajectory precision is the priority but measures only SSIM/PSNR, never quantifying trajectory accuracy.

SoccerChat (arXiv:2505.16630) fine-tuned Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct on a 49,120-QA instruction dataset built from SoccerNet (500 matches, ~764 h, ~300k events in 17 classes): plus/minus-5 s clip extraction around event labels, consecutive-event pairing (1-7 s apart), caption/commentary alignment (captions +3 to +10 s, replay ASR filtered), GPT-3.5 250-300-word descriptions, two QA types (overview-based, detail-based), and jersey-color anonymization ('red-jerseyed team') to force event-dynamics learning over name memorization.
SoccerChat's visual token budget arithmetic: 24 frames per segment at 2.4 FPS x up to 128 visual tokens per frame (16:9 -> 112 patches) = 2,688 tokens per 10-s segment.

On referee QA (XFoul), mean QwQ scores were Q2VL-XF 6.81 (best), SC+XF 6.46, SC-FT-XF 6.14, SoccerChat 3.37, X-VARS 2.91, base Q2VL 2.58 — X-VARS, trained exclusively on XFoul data, scored near the untrained base, showing general pretraining strength dominates narrow fine-tuning data; joint multi-dataset training (SC+XF) beat sequential fine-tuning (SC-FT-XF), which showed catastrophic forgetting on the 16-class task (4.00 vs 6.15).

On six-class soccer action classification, SoccerChat reached mean QwQ 6.80 and weighted F1 0.57 (vs Q2VL base 0.17); but all evaluation rests on the QwQ LLM-as-judge with no human-correlation validation, scores reported as means with no confidence intervals or significance tests, and the data is research-licensed SoccerNet only.

ST-VLM (arXiv:2503.19355v2) fine-tuned a 7B video VLM on 116K kinematic QA pairs; traveled distance = sum_{t=s}^{e-1} ||P_{t+1}^{(i)} - P_t^{(i)}||_2 (frame-to-frame 3D displacements) and speed = distance/(e-s), with direction theta_t = arccos(((P_{t+1}^{(i)}-P_t^{(i)}) dot (P_{s+1}^{(i)}-P_s^{(i)})) / (||P_{t+1}^{(i)}-P_t^{(i)}|| ||P_{s+1}^{(i)}-P_s^{(i)}||)) discretized to 12 clock-face directions.
ST-VLM-7B scored 59.8% average accuracy on STKit-Bench versus LLaVA-OneVision-7B 27.4% (+32.4 pp), GPT-4V 28.5%, and GPT-4o 26.8%; the abstract claims +31.3% over GPT-4V.

ST-VLM per-task results (accuracy / MAE): traveled distance 49.5% / 25.1 m (vs GPT-4V 4.5% / 33.1 m), speed 42.0% / 11.6 km/h, direction 32.0% / 1.7 clocks, direction timestamp 69.0% / 0.61 IoU, multi-object comparisons 74-76% — precise estimation remains crude despite the accuracy gains.

ST-VLM's data ablation showed pseudo-labeling (MonST3R 4D reconstruction + Metric3Dv2 rescaling + Grounded-SAM2 boxes, ~400 s/video on A6000) added +8.7 pp (no tuning 27.9% -> labeled only 51.1% -> plus pseudo-labels 59.8%); paraphrased questions held at 58.2% average and general video benchmarks improved +2.7 pp (65.6 vs 62.9), ruling out template overfitting.

The ST-VLM paper explicitly EXCLUDES movement direction for sports due to complex 3D trajectories — the one kinematic task most relevant to NFL route/angle analysis is the one it dodges; scoring used distance/speed correct if within ±25% of truth, direction correct on exact clock match, timestamp correct if IoU >= 0.5.

DiffOpt (Heo et al. 2024, arXiv:2411.10582) was REJECTED in the deep read for sports tracking: it is single-human, per-video test-time optimization (SMPL pose + world-frame root trajectory from one moving-camera video) that cannot process 22-player broadcast film at season scale, and its AMASS-trained motion-diffusion prior (ground-plane contact only) degrades on contact-heavy motion like tackles.

DiffOpt's motion-diffusion score-distillation prior is L_Diff = E_{t,epsilon}[w(t) ||epsilon_phi(alpha_t x + sigma_t epsilon, t) - epsilon||^2_2] (DreamFusion-style distillation against the AMASS-trained motion diffusion model), combined with a 3-stage optimization: warm-up L2 fit to HMR2.0 init, alternating human update (L_Diff + warm-up) with camera update on DROID-SLAM outputs (learnable rotation bias, translation scale/bias, focal scale, 2D reprojection loss with Geman-McClure robust error), then joint fine-tune.
equation: L_Diff = E_{t,ε}[w(t)‖ε_φ(α_t x + σ_t ε, t) − ε‖²₂]

claim: On trimmed EMDB (mm, G-MPJPE), DiffOpt scored 322.6, best in 5/7 sequences (paper claims 17% G-MPJPE / 18% G-MPVPE over third-best); on untrimmed EMDB it scored 1776.2, 16% better than second-best GLAMR (2113.5), though GLAMR won local MPJPE (90.4 vs 102.5) — while WHAM returned NaN on 'soccer warmup' and SLAHMR returned NaN on all 17 Egobody sequences (complete optimization failures).

DiffOpt ablations: replacing neural motion fields with learnable tensors added +318.2 G-MPJPE, single-stage optimization added +625.1 (catastrophic), no warm-up +262.1, no MDM step +145.2, no fine-tune +205.0.

'The most exciting game' (Backhoff-Veraguas & Beiglbock 2023, arXiv:2305.14037v2) was REJECTED in the deep read: a pure stochastic-analysis paper with no data and no empirical validation — its continuous-path/no-jump idealization (Bernoulli terminal law, no draws, time normalized to [0,1]) is badly mismatched to NFL win probability, which resolves via discrete jumps on discrete plays.

The paper's main theorem (Eq. 1.2): the unique maximum-entropy win-probability martingale satisfies dM_t = sin(pi M_t)/(pi sqrt(1-t)) dB_t with M_0 = x_0, minimizing specific relative entropy with respect to Wiener measure.

The paper defines specific relative entropy h(Q|W^{x_0}) = 1/2 E_Q[integral_0^1 {Sigma_t - log(Sigma_t) - 1} dt] (Eq. 1.3), where Sigma_t is the quadratic-variation density; the closed-form optimal value is (x_0(1-x_0)-1)/2 - log(sin(pi x_0)/pi), which at x_0 = 0.5 equals approximately 0.7696.

In discrete time, maximizing Shannon entropy over martingale transport plans equals minimizing relative entropy with respect to the discretized Wiener measure (telescoping identity) — the justification bridging the paper's discrete setup to the continuous SDE.

Lopez (2019, arXiv:1909.10631v3) showed the famous 'go for it on 4th down' benefit was overstated ~40% because play-by-play records only integer distance-to-go while teams self-select on precise distance: on 4th-and-1, go-teams' median was 0.70 yards from the line vs 0.98 for no-go teams (0.28-yard gap); GAM estimates show 4th-and-inches was attempted ~70% of the time vs ~30% for long 4th-and-1, with conversion ~79% vs ~55%.

Replicating the 4th-down aggressiveness value analysis with integer distance gave +0.35 wins/team/year and 3.8% per-play win-probability-added (95% CI 2.6%-4.9%), while precise tracking-derived distance gave +0.22 wins/team/year and 2.2% (95% CI 0.6%-3.4%) — roughly 40% of the benefit negated, though the CIs overlap substantially so the magnitude is noisy.

The 'squeezing the balloon' diagnostic: conditioning on the 17-variable play-by-play covariate set (yardline, time, score, timeouts, pre-play WP) actually widened the precise-distance imbalance between go and no-go teams — among low-go-probability teams, go-teams were more than half a yard closer — meaning matching on observables can increase imbalance on unobserved tracking covariates.

The NGS tracking-data engineering spec published in the paper: x/y for all 22 players plus ball at ~10 fps from RFID chips, 250,000-350,000 rows/game, no z-coordinate, location accurate to ±12 inches and reliable on 99.999% of players/games over three seasons (football coordinates slightly less reliable), field coordinates fixed per stadium (x: 0-120, y: 0-160/3), ~half of offensive plays must be flipped (x->120-x, y->160/3-y), max speed sometimes recorded during/after a tackle, and year-to-year speed differences after tag updates.

Wolfson & Koopmeiners (2015, arXiv:1501.07179v1) compared information-per-game across leagues with Bradley-Terry logit(pi_{i,j}) = beta_i - beta_j + alpha (alpha = home advantage) and margin-of-victory mu_{i,j} = delta_i - delta_j + lambda, fitting on random within-season subsamples (12.5%-87.5%, 100 reps) and predicting the rest.
equation: logit(π_{i,j}) = β_i − β_j + α; μ_{i,j} = δ_i − δ_j + λ

claim: The NBA was the most predictable league (up to 70% accuracy with 87.5% training; home teams won ~60%, the largest home edge) and accuracy plateaued — 'no better when 75% of games were included than when 25% were' (~25-30 games); the NFL never plateaued within a season — accuracy kept improving as more games were added, worth ~1.4 pp accuracy per game at 87.5% training.

MLB never exceeded 58% accuracy even with 140 games (7/8 of a season) as training and NHL never exceeded 60% (only in 2005-06 when home win probability was 58%); both were rarely more than 2-3 pp better than an always-pick-home baseline, which beat the half-season paired-comparison models in 2007-08 and 2011-12.

Odds ratios versus the always-home baseline at 87.5% training: NBA 1.41, NFL 1.46, NHL 1.09, MLB 1.06; per-game accuracy gains: NBA 0.34 pp, NFL 1.4 pp, NHL 0.13 pp, MLB 0.053 pp; margin of victory added virtually nothing in the NBA ('slightly worse predictions during the 05-06 season').

The paper's central design flaw for deployment: random within-season subsamples use future games to estimate team strength — lookahead bias by construction — so it measures information content, not forecastability; the portable contribution is the sample-sufficiency/plateau analysis, which should be rerun chronologically (rolling-origin, decay-weighted) rather than via random splits.

Goals-above-expected (GAX) is defined as GAX = sum_i (G_i - xG_i), and the Davis & Robberechts (2024, arXiv:2401.09940v2) paper shows these residuals are confounded by training-data composition: elite high-volume finishers over-contribute to the xG training set, so the model misprices their shots and part of the measured 'skill' is self-contamination.

The paper's remedy is multi-calibration: calibrate separately within groups g = position x smoothed shot-volume bin (low < 0.875 shots/90, high > 2.526 shots/90), pulling group xG toward the group's empirical conversion rate with a prior weight of 270 minutes at the position prior (attacker 2.1, midfielder 1.1, defender 0.4 per 90).

Simulation evidence that single-season GAX is mostly noise: a +25% finisher at 150 shots/season has mean GAX 3.70 with SD 3.73 (10,000 repetitions per skill-multiplier/volume cell); a +25% finisher with 100 shots/season outperforms xG in at least 4 of 5 seasons only 70.0% of the time, and a +10% finisher with 125 shots only 41.6% of the time.

The Messi contamination experiment: injecting 4,000 shots from a +25% finisher into xG training dropped Messi's measured GAX from 127.6 to 120.8 (>5%); under the corrected multi-calibrated baseline his GAX instead rose from 127.57 to 149.99 (~17% increase) — Messi's actual record was 375 goals from 1,862 open-play shots.

Mahrez's GAX was 14.61 including deflected shots versus 9.03 excluding them (5.9% of his 289 shots were deflected), showing deflections inflate apparent finishing skill — atypical plays must be excluded from both training and residual evaluation.
For 2015/16 EPL players with >=5 goals (n=63): 50 exceeded standard xG (avg 16.72%), 51 exceeded multi-calibrated xG (avg 20.00%), and 47 exceeded StatsBomb proprietary xG (avg 12.78%).

Kharrat, Lopez Pena & McHale (2017, arXiv:1706.04943v1) adapted basketball-style adjusted plus-minus to soccer using maximal fixed-22-player-lineup segments (129,988 segments from 20,868 games) with design matrix x_tj = +1 home / -1 away / 0 off pitch, estimated by ridge regression alpha-hat = (X^T X + lambda^2 I)^{-1} X^T y (glmnet, multi-response Gaussian, group penalty), preferring ridge over lasso so always-together players split credit equally.

The soccer APM model used time decay w_i = exp(zeta (date_i - ratingDate)/3.5) in half-week units with best hyperparameters lambda=0.042, zeta=0.002, tuned via an ordered-probit match-outcome model minimizing out-of-sample Brier score (10-fold CV x 3).

The ordered-probit model with PM ratings achieved Brier 0.292 (sd 0.003) versus bet365 de-vigged 0.295 on the same games — essentially market-level performance; the raw-PM worked example given is ((-1/60)+(2/30))x90 = +4.5 per 90.

Penalty xG is nearly unpredictable: penalty baseline Brier 0.1845-0.185 versus best model 0.1844 ('penalties are truly random'), while open-play xG improved from baseline 0.0836 to best neural net 0.0673, with inverse distance, view angle, and 'big chance' as dominant features.

Estimated red-card effects in the soccer APM: first dismissal -1.25 (PM) / -1.18 (xGPM) / -0.12 (xPPM), second -0.16/-0.15/-0.01, third approximately 0; home advantage was 'surprisingly very small' at ~0.006/0.005/0.0004.

The expected-points target used xP^H_t = 3*P^HW_t + P^D_t with segment target y_[0,60] = delta-xP^H - delta-xP^A; the Brier score for three-way outcomes was BS = (1/N) sum_i sum_{r=1}^3 (p_{ti} - o_{ti})^2.

League-strength estimates via player movers (mean PM): EPL 0.88, Bundesliga 0.75, La Liga 0.64, Serie A 0.64, Russia PL 0.54, Bundesliga II 0.53, Championship 0.48, Liga NOS 0.39, Ligue 1 0.29, Super Lig 0.20, Eredivisie 0.11 — the odd ordering (e.g., Ligue 1 below Russia) suggests mover-identification artifacts.

Pitwall (Santillana 2026, arXiv:2607.06495v1) calibrated its F1 Monte Carlo engine by optimizing J(theta) = rho_Spearman - 2*BS - 1*ECE via bound-constrained differential evolution over a 12-parameter vector inside physically interpretable bounds, pinning discrete switches per run and recalibrating each config independently (gating rule: never score a component under incumbent parameters).

Pitwall's backtest over 157 races (2018-2026): modal winner hit 64.5%, winner in top-3 90.3%, podium recall 72.3%, mean Spearman rho = 0.749 overall and 0.766 held-out, with no drift across the 2022 regulation change; held-out calibration was combined Brier 0.0745, ECE 0.0297 (win Brier 0.0254 with reliability 0.0014, podium 0.0652, points 0.1381).

Pitwall runs counterfactuals under common random numbers: options (box-now vs +1 vs +2 laps vs stay) simulated under the identical random seed, with option deltas delta-hat_h = P-hat_h(ahead) - P-hat_stay(ahead) and 90% percentile-bootstrap CIs (B=500 resamples on the replication axis at zero extra cost); CRN option-delta signs were stable to <+-0.3 pp at N=2,000 replications.

Pitwall's lap-time model is l(t,a) = f_0^(t) + delta^(t) a + 1[a>k^(t)] s^(t) (a-k^(t)) + epsilon with epsilon ~ N(0, sigma^2_lap); the tyre-cliff evidence gate required >=25% SSE reduction over a linear fit with n>=300 laps (37 circuit-compound cliffs passed from 8,278 stints / 191k laps).
equation: ℓ(t,a) = f₀⁽ᵗ⁾ + δ⁽ᵗ⁾a + 𝟙[a>k⁽ᵗ⁾] s⁽ᵗ⁾(a−k⁽ᵗ⁾) + ε, ε∼𝒩(0,σ²lap)

claim: Pitwall's overtake kernel is P(pass) = sigma(AGP + kp*delta-pace + kt*delta-age) with kp = +0.87, kt = +0.46, fitted on 131,000 adjacent-car battles (4,142 clean passes, 3.2% base rate, fitted through 2023, tested 2024+); the undercut logistic scored Brier 0.168 vs climatological 0.188 (BSS 0.107, base rate 25%, N=828) with gap_before_s coefficient -1.21 and tyre-age delta +0.01.
equation: P(pass) = σ(AGP + kpΔpace + ktΔage), kp=+0.87, kt=+0.46

claim: Pitwall's key calibration lesson: the components encoding the most domain knowledge (overtake kernel, compound normalization, rich language targets) were exactly the ones gated OFF the calibrated/production paths — Brier-optimal is not decision-optimal and vividness is not faithfulness; e.g., the 2025 Spanish GP lap-46 box-now call was 72.9% under raw bases vs 23.4% after canonical ordering projection, flipping the recommendation to stay-out.

Pitwall's language layer uses 10 typed claim types with a verifier that checks every extracted claim against engine state before publication; Phi-4-mini runs production (greedy decoding, 8-bit quantization OK, 4-bit reintroduces hallucination) and degrades to generic phrasing on sparse contexts where 1B/7B bases invent drivers; GPT-4o briefing candidates were admitted only with >=1 checkable claim and 0 contradicted claims (2,494/81.9% admitted).

DeepDIVE (Wong et al. 2025, arXiv:2501.08710v2) proves (Proposition 1) that log p_theta(x,y) = L(theta,phi;x,y) + D_KL(q_phi(a,b|x) || p_theta(a,b|x,y)), where L(theta,phi;x,y) = E[log p_theta(y|a,b,x)] (forecast loss) + E[log p_theta(x|a,b)] (reconstruction loss) - D_KL(q_phi(a,b|x) || p_theta(a,b)) — so reconstruction + forecasting provably form a single non-conflicting ELBO on the joint log-likelihood.
equation: L(θ,φ;x,y) = E[log p_θ(y|a,b,x)] + E[log p_θ(x|a,b)] − D_KL(q_φ(a,b|x)‖p_θ(a,b)))

claim: DeepDIVE splits the latent space z=[a||b] into supervised 'marginal' dims b (supervised by sequence-level labels via a Naive-Bayes-derived loss assuming independence among marginal dims conditional on input) and unsupervised 'conditional' dims a, fused via cross-attention; Theorem 1 justifies RBF prior components plus cross-entropy with interleaving training under a mixture-of-log-concave prior.

DeepDIVE on the Gait dataset (30 runs): reconstruction RRSE 11.1627, forecast RRSE 16.0582, MIG 0.0473 — best on all three versus conditional-only (11.8835/16.4434/0.0155), marginal-only (28.2268/27.7309/0.0464), and beta-TCVAE (29.3563/33.7654/0.0081); on Electricity: recon 1.5803, forecast 0.0998 versus conditional-only 2.5562/0.1062.

DeepDIVE collapses at long horizons: at horizon 24 on Electricity it scored RRSE 1.0000 — no better than the mean baseline — while AutoCTS (0.0947) and LightCTS held, so the paper's 'comparable to SOTA' claim holds only for short horizons; multi-task sharing can hurt the primary objective.

DeepDIVE's Naive conditional-independence assumption among marginal dims is violated by its own data (the paper's Fig. 2 shows gait type and stride length are correlated), and Assumption 2 (representative training distribution) explicitly fails on the gait dataset, yet results are reported anyway.
Online calibration error is defined as CE_T = sum_i (N_i^T / T) * |M_i - p_i^T| and epsilon-calibration error as epsilon-CE_T = max(CE_T - epsilon, 0) (Gupta & Ramdas 2022, arXiv:2204.13087v2).
equation: CE_T = Σ_i (N_i^T/T)·|M_i − p_i^T|; ε-CE_T = max(CE_T − ε, 0)

claim: POTC-Cal ('Predict-Then-Choose') is a deterministic online forecasting protocol achieving O(1/T) calibration error on interval forecasts without randomization (Theorem 1: epsilon-CE_T <= m/T), versus the Omega(1/sqrt(T)) lower bound for any classical randomized point-forecasting strategy (Theorem 3) — while deterministic point forecasts are uncalibratable (Theta(1)).

POTC-Cal maintains a 2epsilon-grid {M_1,...,M_m} subset of [0,1], tracks per-bin deficit/excess statistics, and outputs a single point or an adjacent pair (interval width <= 2epsilon) per round, with the realized y_t selecting which endpoint counts; the Bernoulli appendix epoch schedule K_k = ceil((0.85 log T_k/epsilon)^2 * (log log(T_k/2) + 0.72 log(5.2 m T_k^2))) gives E[epsilon-CE_T] <= O(poly log T / T).
equation: K_k = ⌈(0.85 log T_k/ε)²·(log log(T_k/2) + 0.72 log(5.2 m T_k²))⌉

claim: The calibration guarantee covers calibration but not sharpness (a constant 0.5-forecaster is perfectly calibrated); the m/T bound scales with grid size m (fine grids weaken the constant); interval outputs are awkward for point-probability products; and the paper's open problems include a matching lower bound for POTC, more than two choices per round, and multidimensional forecasts.

D'Agostini (2020, arXiv:2012.04455v1) derives the closed-form ratio-of-Gammas (Beta-prime) posterior for the ratio of two Poisson rates: f(rho_z | alpha_1,beta_1,alpha_2,beta_2) = [1/B(alpha_1,alpha_2)] * beta_1^{alpha_1} beta_2^{alpha_2} * rho_z^{alpha_1-1} (beta_2 + rho_z beta_1)^{-(alpha_1+alpha_2)}.

With flat priors, the ratio posterior has closed form f(rho = r_1/r_2 | x_1+1, T_1, x_2+1, T_2) = [(x_1+x_2+1)!/(x_1! x_2!)] * T_1^{x_1+1} T_2^{x_2+1} * rho^{x_1} (T_2 + T_1 rho)^{-(x_1+x_2+2)}, with summaries mode(rho) = (x_1/T_1)/((x_2+2)/T_2), E(rho) = ((x_1+1)/T_1)/(x_2/T_2) for x_2>0, and sigma(rho) = (T_2/T_1)*sqrt[((x_1+1)/x_2)*((x_1+2)/(x_2-1) - (x_1+1)/x_2)] for x_2>1.

Prior elicitation recipe: conjugate Gamma(alpha_0, beta_0) posterior is Gamma(alpha_0+x, beta_0+T), with alpha_0 = mu_0^2/sigma_0^2 and beta_0 = mu_0/sigma_0^2 (eqs. 54-55); a belief r = (5 +/- 2) s^-1 maps to alpha_0 = 6.25, beta_0 = 1.25 s, equivalent to having observed ~5 counts in 1.2 s from a flat start; setting alpha_0 slightly above 1 forbids r=0 while staying vague.

The paper's toy comparison (x_1=3, T_1=3 vs x_2=6, T_2=6) gave Model A [flat on r_1,r_2] rho = 1.33 +/- 0.94 versus Model B [flat on (rho,r_2)] rho = 1.60 +/- 1.20 — wider and shifted — showing rate-ratio inferences are prior-parametrization dependent, which undercuts any claim of objectivity; MCMC histograms agreed 'excellently' with the closed forms.

Cross-influence result: flat priors on r_1, r_2 induce f(rho) = 1/2 for rho <= 1 and 1/(2 rho^2) for rho > 1, so P(1/10 <= rho <= 10) = 9/10; for combining ratios across instances with constant rho, pool counts directly (x_tot = sum x_j, T_tot = sum T_j) rather than taking weighted averages.

Xu Sun (2015, arXiv:1411.6243v2) proposed structure regularization via sample decomposition — splitting structure-size-n training samples into alpha mini-samples of size n/alpha — but the deep-read verdict is REJECT: it is NLP sequence-labeling theory/experiments (CRFs, structured perceptrons) with no transfer path to NFL pick modeling.

Structure regularization's decomposed objective is R_{alpha,lambda}(g) = (1/(mn)) sum_{j=1}^{m alpha} L_tau(g, z'_j) + (lambda/2) ||g||^2_2 with alpha in [1,n]; Theorem 9 gives a generalization bound R(f) <= R_e(f) + 2 tau Delta-bar + complexity terms scaling with stability Delta-bar and sqrt(log(1/delta)/(2m)) w.p. >= 1-delta, and Theorem 7 shows stability Delta-bar shrinks with alpha.

Structure regularization beat WeightReg/WeightAvg across all four tasks and both model types (Table 1: POS-Tagging 97.36% vs 97.33%; Bio-NER F1 72.43% vs 72.28%/72.65%; Word-Seg F1 97.50% vs 97.19%/97.5%) with significance POS p<0.01 and Act-Recog p<0.0001, plus substantial wall-clock training speedups — but GSE has no structured-prediction component, leaving only the portable intuition that simpler structures generalize better.

Horton & Lucey (Stats Perform, 2026, arXiv:2511.18730v1) built an axial transformer that jointly forecasts end-of-match totals of 12 player actions, team totals, and game outcome, updated ~150 times per soccer match at event timesteps — ~505 predictions per timestep x ~150 timesteps = ~75,000 live predictions per game with sub-second inference on commodity CPU.

The model uses a grid E_0 in R^(HxWxD) (H = agents = players+2+1, W = timesteps, D=128 embeddings per modality: player/team/game x pre-game/live x strength/context) with L=4 axial transformer layers combining row (temporal, strict upper-triangular causal mask) and column (agent, current timestep) attention; an equivalence theorem shows axial attention is identical to sequential masked attention on row-major unraveling with M := M^row + P(M^col)P^T, at complexity O((H+W)HW) vs O(H^2 W^2).

The axial combination rule is R = [N^row/(N^row+N^col)] elementwise R^row + [N^col/(N^row+N^col)] elementwise R^col (Algorithm 1 line 17), with the self-cell masked in one of the two ops; masked attention is Attention(K,Q,V,M) = softmax(A)V with A = (M + KQ^T)/sqrt(d).

The paper's full model beat all four ablations (no-agent-attention, no-temporal-attention, no-pre-game-context, stacked axial) on mean log-probability for every one of 12 targets; target log-prob/calibration-error pairs included goals -0.111/0.002, assists -0.088/0.001, shots -0.515/0.021, passes attempted -3.039/0.074; ablation gaps (e.g., goals -0.111 vs -0.124 no-temporal, accurate passes -2.765 vs -3.199) showed temporal dynamics contribute most, pre-game context second, agent interaction third.

Rare-event heads (red cards, own goals) were near-degenerate zero-mass predictors (zero-category mass >= 0.84 and >= 0.97); the paper has no external baselines (self-referential calibration+ablation only) and consistency constraints (shots-on-target <= shots) emerge from shared embeddings only, with no hard constraints.

The study trained on 62,610 soccer matches (28 competitions, Opta event data via Stats Perform, proprietary): 58,501 games from 2016-17 to 2023-24 for training and 4,109 games of partial 2024-25 (through 15 Dec 2024) for test, using shared-over-agents-and-timesteps linear heads to per-target distribution parameters (Bernoulli, Poisson, log-Gaussian, model-free discrete) with Poisson-NLL summed per target, Adam LR 0.0003, cosine annealing, batch 30, ~150k steps, ~15 h on one NVIDIA A10.

Zhong et al. (2023, arXiv:2311.08007v4) defined a distance map D_t(x,y) = ||V_{0->t}(x,y)|| * cos(theta) / ||V_{0->1}(x,y)|| for velocity disambiguation in video frame interpolation, where V_{0->t} is the motion field from frame 0 to intermediate time t, V_{0->1} is full inter-frame motion, and theta the angle between them; the deep-read verdict is REJECT — no prediction-modeling application and generated/interpolated footage is prohibited by Garrett's standing video rule.

Adding the distance map plus iterative reference-based estimation to RIFE on Vimeo90K improved LPIPS 0.105 -> 0.086 and NIQE 6.663 -> 6.220; the multi-frame refiner reached PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/NIQE 28.34/0.928/0.089/6.173 versus the ground-truth-map upper bound 31.63/0.952/0.062/5.990, showing estimated maps capture roughly half the ideal gain; cost on A100 at 448x256 was 0.10 s, 30.68 MB.

Schulte, Liu & Li (2018, arXiv:1802.08765v1) built logistic regression model trees (LMT) for NHL draft prospects 1998-2008: the tree partitions feature space and each leaf fits p_i = P(g_i > 0) = P(plays >= 1 NHL game in 7 years), built with LogitBoost via Weka LMT and final leaf weights refit by maximum likelihood; the binary target is a zero-inflation solution (an M5P regression tree on game counts collapsed to a stump on CSS rank) that doubles as a success ranking.

LMT rankings beat draft order in all four temporal out-of-sample splits (train 3 draft years, test a later year), SRC of draft order / LMT accuracy / LMT SRC: train 1998-2000 -> 2001: 0.43 / 82.27% / 0.83; -> 2002: 0.30 / 85.79% / 0.85; train 2004-2006 -> 2007: 0.46 / 81.23% / 0.84; -> 2008: 0.51 / 63.56% / 0.71 — with a sharp uninvestigated accuracy drop in 2008 showing temporal regime sensitivity.

The 2004-2006 learned prospect groups: CSS rank <12 -> 82% play >=1 game; CSS >=12 & regular-season points <12 -> 16%; points >=12 then plus-minus negative -> 37%, neutral -> 61%, positive -> 92% (with >10 playoff assists, n=13, median 128 games); group weights: CSS rank -17.9 (Group 1), regular-season points +14.2 (Group 2), plus-minus +13.16 (Group 3), goals +3.59 (Group 5, 64.8% forwards) vs -2.17 (Group 2, 61.6% defensemen); log-odds explanation vs group mean = sum_j w_j (x_ij - xbar_gj).

Case studies validating the model tree's discovered groups: Kyle Cumiskey (unranked by CSS, model's top in his group, drafted 222nd, played 132 NHL games, won the 2015 Stanley Cup), Brad Marchand (CSS 80, top of group 6), Milan Lucic (tops Group 5); Sidney Crosby and Patrick Kane topped Group 1; ~50% of draft picks never play an NHL game (Tingling et al. 2011).

Oko et al. (2026, arXiv:2609.12651v1) refined RLHF distortion bounds: Theorem 3.1 gives Dist(pi_Borda) <= C1*beta + 4 (improving the prior O(beta^2)), and Theorem 4.1 gives Dist(pi_RLHF) <= C2*min{e^B*tau, B, B*tau^{-1}+1}*beta + 4; at B=0 (preference data on-policy, mu = pi_ref) RLHF is an O(beta)-distortion utilitarian aligner, matching the algorithm-independent Omega(beta) lower bound — the exponential blowup in BT temperature was a distribution-mismatch artifact.

Distortion (alignment) is defined as Dist(pi) = max_{pi': KL(pi'||pi_ref) <= tau} E[u] / E_{u~D, x~pi}[u(x)]; Assumption 2.1 (distribution mismatch) is max_x log(pi_ref(x)/mu(x)) = B < infinity; empirically, max pairwise reward differences were Delta-r = 108.8 (Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B) and 25.4 (UltraRM-13B) across 5,000 preference instances — practical reward models operate in the BT nonlinear regime.
equation: P(i prefers x over y) = σ(β(u(x) − u(y))), σ(t) = 1/(1+e^−t)

claim: The RLHF-distortion paper was REJECTED in the deep read for GSE purposes: it is LLM-alignment theory with no sports-relevant method, data, or transfer path; its synthetic experiment (beta=10, B=11.5, mirror descent eta=1e-3) showed on-policy preference data -> distortion converges to 1 while mismatched data -> distortion grows and average reward declines.

The HypoArena benchmark (arXiv: 'Before the Action') defined 'Prospective Hypothesis Discovery' (PHD) — constructing grounded, discriminative, testable hypothesis sets from conclusion-free observations — and ranked 15 frontier LLMs on 988 cases via pairwise LLM-as-judge arena with Bradley-Terry-Davidson aggregation (5-level verdicts mapped to win shares {1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.0}, tie parameter theta, 1500 baseline, position debiasing) plus six-dimension rubric scoring (q_i = (g_i + l_i + j_i)/3; Q_set = (b+d+u)/3).

HypoArena leaderboard (BTD / win rate, baseline mode): claude-sonnet-4.6 1654.0/71.3%, claude-opus-4.6 1652.7/71.4%, gpt-5.4 1631.4/70.7%, reference 1590.5/57.8%, kimi-k2.6 1582.7/58.2%, glm-5.1 1581.9/59.1%, deepseek-v4-pro 1535.4/46.1%, kimi-k2.5 1289.5/9.2% (bottom) — a >360-point spread with clear stratification.

HypoArena findings: the structured-analytic Agent mode vs zero-shot baseline delta ranged +88 (kimi-k2.5) to -60 (claude-opus-4.6) with Spearman rho = -0.10 against baseline strength — structured analytic skills are model-dependent and sometimes harmful; human alignment was Kendall tau = 0.90, Spearman rho = 0.98 on 1,500 expert pairwise comparisons (per-domain tau 0.97 Fin -> 0.53 Bio); arena score spread (345-490 pts/domain) vs rubric (<1 point on a 1-5 scale) showed rubric compression; accepted ICLR papers' hypotheses were more competitive (+47 BTD).

The HypoArena paper was REJECTED in the deep read: no sports data, no predictive model, no GSE-transferable statistics — the sole transferable element (pairwise arena + BTD ranking for open-ended outputs) duplicates Bradley-Terry machinery already in the corpus.

A single Bradley-Terry ranking fit to pairwise comparisons is misspecified under heterogeneous preferences and can shut out a cohesive subgroup, so the paper formalizes gamma-approximate local stability as a checkable fairness criterion: a committee W_k of size k is gamma-approximately locally stable if max_{a not in W_k} Pr_{i~D}[a >_i W_k] <= gamma/k (a >_i W_k = user i prefers a to every member of W_k); a ranking is stable if every top-k prefix is.

The stability estimator is gamma-hat = k * (max_{a not in W_k} (1/n) sum_i 1[a >_i W_k]), with gamma-hat <= 1 meaning stable; empirically on LMArena semi-synthetic data the BT ranking violated stability at k = 4, 5 (phi=0.1) and k = 5 (phi=0.5) while Algorithms 2 and 3 (committee ranking via geometric checkpoints, committee sizes k_r = floor(lambda^{r-1}), lambda=2 best theory; heuristic single-addition decomposition) were stable for all k and all phi.

Pluralistic-leaderboards load-bearing limitations: the guarantees require adaptive per-user battle-pair selection and offline/pre-collected data is explicitly out of scope, so on fixed historical datasets only the diagnostic gamma-hat criterion ports cleanly, not the constructions; the stronger PSC notion is unverifiable from k-wise comparisons (no deterministic algorithm can check it; randomized success <= k/(k+1)); and an identity in the appendix shows BT over all pairs is equivalent to Borda count is equivalent to Elo over all pairwise comparisons.

Committee construction Alg. 1 (iterated rounding) uses T = ceil(10 log(k/epsilon)) rounds with alpha = 1/2 + 4 epsilon, beta = 1/4 + 2 epsilon and sub-committee sizes k_t = max{1, floor((1-alpha) alpha^{t-1} k)}; Theorem 3.1 promises a (16+O(epsilon))-approximately stable committee w.h.p. 1-delta with d = O((k/epsilon^2) log(m/(epsilon delta))) comparisons per user (epsilon=0.01 -> factor 18.97; epsilon=0.05 -> 39.2); Alg. 1 at k=5, phi=0.5 used 18,540 users with median 38 comparisons/user.

Across all 268 UEFA club-competition penalty shootouts (2000/01-2025/26), none of five two-sided binomial tests (first-mover, home-mild, home-strict, two momentum proxies) was significant even at the 10% level; team-strength logistic regressions P(win) = 1/(1+exp(-(beta_0 + beta_1*strength_diff + beta_2*venue))) found venue and strength coefficients insignificant regardless of strength measure — favorites with >=100 Elo points failed to win 50% of shootouts, directly contradicting prior studies that found ~20 pp advantages for strong favorites in broader domestic-cup-heavy samples.
equation: P(win) = 1/(1 + exp(−(β_0 + β_1 · strength_diff + β_2 · venue)))

claim: The sole shootout exception — 2020-2025 one-legged matches where home teams won only 7 of 20 (35%), significant below 50% at the 10% level — disappeared under the strict venue definition and is multiple-comparison noise across 26 rolling specifications (the paper's own flagged inference); the authors caveat that the logistic regressions are in-sample, n=268 is small for detecting modest effects, and the homogeneous elite-vs-elite sample is both the innovation and the limitation.

The shootout dataset covers 268 UEFA club-competition shootouts (Champions League, Europa League, Conference League including qualifiers), 139 of 268 (51.9%) in the last six seasons (COVID one-legged qualifiers 2020/21, abolition of the away-goals rule, new Conference League), with strength from Football Club Elo Ratings (authors prefer Elo to betting odds, citing odds biases), and robustness checks repeating all tests on first-20-season vs last-6-season subsamples plus 26 rolling-window logistic regressions.

The score-driven dynamic Plackett-Luce model splits team strength into fixed effects plus mean-reverting AR(1) dynamic component plus regression covariates: f_{i,t} = omega_i + sum_j beta_j x_{i,t,j} + u_{i,t} with u_{i,t} = phi u_{i,t-1} + 1_{i in P_{t-1}} alpha nabla_i(f_{t-1}|y_{t-1}); strengths are computed only for participants P_t, non-participants' u decays toward 0 when phi in (-1,1), identified by sum_i omega_i = 0; it is fitted by penalized ML with penalized log-likelihood L_Pen(theta) = sum_t l(f_t|y_t) - lambda sum_t sum_{i in P_t} f_{i,t}^2 and standard errors s-hat-e[theta-hat] = sqrt(diag[-T H(theta-hat)^{-1}]).

The Plackett-Luce probability (Eq. 1) is P[y|f] = product_{r=1}^N exp(f_{r-th})/sum_{s=r}^n exp(f_{s-th}) with log-likelihood l(f|y) = sum_i f_i - sum_{r=1}^N ln(sum_{s=r}^N exp(f_{s-th})) (Eq. 3), and the score (Eq. 5) is nabla_i(f|y) = 1 - sum_{r=1}^{y(i)} exp(f_i)/sum_{s=r}^N exp(f_{s-th}), which has zero expectation and variance equal to the Fisher information.
