equation: P[y|f]=Π_{r=1}^N exp f_{r^th}/Σ_{s=r}^n exp f_{s^th}; ∇_i(f|y) = 1 − Σ_{r=1}^{y(i)} exp(f_i)/Σ_{s=r}^N exp(f_{s^th})

claim: The fitting-discipline lesson from the paper's section 4.4: bound phi in [0,1) and alpha >= 0, because unbounded MLE drifts to a spurious persistent model (phi -> 1) with negative alpha whose standard errors collapse to ~=0; always use multiple starting points — a pathology unreported in Holy & Zouhar 2022.

IIHF World Championship final model (AIC 1531.978 vs static 1577.664): Last WJC 0.853***, Last WC 0.674**, Avg. Age -0.191*** (younger better), IIHF Exp. 0.053***, NHL Exp. 0.002* — the IIHF coefficient is ~25x the NHL coefficient despite 11x fewer games/season, but this is confounded because the WC runs during the NHL playoffs so WC rosters systematically miss the best NHL players (selection, not causation); hosting was insignificant; phi = 0.736.

On 16 rolling one-step-ahead editions (lambda=0.01 optimal for both), the World Championship final model averaged log-likelihood -22.783 vs static -23.321 (P(champion) 0.166, P(medals) 0.045, P(playoffs) 0.027, MAE 1.999, RMSE 2.627) and the WJC -10.794 vs -11.004 — but WITHOUT penalization (lambda=0) the static model beat the final model, so penalization is required for the covariate model to win; lag-1 rank autocorrelation was 0.715 (WC) vs 0.566 (WJC), mirroring the phi estimates 0.736-0.850.

World Junior Championship final model (AIC 888.157 vs static 913.877): hosting 0.488**-0.673*** significant in every model, past results insignificant, Height -0.142* (shorter better), Weight 0.123* (heavier better), IIHF Exp. 0.897***; phi = 0.796-0.850.

A Bayesian longitudinal hidden Markov model with two latent states (cold/hot), logistic mixed-regression transition probabilities and Bernoulli observations, fitted to all 11,042 shots of the 2005-06 Miami Heat (105 matches, 5,922 made), found the team showed 'something more like a cold hand instead of a hot hand': generic-match transitions P(C->H)=0.38 vs P(H->C)=0.59, stationary distribution Delta^(C)=0.61 vs Delta^(H)=0.39, and cold streaks (>3 consecutive shots, threshold 'arbitrary') ~0.25 vs hot streaks <0.1 — cold streaks ~3x more likely.

The hot-hand HMM's hidden-state observation logits were logit(gamma_in^C) = alpha_C + alpha_d X_in + alpha_FT I_FT(in) + a_i and logit(gamma_in^H) = alpha_H + alpha_d X_in + alpha_FT I_FT(in) + a_i with a_i ~ N(0, sigma_a^2), covariates shared across states with only intercepts differing; posterior means included beta_CH = -0.49 (-0.58,-0.39), beta_HC = 0.38 (0.27,0.49), delta_C = 0.55 (0.43,0.68), alpha_d = -0.42 (-0.51,-0.33), alpha_FT = 6.37 (5.16,7.75).
equation: logit(γ_in^C)=α_C+α_d X_in+α_FT I_FT(in)+a_i; logit(γ_in^H)=α_H+α_d X_in+α_FT I_FT(in)+a_i

claim: The hot-hand paper's 'hot' state intercept was degenerate: alpha_H = 12.59 (95% CI 10.52, 14.97), implying make probability ~= 1.0 at any distance — the 'hot' state is a fitted artifact absorbing easy makes rather than a real regime — a known failure signature whose detection must gate any port of the model.

Stationary state probabilities in the hot-hand HMM follow Delta_i^(C) = p_i^(HC)/(p_i^(CH)+p_i^(HC)) and Delta_i^(H) = p_i^(CH)/(p_i^(CH)+p_i^(HC)) (Eq. 8), with geometric sojourn times P(tau_i^(j)=n) = [p_i^(jj)]^n (1-p_i^(jj)) (Eq. 10); occupancy in a 120-shot match was posterior mean 74.05 shots cold vs 46.85 hot, and the initial state was 'practically irrelevant'.

The hot-hand paper had no train/test split, no cross-validation, and no predictive checks — purely inferential on one team and one season — with no opponent-strength covariate (a 'cold' stretch against a good defense is indistinguishable from a real cold hand), a text/table inconsistency on SD(alpha_d|D) (0.03 vs 0.05), and the distance effect forced identical across states.

Van Kesteren & Bergkamp (2022, arXiv:2203.08489v2) fitted a Bayesian multilevel rank-ordered logit (Plackett-Luce) model to F1 2014-2021 (160 races / 51 drivers / 19 constructors, Ergast API): p(y_r|theta_r) = product_{i=1}^{m_r-1} exp(theta_i)/sum_{j=i}^{m_r} exp(theta_j), with latent ability theta_c = theta_d + theta_ds + theta_t + theta_ts (each cross-classified random effect ~ N(0,sigma^2)), logit link and no intercept so parameters are log-odds ratios of beating an average competitor (theta_d=0.3 => P(beat average) ~= 0.57, Elo-like).
equation: p(y_r|ϑ_r) = ∏_{i=1}^{m_r−1} exp(ϑ_i)/Σ_{j=i}^{m_r} exp(ϑ_j); ϑ_c = θ_d + θ_ds + θ_t + θ_ts

claim: The F1 model found ~88% of outcome variance comes from the constructor: sigma_c=1.63 [89% CI 1.14,2.27], sigma_cs=0.73, sigma_d=0.54, sigma_ds=0.35, i.e. ~88% constructor (89% CI [0.775,0.945]), consistent with Bell et al. (2016) 86%; model selection by LOO-CV ELPD showed the basic model beats wet-race-slope and circuit-slope extensions (differences within SE, -1.07 +/- 6.35) — parsimony wins.

Counterfactual from the F1 model: Hamilton in an Alfa Romeo vs Raikkonen in a Mercedes in 2021 gave E[pi_{ham>rai}] = 0.36 — the car beats the driver — via pi_{ham>rai} = exp(theta_{ham:alfa:2021})/(exp(theta_{ham:alfa:2021})+exp(theta_{rai:merc:2021})); 2021 points/race were shrunk at extremes (Verstappen expected 15.30 [12.32,18.00] vs 18.00 observed; Hamilton 14.58 [11.45,17.50] vs 17.59).

F1 model caveats: the authors state it is 'probably not suitable for prediction' (year effects unknowable pre-season) and assume no driver-x-constructor interaction — the exact interaction a sports league cares about (a star elevating a weak roster); excluding non-finishers shrank effects toward 0 (including all data moved Maldonado from 19th to 6th-worst — reliability is part of skill if included); fit in Stan with 8 chains x 1250 post-warmup, all R-hat < 1.01, ESS > 2500.

Zhou et al. (2020, arXiv:2012.06366v1) proved a negative result: PageRank-based sports rankings beat the plain win ratio only in a tiny low-randomness early-season corner and are worse everywhere else — across 18 leagues (MLB/NFL-adjacent data from sports-reference.com and win007.com), PageRank beats WinRatio only when randomness delta is small AND season fraction P is small, with the delta threshold shrinking as P grows; the vast majority of real datasets have delta > 0.15 where PageRank brings no improvement and is significantly worse for high-delta sports late in the season.

Bi-directional PageRank (S_i = P_i - Q_i, with Q_i = PageRank on reversed winner->loser edges) beat WinRatio only at P ~= 0.1 or lower per league (averaged over all leagues the threshold is P = 0.035, and WinRatio never lost by more than 0.03 in Kendall tau); the mechanism is that a single upset perturbs only two teams' win ratios but propagates through the whole PageRank network, so with many upsets (high delta) the accumulation is detrimental; no fraction of removed/reversed upsets (eta) lets PageRank/BiPageRank beat WinRatio.

Calibration of the outcome model P(i,j) = [1 + e^{-(Delta-w_{i,j} + H)/delta}]^{-1} found baseball most random and basketball least (CBA least random of 17 leagues), with H in [0, 0.25] and CBA's H/delta 5.4x baseball's; PageRank used alpha=0.15 loser->winner edges with dangling-node correction P_i = (1-alpha) sum_j P_j w_{ji}/s_j^{out} + alpha/N + (1-alpha)/N sum_j P_j delta(s_j^{out}).
equation: P_i = (1−α)Σ_j P_j w_{ji}/s_j^{out} + α/N + (1−α)/N Σ_j P_j δ(s_j^{out}), α=0.15

claim: The PageRank paper's real-data ground truth was the final win-ratio ranking, which structurally favors WinRatio, yet the early-season PageRank edge survived it; the verdict is REJECT as a guardrail — no PageRank-family method in the team-strength pipeline, licensing exactly one conditional use: BiPageRank on the first ~3.5% of games (roughly NFL weeks 1-2).

Montagna, Orani & Argiento (2019, arXiv:1909.03802v1) built Bayesian isotonic logistic regression with constrained B-splines: Y_{ij}|p_{ij}(x) ~ Bernoulli(p_{ij}(x)), logit p_{ij}(x) = f_i(x) + (alpha_i - alpha_j) (serve curve + Bradley-Terry ability difference), f_i(s) = sum_{m=1}^M beta_{i,m} b_m(s) with B-splines order k=4, M=9, knots (1,1,1,1,2,3,4,7,11,15,15,15,15) on [1,15]; partial monotonicity enforced via beta_{i,m} := beta_{i,m-1} - epsilon_{i,m} with epsilon_{i,m}|r_epsilon,s_epsilon ~ Gamma(r_epsilon/s_epsilon^2, (r_epsilon/s_epsilon)^2), r_epsilon,s_epsilon ~ U(0,10) — first m_{L0}-k coefficients free (rich-data region learns freely), constrained beyond L0=3; Proposition 1 states a non-increasing restricted control polygon implies the spline is non-increasing on [L0,U].
equation: logit p_{ij}(x) = f_i(x) + (α_i − α_j); β_{i,m} := β_{i,m−1} − ε_{i,m}, ε_{i,m}|r_ε,s_ε ~ Gamma(r_ε/s_ε², (r_ε/s_ε)²)

claim: Partial monotonicity won all four model criteria on ATP/WTA tennis serve-advantage-vs-rally-length data (Table 3): LPML -52,739.1, WAIC 105,747.6, DIC 105,828, RMSE 19.32 vs exponential baseline -52,813.7/105,821.3/105,876/22.52, unconstrained -52,760.4/105,853.9/105,818/20.71, fully monotone -52,744.9/105,790.4/105,875/20.37 — 'no dramatic difference', so the win is principled shape plus sparse-region uncertainty, not fit leaps; unconstrained splines learned implausible increasing segments at intermediate rally lengths.

Tennis serve-advantage estimates: P(server wins | x=1) = 0.83 men (95% CI 0.75-0.94), 0.69 women (0.55-0.83); at rally length x=15: men (0.51,0.64), women (0.46,0.55); Djokovic had the best baseline rally ability (alpha=0.35); by surface — clay: Nadal 0.52, grass: Federer 0.28, hard: Djokovic 0.34; Serena top WTA baseline 0.26 (0.18-0.35); conclusion: top players separate on rally ability, not serve.

The data covered 145,510 ATP rallies (130,577 short <=4 shots) and 81,880 WTA rallies (71,592 short) from point-by-point Grand Slam singles 2012+ scraped by Jeff Sackmann (also in R package deuce); train 90 servers, test 50 (ATP)/49 (WTA) hold-out servers; fit by Gibbs via rjags (20,000 draws, 1,000 burn-in, thinning 20) with model comparison by LPML/WAIC/DIC/RMSE.

Limitations of the constrained-spline model: knot/L0 are hand-tuned (sensitivity in unpublished thesis), Gibbs/rjags is dated (NUTS-friendly for Stan), and sum-to-zero identifiability (alpha_i ~ N(alpha_0, sigma^2_alpha), sum alpha_i = 0) is awkward for streaming.

Masarotto & Varin (2012, arXiv:1301.2954v1) defined the adaptive ranking lasso: Bradley-Terry with an L1 penalty on all pairwise ability differences, argmin{-l(mu,tau) + lambda sum_{i<j} w_ij |mu_i - mu_j|} (Eq. 4), reformulated via theta_ij = mu_i - mu_j as a constrained ordinary lasso (generalized fused lasso, no natural order), with adaptive weights w_ij = |mu-hat_i^(mle) - mu-hat_j^(mle)|^{-1} (Eq. 7), epsilon=10^-4 ridge stabilization for undefeated/winless teams, lambda via AIC/BIC, and Augmented Lagrangian computation; the BT model is pr(Y_ijr=1) = exp(tau h_ijr + mu_i - mu_j)/(1+exp(tau h_ijr + mu_i - mu_j)) with home indicator h_ijr in {-1,0,1} and identifiability sum mu_i = 0.
equation: argmin{−ℓ(μ,τ) + λ Σ_{i<j} w_ij|μ_i − μ_j|}; w_ij = |μ̂_i^{(mle)} − μ̂_j^{(mle)}|⁻¹

claim: On NFL 2010-11 held-out-half negative log-likelihood (100x random halves): MLE 139.90 | 137.30 | 0.59 (mean | median | fraction better-than-coin); Lasso-AIC 119.10 | 111.70 | 0.60; Lasso-BIC 117.20 | 109.30 | 0.58; Hybrid-AIC 135.20 | 131.90 | 0.60; Hybrid-BIC 131.60 | 127.30 | 0.60 — AIC-lasso ~=15% mean / 19% median better than MLE, BIC-lasso ~=16% mean / 20% median, while the hybrid (lasso groups + MLE refit) was only marginally better than MLE, supporting the adaptive ranking lasso without refitting.

Ranking-lasso NFL 2010-11 groupings: New England 14-2 shrank from MLE 2.59 to lasso-AIC 1.40 / BIC 1.13, and bottom-tier teams (Houston, Tennessee, Seattle, Cincinnati, St. Louis) fused to shared -0.21 (AIC) / -0.12 (BIC); in NCAA hockey the lasso grouped the top four (Denver, Miami (Ohio), Wisconsin, Boston College — the eventual champion) at identical 0.58 (AIC) / 0.41 (BIC).

Ranking-lasso limitations: random-half CV within one season is not time-ordered (absolute NLLs optimistic, relative ranking stands), single season each sport, lambda by AIC/BIC not CV, no comparison vs Elo/Glicko or plain L2 ridge, and n=32 is a small-sample regime where shrinkage trivially helps.

The Strong Aggregating Algorithm (SAA, Vovk & Zhdanov 2008, arXiv:0710.0485v2) gives a regret-bounded way to combine expert probability forecasts online under multiclass Brier loss lambda(omega, gamma) = sum_o (gamma{o} - delta_omega{o})^2 (omega = realized outcome, gamma = predicted distribution, delta = Kronecker delta): the regret guarantee is L_N <= min_k L_N^k + ln K — the learner's cumulative Brier loss is at most the best expert's plus ln K — with optimal mixability learning rate eta = 1, updating expert weights multiplicatively by exp(-eta*loss).
equation: L_N ≤ min_k L_N^k + ln K; λ(ω, γ) = Σ_o (γ{o} − δ_ω{o})²

claim: SAA was tested on 6,473 soccer matches (2005/06-2007/08, 8 bookmakers as experts) and 10,087 tennis matches (2004-2007, 4 bookmakers) using implied probabilities from normalized inverse odds; the paper reports the regret bound is 'reasonably tight' for football and 'particularly tight' for tennis — realized cumulative loss sat close to best-expert loss + ln K.

SAA limitations recorded in the ledger: bookmakers as experts are highly correlated (copy each other's lines), so best-expert-in-hindsight is a weak competitor; SAA inherits shared miscalibration of all experts; Brier loss is symmetric with no special protection in the tails where edges live; the online protocol assumes immediate outcome revelation (frays for futures/correlated slates); and the 2005-2008 data predates modern market microstructure.

Goncalves et al. (arXiv:2510.16008, 2025) forecast short-term price moves in Betfair betting-exchange markets with a novel multi-head convolutional attention: split the multivariate time series into per-variable series, apply 1D conv per path (softmax, last layer 1 channel -> TimeSteps vector per variable), concatenate into a TimeSteps x Variables attention map; multi-channel stacked convs capture multi-scale local patterns, plus a novel 'roll padding' that pads the VARIABLES dimension by copying from opposite sides (cylinder, not torus) while keeping the time dimension valid — preserving variable correlations without zero-padding distortion.
equation: c_i = Σ_i α_i h_i, α_i = softmax(x_i^l)

claim: Weight of Money is defined as WoM = Amounts Bid / (Amounts Bid - Amounts Ask) (Eq. 6, as printed), and the exchange trading layer used Profit Back = Amount Back x (Price Back - 1) and Liability Lay = Amount Lay x (Price Lay - 1) (Eqs. 2-5), with prediction class mapped to mechanism (weak -> swing, strong -> trailing-stop), target = mean of max tick variation per class, stop-loss = 80% of target (swing) / 60% (trailing-stop).
equation: WoM = Amounts Bid / (Amounts Bid − Amounts Ask)

claim: On Betfair UK to-win horse racing pre-live 10-minute windows (2 frames/sec, 2014-09-01 to 2016-08-29, 14,421 races, 3-25 runners/race), 5-run accuracies on a 5-equal-frequency-class target (~20% baseline) were: LSTM + Conv1D multi-head attention mean 30.05% (best run 30.92%, min 29.71) — ~11 pp above baseline; plain LSTM 28.40%; CNN 23.81% -> CNN+roll padding 24.30%; WaveNet 25.89% -> WaveNet2D+roll 28.64%; real deployment accuracy on final test = 28.26%.

The best exchange model was extremes-biased: per-class recall strong down 46.38%, strong up 44.71%, neutral 27.71%, weak down 10.47%, weak up 9.89 (precision strong up 36.54%, strong down 23.70%); its 30-day production simulation (category #41: strong up -> trailing stop, target 6 ticks, stop 4 ticks) did 134 trades (54 greens, 36 reds, 44 null; positive ticks 134 vs negative 87 at GBP 3 stake) but ROI was lower at GBP 100 stake (50 greens/39 reds) due to market absorption.

The exchange paper's 9-indicator data engineering (integral of price change runner/competitor, liquidity variation ask/bid, volume variation+direction, price variation from sequence start runner/competitor, WoM runner, WoM others) used 10% tail truncation per histogram and [-1,1] normalization; a rule-based market-regime decision tree (favorite? x runners x price x liquidity -> 54 categories, only 9 with >=1,200 examples trained from scratch) gated model training.

Brown et al. (arXiv:2411.09085, 2024) built a Transfermarkt-weighted Massey: weighted least squares X^T W X r* = X^T W y (Eq. 16) with home advantage as an extra parameter y_k = r_i - r_j + r_h x_k (Eq. 17), final rating r = r-hat + r_TM — an equal-weighted sum of the WLS solution and the Box-Cox-transformed, [0,1]-standardized average Transfermarkt lineup value; plus a Transfermarkt ordered-probit regression y*_ijg = (h_ig - h_jg) beta_h + (TM_ig - TM_jg) beta_TM + epsilon with TM = log lineup market value.
equation: Xᵀ W X r* = Xᵀ W y; r = r̂ + r_TM

claim: Time-weighted Colley is W_k = exp((t_k - t_0)/(t_f - t_0)) with weighted wins/totals w*_i, t*_i and (2 + t*_i) r*_i = 1 + (w*_i - l*_i)/2 + S* (Eqs. 11-14); Massey is r_i - r_j = y_k with Mr = p and r_i = p_i/G_i + sum_j (g_ij r_j)/G_i — rating = avg point spread + avg opponent rating (Eqs. 4-6); discounting draws (no merit) in Colley improved predictions over awarding half-wins.
equation: (2 + t*_i) r*_i = 1 + (w*_i − l*_i)/2 + S*; r_i = p_i/G_i + Σ_j (g_ij r_j)/G_i

claim: End-of-season Kendall's tau (47,198 games across English PL, Championship, League One, League Two 2010-2024, 204 unique teams): Transfermarkt-weighted Massey best everywhere — PL 0.5887, Championship 0.2737, League One 0.2881, League Two 0.1655 (vs unweighted Massey 0.5498/0.2118/0.2426/0.1061, Colley lower); in-season PL Brier: Betting Odds 0.1842 < T.M.-weighted Massey 0.1888 = T.M. Regression 0.1888 < Massey 0.1912 < Colley 0.1945 < Null 0.2121, same ordering in all leagues; pairwise t-tests: T.M. Massey - Massey = -0.0024 (PL, significant), Betting Odds - T.M. Reg = -0.0044 to -0.0065 (odds still best).

Two substantive findings: (1) the PL-vs-lower-league predictability gap DISAPPEARS after removing dominant teams (Big Six / Bayern / Old Firm) — the gap is team disparity, not forecasting skill (same pattern in Germany/Scotland); (2) the wisdom-of-crowd test FAILS — Transfermarkt values with no user discussion (lower leagues, moderator-set) predict just as well relative to odds as heavily-discussed ones, so predictive power comes from values tracking salaries/contracts, not crowd wisdom.

Draws were 24% (PL) to 27% (League One) of matches; the equal 0.5 weighting of r-hat and r_TM is arbitrary (authors flag weight optimization as future work); Transfermarkt values are partly endogenous and lower-league valuations sparse.

Boudreaux et al. (arXiv:2201.01168, 2021) compared contest-success functions as estimators of MLB team quality: general Pythagorean (Tullock) EWP_{i,j} = rs_{i,j}^alpha/(rs_{i,j}^alpha + ra_{i,j}^alpha) with James restricted alpha=2; linearized Tullock ln(1/EWP - 1) = alpha*ln(ra/rs); difference form EWP = 1/(1+e^{alpha(ra-rs)}); serial form min(EWP, 1-EWP) = min(rs,ra)^alpha/(2*max(rs,ra)^alpha) with estimated alpha=1.032 — each transformed linear in noise parameter alpha and fit via OLS on 390 MLB team-seasons (2003-2015, mean wins 80.98 SD 11.15, mean runs 729.24 SD 81.46).

OLS estimates of alpha (390 MLB team-seasons): Tullock 1.859 (t vs H0=0: 50.07***, vs H0=2: 3.79***), R^2=0.866, RMSE 4.069/4.0722 wins; difference 0.00254 (t vs 0: 49.88***), R^2=0.865, RMSE 4.081; serial 1.032 (t vs 0: 52.56***, vs 2: 49.31***), R^2=0.877, RMSE 3.6836; LOOCV (train 389, validate 1, x390) root MSE: Tullock 4.0836, difference 4.0926, serial 3.6964; LOOCV MAE: 3.2807, 3.2932, 2.9357.

The serial CSF reduces LOOCV root MSE by ~0.39 wins versus optimized Tullock — 5x the root-MSE reduction achieved by moving from James' restricted alpha=2 to the OLS-optimized alpha — and both the serial (alpha=1.032) and Tullock (alpha=1.859) estimates decisively reject H0:alpha=2 at 49-52 sigma; the authors claim estimates of team win proportion typically within ~.025 units of true win proportion (~4 wins/162 games).

Pythagorean-CSF limitations: MLB only (not tested in other leagues; authors flag NFL/NBA as future work); the serial CSF is anonymous/symmetric and cannot absorb sport-specific asymmetries (NFL home field, schedule strength) without modification; LOOCV is within-sample in time (alpha estimated on the full sample including future seasons); single-input (runs) model; the NFL analog (points) is a coarser signal over 17 games vs 162.

Barnes & Barnes (2021, arXiv:2104.08236v1) built a regression neural network that outputs (mu, sigma) and learns via an abstention loss to abstain on predictions it is not skillful at, hitting a user-specified abstention setpoint: abstention loss (Eq. 4) L(x_i) = -q_i log p_i - alpha log q_i with q_i = min(1.0, (kappa/sigma_i)^2), kappa = P_90% of validation sigma after spin-up; the abstention rule is abstain iff sigma_i > tau where tau = coverage-setpoint percentile of validation sigma; two-stage training (spin-up N epochs on NLL L = -log N(y_i; mu_i, sigma_i), then abstention loss) with a PID controller on alpha (velocity algorithm, 6-batch/192-sample evaluation windows) to hit setpoints in {0.1,...,0.9}.
equation: ℒ(x_i) = −q_i log p_i − α log q_i, q_i = min(1.0, (κ/σ_i)²)

claim: On the forecasts-of-opportunity variant (29% true opportunity fraction), controlled abstention network error was below the best baseline ANN at every coverage, especially below 30% coverage; the constant-alpha variant identified ~24% coverage vs the true 29%, and PID slightly outperformed constant-alpha; on corrupt inputs (constant alpha=0.05) it correctly identified 70% coverage (= 30% corrupted fraction) and beat the baseline ANN.

The baseline ANN's standardized errors z_i = (y_i - mu_i)/sigma_i were empirically ~= N(0,1) (mean ~= 0, std ~= 1 on train and test), justifying the (mu, sigma) probabilistic reading and making post-hoc sigma thresholding 'a simple yet powerful method' in its own right; ridge (L2=0.1) + abstention combined beats either alone, though regularization narrows the CAN-vs-baseline gap.

The paper's data was a synthetic climate benchmark (Mamalakis et al. 2021, public): 900 grid-point SST anomaly maps, 8,000/5,000/5,000 splits, plus a synthetic 1D example where the paper is internally inconsistent on coverage (section 4.1 says the line holds 30% of samples, results discussion says 20% — treat coverage numbers as approximate); percentile thresholds (tau, kappa) frozen on validation sigma break under distribution shift, so tau must be recalibrated each season.

Mitton et al. (2026, arXiv:2509.21514v4) added a no-retraining selective-prediction layer to deployed knowledge-tracing models: M=100 stochastic forward passes with dropout active at inference, total uncertainty = entropy of the aggregated predictive distribution H = -sum_k p-bar_k log p-bar_k with p-bar_k = (1/M) sum_m p_k^(m), selective signal = std/variance of predictions across MC samples, abstaining the most-uncertain fraction to hit target coverage (c=0.80); BALD epistemic uncertainty = total entropy - mean MC-sample entropy.
equation: H = −Σ_k p̄_k log p̄_k, p̄_k = (1/M)Σ_m p_k^(m)

claim: At c=0.80, MC-Dropout variance lifted accuracy +2.3-3.0 pp, AUC +1.9-2.4 pp, and F1 +1.4-4.3 pp across three architectures (baselines AKT 72.44%, SAKT 72.27%, DKT 72.20%; AUC 76.20-76.75%), with no retraining and bootstrap CI margins +-0.13 pp (accuracy), never crossing zero; deferred-set error rate was 1.45-1.60x the kept set (2.3-2.5x on hardest questions, >1.0 in every difficulty quartile); the IRT baseline lifted only 0.41-0.46 pp AUC vs MC-Dropout's 2.0-2.4 pp — MC variance is ~5x stronger.

BALD variance decomposition showed heuristic proxies capture almost none of the model-native epistemic signal: difficulty alone 0.4-1.5%, +ability 0.8-1.8%, +IRT ambiguity 1.1-3.7%, +4-level coverage <=3.8% linear, nonlinear random-forest bound 9.8-23.2%, leaving 76.8-90.2% unexplained — classical heuristic proxies (like matchup difficulty or consensus) cannot recover the epistemic signal, a disciplining result for any abstention design.

Fairness of the selective layer: abstention ran 16-23% across ability quartiles with the weakest students lowest at 16-17% (not disproportionately deferred); the data was the Eedi mathematics learning-platform dataset (4,257 questions, 11,994 train students / 1,199,266 interactions, 1,493 validation students / 149,278 interactions, student-disjoint splits); the paper flags deep ensembles and temperature-scaled softmax as stronger baselines it did NOT test; calibration caveat: mean entropy correlates -0.62 with question difficulty (class-imbalance artifact).

Lucena (2018, arXiv:1809.07751) proposed SplineCalib: non-parametric logistic regression of calibration-set outcomes on natural-cubic-spline expansions of model scores, minimizing J(f) = -sum_i [y_i log f(x_i) + (1-y_i) log(1-f(x_i))] + 1/2 lambda integral f''(t) dt (Eq. 1); Algorithm 1 samples 200 knots from unique score values, expands into natural cubic spline basis N_1=1, N_2=x, N_{k+2}(x)=d_k(x)-d_{K-1}(x) with d_k(x)=[(x-phi_k)_+^3 - (x-phi_K)_+^3]/(phi_K-phi_k), then runs CV-L2 logistic regression choosing lambda* by CV log-loss, f(z)=logistic(X_natural(z) beta-hat).
equation: J(f) = −Σ_i [y_i log f(x_i) + (1−y_i) log(1−f(x_i))] + ½ λ ∫ f''(t) dt

claim: SplineCalib's compact-logit pre-transform for overconfident models (Algorithm 2) is G_epsilon(x) = ((1-2 epsilon)/(2 log((1-epsilon)/epsilon))) * log(x/(1-x)) + 1/2 for x in [epsilon, 1-epsilon], x otherwise, with epsilon = 10^(r-1), r = floor(log10(min(1-p_i))); the multi-class extension (Algorithm 3) fits per one-vs-rest column then renormalizes f_i(x_i)/sum_j f_j(x_j); the cross-validated variant (Algorithm 4) stacks 5-fold out-of-fold predictions into the calibration set, fits the calibrator, and trains the final model on full data.

SplineCalib results: MIMIC-III ICU mortality RF log-loss — uncalibrated 0.2525, isotonic 0.2592, Platt 0.2535, SplineCalib 0.2442 (best); UCI Adult naive Bayes — uncalibrated 0.7448, isotonic 0.3976, Platt 0.4287, SplineCalib 0.4032, compact-logit 0.3934 (best calibrated); CIFAR-10 CNN (800 epochs) — uncalibrated 0.4361, clipped 0.4150, SplineCalib 0.3633, accuracy 87.64% -> 87.88%; cross-validated variant log-loss 0.3704 -> 0.3286, accuracy 88.86% -> 89.04%; the key claim is that a 40k-train + 10k-calibrate calibrated model beat the uncalibrated model trained on the full 50k.

SplineCalib caveats: the paper reports no confidence intervals on the log-loss gains, CIFAR accuracy gains are small (+0.24 pp, +0.18 pp), and there is no time-series validation — NFL non-stationarity requires time-ordered splits; code is the ml-insights package (pip install ml_insights) with notebooks at github.com/numeristical/introspective.

Lang et al. (ECMWF, 2024, arXiv:2412.15832) trained a machine-learned weather ensemble directly on a proper-score loss instead of MSE: CRPS({x_j},y) = (1/M) sum_j |x_j - y| - (1/2M^2) sum_{j,k} |x_j - x_k|, fair CRPS replacing 1/2M^2 with 1/2M(M-1), and almost-fair CRPS afCRPS_alpha = alpha*fCRPS + (1-alpha)*CRPS = (1/M) sum_j |x_j-y| - (1-epsilon)/(2M(M-1)) sum_{j,k} |x_j - x_k| with epsilon = (1-alpha)/M, alpha=0.95.

The afCRPS positive-terms rearrangement (Eq. 4, fp16-stability fix) is afCRPS_alpha = (1/2M(M-1)) sum_j sum_{k != j} (|x_j - y| + |x_k - y| - (1-epsilon)|x_j - x_k|), non-negative per term by the triangle inequality for epsilon >= 0; the degeneracy-fix rationale: pure fCRPS has a degeneracy where if M-1 members equal the observation the remaining member is unconstrained (zero gradient), and the (1-alpha) CRPS admixture removes it.

AIFS-CRPS (50-member) beat the 9km physics-based IFS ensemble on most upper-air (500 hPa geopotential, 250 hPa wind) and surface (2m temperature) variables — lower CRPS and RMSE, higher anomaly correlation, improvements 5-20% (degraded above 100 hPa); tropical 200 hPa temperature mean RMSE was ~0.1 K lower than IFS; subseasonal (2-6 week) forecasts improved vs operational IFS with lower biases and better MJO skill; realistic spectra were maintained to long leads with reference-field truncation (without it, spurious small-scale energy growth).

The AIFS training used per-variable loss scaling plus pressure-dependent weighting w_pl = plev/1000 (min 0.2); the graph transformer trained in 4 stages (300k/60k/~45k iterations, AdamW beta 0.9/0.95, wd 0.1) on ERA5 reanalysis (N320 ~31km; O96 ~1°) with operational IFS analysis, verified against ECMWF analysis + radiosonde + SYNOP for forecasts initialized 00/12 UTC 2024-02-01 to 2024-09-30; inference ran ~1 min (O96) / ~4 min (N320) per 15-day single-member forecast on NVIDIA A100 40GB.

An arXiv 2024 IIT Guwahati paper applied correspondence analysis (CA) to 1,088,570 ball-by-ball cricket short-text commentaries to mine per-player strength/weakness rules: a confrontation matrix N (batting-response x bowling-delivery co-occurrence from unigram/bigram features; 19 batting x 12 bowling features); dependency via independence-axiom violation P(bf intersect wf) = alpha*P(bf)*P(wf) with alpha=1 independent, alpha<1 dependent; CA = SVD of normalized, centered N -> principal components F (batting), G (bowling), minimizing sum of squared distance of feature points to the reduced subspace.

CA-derived rules: for a batsman, a strength rule pairs an attacked batting feature with the bowling partner = argmax_j <F_attacked, G_j>, weaknesses mirrored (beaten); bowler rules mirrored (strength = opponent beaten); t-SNE on 31-dim per-player rule vectors clustered similar players (short-pitched-ball attackers: Warner, Collingwood; leg-line attackers: Smith, Kayes, Edwards; beaten-by-away-movement cluster); max 228 rules/player (19x12), 12+12 evaluated, 4 dominant presented.

Steve Smith's CA-derived rules matched the domain expert (Sanjay Manjrekar ESPNCricinfo video 2017-06-01) verbatim in substance: strengths = attacks leg-stump deliveries, attacks slow deliveries; weaknesses = beaten by swinging deliveries, beaten by move-away deliveries; Procrustes train/test biplot stability Delta^2_12 (lower = better): Root 0.09, Karunaratne 0.11, Smith 0.17, Pujara 0.27, Elgar 0.28, Kohli 0.30, Warner 0.47, Williamson 0.47.

Lipiecki, Uniejewski & Weron (Energy Economics, arXiv:2404.02270v2) compared QRA, Conformal Prediction, and Isotonic Distributional Regression for converting point forecasts into probabilistic forecasts on German/Spanish day-ahead electricity prices: QRA q-hat(alpha|p-hat) = [1, p-hat^ave] * beta_alpha with beta from pinball-loss minimization (most compute-intensive); CP symmetric intervals from absolute-error nonconformity scores in rolling calibration windows; IDR (Henzi et al. 2021) (F-hat_1(z),...,F-hat_m(z)) = argmin sum(eta_i - 1{p_{i,h} <= z})^2 s.t. eta_1 >= ... >= eta_m, eta_i in [0,1] via abridged pool-adjacent-violators with linear interpolation between sorted point forecasts and extrapolation clamped to endpoints.
equation: (F̂₁(z),…,F̂_m(z)) = argmin Σ(ηᵢ − 1{p_{i,h} ≤ z})² s.t. η₁ ≥ … ≥ η_m, ηᵢ ∈ [0,1]

claim: The ensemble LEAR-Ave (vertical averaging of the three predictive distributions over calibration windows m in {28, 56, 91, 182}) achieved the lowest CRPS in both markets and all four subperiods: Germany CRPS 1.310 / 3.970 / 10.199 / 4.215 (2020/2021/2022/2023), Spain 0.938 / 3.832 / 6.983 / 4.369; the CPA test (Giacomini-White 2006, Delta_d = phi' X_{d-1} + epsilon_d) showed LEAR-Ave significantly outperforms ALL models in both markets, evaluated on CRPS over 99 percentiles with skill score SS = 1 - sum CRPS^model / sum CRPS^{LEAR-N} over rolling 182-day windows.

Shapley decomposition of the winning ensemble: IDR contributed the most — its 2023 contribution exceeded 75% in both markets — while CP contributed least; IDR was the most volatile component but the most valuable diversifier; all LEAR-based models, even Gaussian-error LEAR-N, significantly outperformed the much more complex DDNN-JSU (Johnson's SU distributional neural nets), which collapsed during the energy crisis (Germany 2022: 13.375 vs LEAR-Ave 10.199; Spain 2022: 8.299 vs 6.983).

On tails (APS_20, extreme 20 percentiles), LEAR-Ave was best in all subperiods except the first German subperiod (DDNN-JSU insignificantly better) and Spain 2023 (LEAR-IDR best); compute cost was LEAR+postprocessing ~2:45-3:15 h on a 64-core server vs DDNN-JSU 6:00-6:30 h (DDNN hyperparameter optimization would take weeks; IDR itself takes 15-20 s); IDR was regime-dependent — poor for 182-day windows ending Dec 2019-Apr 2021, Dec 2021-Apr 2022, Aug 2022-Apr 2023 (Germany), excelling in calm periods following volatile ones; the test covered 2015-01-01 to 2023-12-31 German/Spanish day-ahead prices (4.5-year out-of-sample 2019-06-27 to 2023-12-31, covering COVID and the Ukraine-war energy crisis).

Agrawal, Wang & Ye (2008) studied parimutuel call-auction betting over permutation outcome spaces (n! outcomes): they proposed 'Proportional Betting' with polynomial-time pricing via a compact LP, max pi'x - e'v - e'w s.t. v_i + w_j >= sum_k(x_k A_k)_{ij} (polynomial via matching-polytope integrality), versus the CPCAM primal max pi'x - r + mu sum theta_i log s_i s.t. sum_k a_ik x_k + s_i = r whose parimutuel prices are the dual variables; the deep-read verdict is REJECT — pure theory with zero empirical results, no data, and no predictive method for a pick publisher.
equation: max π'x − e'v − e'w s.t. v_i+w_j ≥ Σ_k(x_k A_k)_{ij}

claim: The paper reconstructs a joint distribution over rankings from marginal prices via maximum entropy: min sum_sigma p_sigma log p_sigma s.t. sum_sigma p_sigma M_sigma = Q -> p_sigma = e^{Y.M_sigma - 1}, an n^2-parameter exponential-family form whose exact computation is #P-hard (reduction from (0,1)-matrix permanent), with a (1-epsilon)-FPTAS in poly(n,1/epsilon,1/q_min) via the Sinclair Jerrum-Vigoda permanent approximation.

Complexity results: fixed-reward matching is NP-hard (MAX-2-SAT reduction, Theorem 3.1); proportional-betting pricing is polynomial with a unique doubly-stochastic marginal price matrix Q (Theorem 4.4) — marginal prices are unique and parimutuel; the proportional-betting organizer problem is polynomial (O(n^2+m) variables/constraints).

Vukcevic & Keser (arXiv 2024) derived the constrained generalized multivariate Kelly solution for sizing a small set of simultaneous correlated bets: the core first-order condition (quoted exactly) is sum_i p_i k_{ij} / (1 + sum_j f_j k_{ij}) = 0, solved for the fraction vector f via Newton-Raphson over discrete joint outcomes with probabilities p_i and payoff vectors k_{ij}, with long-only (f_j >= 0), leverage-cap (sum f_j <= 1), max-allocation-per-position, and permanent-capital-loss P(loss >= K) <= P constraints enforced by enumerating all 2^{N_l} active/inactive constraint combinations and keeping the feasible optimum.

On constructed scenarios (no empirical dataset — all numbers are model outputs on stipulated inputs): five identical 50%-loss/100%-gain 50/50 candidates gave unconstrained Kelly 35% each (75% leverage implied) -> no-leverage constraint 20% each -> with P=5%/K=50% permanent-loss constraint 2% each; the 5-asset example portfolio sized A 30%, B 8%, C 30%, D 2%, E 30% with expected gain $0.32 per dollar wagered, cumulative loss probability 16%, and claimed 60%-capital-loss probability 0.008%.

The multivariate-Kelly paper's complexity is 2^{N_l} — infeasible beyond small N (with 20 candidates and all constraints, ~4 trillion nonlinear systems) — and Newton-Raphson nonconvergence can silently discard the true optimum (flagged in the paper); the solution assumes known outcome probabilities, fully enumerated discrete joint outcome space, log utility, simultaneous resolution, and no sequential rebalancing, implemented in the Rust crate `charlie`.

Wan et al. (arXiv:2011.06430v2) built a news co-occurrence network of 87 companies from 7 years of Reuters news (145 frequent orgs, 87 with Bloomberg tickers, 9 sectors): Louvain community detection found 7 groups vs 9 Bloomberg sectors, with median in-sector edge weight 0.0157 vs out-sector 0.00229; edge weight e_{ij} = cosine similarity of news-coverage row vectors; Louvain modularity Q = (1/2m) sum_{i,j} (e_{ij} - k_i k_j/2m) delta(C_i, C_j); entities extracted via NCRF++ NER (char-CNN + word-LSTM + CRF, trained on CoNLL 2003).
equation: Q = (1/2m) Σ_{i,j} (e_{ij} − k_i k_j / 2m) δ(C_i, C_j)

claim: Sentiment shocks propagate to network neighbors (Mann-Whitney, p<0.01), but asymmetrically: in Group 1 (financials) negative shocks propagate significantly while positive ones don't, with the same asymmetry in Groups 3, 5, 6, while consumer groups 2 and 4 are symmetric; post-event CAR diverges — positive sentiment -> upward drift, negative -> decline — with few significant pre-event CAR deviations; both event types elevate volatility, lingering for days in some groups; the volatility proxy was sigma(t) ~= |log(P(t)/P(t-1))|.

The news-network study is associational, not a trading strategy — no predictive backtest, and no single headline effect size was quoted (results are figure-based significance patterns, not point estimates); the event-study discipline included a manual causality check sampling event-day articles to exclude pure market-commentary pieces, guarding against circularity.

Dierckx, Davis & Schoutens (KU Leuven, arXiv:2009.07947) predicted next-day direction of AAPL implied volatility (VIX formula: VIX = 100*sqrt[(2/T) sum (Delta-K_i/K_i^2) e^{RT} Q(K_i) - (1/T)(F/K_0 - 1)^2], interpolated to 30-day term; target y_i^* = ivol_{i+1} - ivol_i, y_i = 1 iff y_i^* > 0, class split 59% down / 41% up) from 78 engineered features (market + Google News counts + Wikipedia page views, 486 daily vectors Jan 2016-Dec 2017) with walk-forward validation (379-day/78% train window, next day OOS, 106 splits, standardization + feature selection re-run inside each fold; metric = balanced accuracy).

Balanced-accuracy results (Table 9): market-only LR 63.3%, SVM 64.2%, AdaBoost 53.7%; news+wiki only 52.3/50.5/55.0; market+wiki 52.8/55.6/AdaBoost 63.0%; market+news 51.8/53.3/49.0; all 61.3/59.1/57.3 — market data alone beats alternative data under linear models (best overall SVM 64.2% vs 50% chance and 59% majority-class baseline on 106 OOS points), but AdaBoost on market+Wikipedia hit 63.0% while LR collapsed to 52.8% on identical features — a non-linear interaction between Wikipedia page-traffic features and IV moves that linear models miss.

The alternative-data study is an honest negative for linear models: Google News counts were the least effective feature family, alternative data did NOT improve LR/SVM, and the authors used sklearn defaults with no tuning, a binary target ignoring magnitude and neutral moves, and predicted probabilities never checked against precision/move size; they also argued Random Forests clash with sequential data and excluded them.

The R PlackettLuce package paper (Turner, van Etten, Firth, Kosmidis; JSS, arXiv:1810.12068v2) ships generalized Plackett-Luce machinery for subset rankings and arbitrary-order ties (Davidson-Luce), pseudo-comparison regularization, quasi-standard errors, and PL trees: the augmented likelihood adds weight-0.5 pseudo-wins/losses vs a hypothetical average-worth item, giving finite MLEs in disconnected networks and shrinking worths toward equality; quasi-variances satisfy Var(log w-hat_i - log w-hat_j) ~= qvar_i + qvar_j, giving reference-free contrast uncertainty; PL trees recursively partition on ranking-level covariates via parameter-instability tests to find subgroups with different worth structures.
equation: Var(log ŵ_i − log ŵ_j) ≈ qvar_i + qvar_j

claim: PlackettLuce benchmark: 5,000 sub-rankings of 10 items from 100 with ties to order 4 fit in 18.1 s / covariance 14.8 s on a 2.10 GHz i7 / 16 GB; the NASCAR example covered 36 races, 87 drivers (42-43 per race); the paper's explicit warnings: PL trees can be unstable, high-order ties grow combinatorially in memory/time, and online/streaming estimation plus spatiotemporal extensions are listed as future work, not implemented; no predictive baseline comparison — validation is correctness + performance.

O'Brien, Gleeson & O'Sullivan (arXiv:2009.01206v1) tested whether fantasy success is skill or luck on 901,912 FPL managers' full 2018/19 season (~50M API calls to fantasy.premierleague.com; ~6M managers in 2019/20, ~3.8M with >=1 prior season, 13 seasons of pairwise overlap): season-to-season points correlation was 0.42 (2018/19 vs 2017/18, n~=3M) with the 13-season matrix 0.13-0.47 decaying with gap — persistent skill over a decade; +1 year of experience = +22.1 points/season (R^2=0.082); the winner scored 2659.

The FPL paper's perfect-foresight transfer-regret metric is y_G(x_i,x_j) = sum_k 1[q_G(x_k)<=q_G(x_i)] * 1[p_G(x_k)>p_G(x_j)] / sum_l 1[q_G(x_l)<=q_G(x_i)] (the fraction of same-cost-or-cheaper alternatives that outscored the chosen transfer); top tiers' transfer-regret CCDFs decay faster (consistently nearer-optimal replacements), captaincy points distributions shift right with tier, and team value at GW19 predicted +21.8 final points per +GBP 1M (R^2=0.169) with top-10k values diverging upward from GW1.

FPL template-team detection: the player co-occurrence matrix A^G_ij (# teams containing both i and j) with hierarchical clustering (k=4, elbow on WSS) showed the 3 smallest clusters contain only 5.13% (32/624) of players yet anchor most squads; Jaccard similarity J^G(i,j) = |T_i cap T_j|/|T_i cup T_j| between manager squads (100 teams x 10,000 resamples per tier-pair per GW) rises with tier and oscillates — consensus forms then dissolves — and GW1 already showed high similarity among top managers (shared pre-season information); top tiers beat lower tiers every GW, largest gaps at GW1 (top-10^3 averaged 88.16 vs 63.17 — preparation before a ball is kicked), DGW35, BGW33.

FPL chip timing: 79.4% of top-10k played Bench Boost in DGW35 vs 28.9% of the rest, with returns 23.2 vs 13.8 points; the dominant sequence was Free Hit DGW32 -> Wildcard GW34 -> Bench Boost DGW35 (long-horizon planning); 85.05% used all chips (top-manager-biased sample).

Yazbek et al. (2021, arXiv:2103.13736) tested Siamese networks feeding LightGBM LambdaRank / XGBoost pairwise rankers for end-of-season team ranking in NBA (2014-2018, 2,460 games/season, 30 teams, 14 box-score features per side) and Super 15 Rugby (2017-2020, 120 games/season, 15 teams, 38 seasonal stats): contrastive loss J(theta) = (1-Y)(1/2)(D_{a,b})^2 + (Y)(1/2)(max(0, m-D_{a,b}))^2 with Y=0 win / 1 loss and D_{a,b} = Euclidean distance between embeddings; triplet loss J(theta) = max(D(a,p) - D(a,n) + m, 0) with anchor a, positive p (same class), negative n (different class).

Triplet-loss embeddings beat plain boosters: NBA LightGBM(Triplet) — mAP 0.867 +/- 0.15, Spearman 0.870 +/- 0.11, NDCG 0.980 +/- 0.00 vs naive 0.704/0.640 and plain XGBoost 0.857/0.900/0.976, playoff hits 8/8 East + 7/8 West; Rugby XGBoost(Triplet) — AP 0.921 +/- 0.04, r_s 0.793 +/- 0.00, NDCG 0.982 +/- 0.03 vs naive 0.462 — while plain LightGBM/XGBoost without SNN LOST to naive on rugby (0.381/0.421 vs 0.462), making representation learning load-bearing; triplet > contrastive in both sports but the margin was 'smaller than expected'.

The paper has a leakage flaw: end-of-season aggregate stats were used to predict games WITHIN that same season — overstating true forecasting power; there was no consistent winner across sports (LightGBM-Triplet wins NBA, XGBoost-Triplet wins rugby); huge error bars (e.g., NBA XGBoost-Contrastive mAP 0.745 +/- 0.26) make the SOTA claims shaky; all six models missed Utah over Denver in 2017/18; the tally-rank aggregation (predicted game similarity score added to a team's tally on predicted win, subtracted on loss; tallies sorted descending -> standings) is heuristic, not learned.

Mallepalle, Yurko, Pelechrinis & Ventura (2019, arXiv:1906.03339) recovered raw pass locations from NFL Next Gen Stats pass-chart images (scraped from nextgenstats.nfl.com, 2017-2018, 500+ games; >27,000 passes modeled) via K-Means++ clustering to identify passes/field locations plus DBSCAN noise removal and greedy record linkage validated against Big Data Bowl tracking, with median coordinate deviation 1.7 yards vs Big Data Bowl tracking; code + dataset at github.com/ryurko/next-gen-scrapy.

The CPAE pipeline used a 2-D Naive Bayes shrinkage surface P-hat*_G(Complete|x,y) = [N_g f-hat_g(x,y) P-hat_g + N_Median f-hat_NFL(x,y) P-hat_NFL] / [N_g f-hat_g(x,y) + N_Median f-hat_NFL(x,y)] — weight shifts from league prior to group data as attempts N_g grow — plus league-wide GAM for P(Complete|x,y) smooth in distance-from-LOS and distance-from-field-center, attempt density via 2-D KDE, and CPAE_g = integral integral P-hat*_{g,league}(Complete|x,y) f-hat_g(x,y) dx dy (spatial-density-weighted integral of the above-league-average completion surface).
equation: P̂*_G(Complete|x,y) = [N_g·f̂_g(x,y)·P̂_g + N_Median·f̂_NFL(x,y)·P̂_NFL] / [N_g·f̂_g(x,y) + N_Median·f̂_NFL(x,y)]; CPAE_g = ∫_X∫_Y P̂*_{g,league}(Complete|x,y)·f̂_g(x,y) dx dy

claim: Open-data CPAE correlated with official NFL NGS CPAE at rho = 0.81 (2017) and 0.91 (2018) despite a strictly weaker model (no play context: no down/distance/pressure/coverage); CPAE year-over-year stability was 0.41 (p < 0.05); 2018 QB CPAE leaders: Brees +6.14%, Fitzpatrick +3.42%, Foles +3.42%, Wilson +3.39%, Ryan +3.22%, Wentz +3.08%; worst: Bortles -5.04%, Driskel -4.83%, Rosen -4.54%; 2018 defense CPAE (negative = better): Ravens -5.24%, Bears -2.43%, Rams -2.35%; worst: Buccaneers +6.89%, Falcons +4.31%; 4 of the top 5 CPAE defenses made the 2018 playoffs.

League-wide 2018 completion profile: 66.5% of targets within 10 yards of LOS, 89.2% within 20; median predicted completion 76.8% (<=10 yd), 69.7% (<=20), 28.0% (beyond 20); deep middle 30.5% vs deep sidelines 22.7%; defense surfaces agree with DVOA (2018 Bears -26.9% DVOA, below-average allowed completion field-wide).

Bittner, Nussbaumer, Janke & Weigel (2006, arXiv:physics/0606016v1) fitted soccer goal distributions with microscopic 'self-affirmation' feedback models where scoring changes subsequent scoring probability: Model A (additive) p(n) = p_0 + n kappa; Model B (multiplicative) p(n) = p_0 kappa^n (clipped to [0,1]); Model C (coupled): home goal -> p_h x kappa_h, p_a / kappa_a and vice versa; exact distribution via Pascal recurrence P_N(n) = [1-p(n)]P_{N-1}(n) + p(n-1)P_{N-1}(n-1), O(N^2), N=90 Bernoulli steps.

Poisson was rejected everywhere on soccer goals: chi^2/dof 6.53-12.8 (e.g., Bundesliga home lambda=2.01 +/- 0.02, chi^2/dof=6.53; Oberliga away lambda=1.05 +/- 0.01, 12.8) with tails fatter than Poisson; NBD fit well (chi^2/dof 0.68-4.09; Bundesliga home p=0.11 +/- 0.01, r=15.9 +/- 2.10; Bundesliga r ~= 2x Oberliga r); Model B fit World Cup qualification extremely well — away scores better than GEV ('each goal motivates more than the previous — true football fever'); GEV never best for German leagues (xi small and mostly negative, Weibull; xi=0 Gumbel rejected).

Home-away goal correlation was weak but significant negative: R = -0.015 +/- 0.011 (Oberliga), -0.031 +/- 0.009 (Bundesliga); larger feedback kappa in Oberliga than Bundesliga ('more encouraging' scoring; alternatively West teams switched to defensive mode when leading) and much larger kappa in Frauen-Bundesliga (fatter tails), paralleling WC qualification; sum/difference consistency: P_Sigma(sigma) = sum_n P_h(n) P_a(sigma-n), P_Delta(delta) via modified Bessel I_delta (Poisson case).

The continuum limit of Model A is exactly the negative binomial with r = p_0/kappa, p = 1 - e^(-kappa N) (Appendix A proof) — so NBD arises both as compound-Poisson (non-contagious) and as the limit of contagious Model A, meaning fit quality alone cannot prove the feedback mechanism (spurious contagion caveat [37]); data spanned Bundesliga 1963/64-2004/05 (~12,800 matches), Oberliga GDR 1949/50-1990/91 (~7,700), Frauen-Bundesliga 1997/98-2004/05 (~1,050), FIFA World Cup qualification 1930-2002 (~3,400), plus 14 further European premier leagues.

Szabadary et al. (2025, arXiv:2506.21802v1) formalized conformal prediction as a binary classifier with reject option: reject rule m(x,epsilon) = reject-empty if |Gamma^epsilon(x)|=0 (novelty rejection); accept Gamma^epsilon(x) if |Gamma^epsilon(x)|=1; = reject-ambiguity if |Gamma^epsilon(x)|=2 (ambiguity rejection); accept iff epsilon in I_x = [gamma_x, c_x); online smoothed CP gives sigma := P(err | S) = (epsilon - P(E)) / P(S) with estimator sigma-hat = (n epsilon - e)/s converging to sigma a.s. — error rate = sigma, reject rate = 1 - P(S); bounds P(E) <= epsilon <= 1 - P(D) hold so sigma in [0,1].
equation: σ := P(err | S) = (ε − P(E)) / P(S); σ̂ = (nε − e)/s

claim: The paper's key fix is the offline inductive CP correction: epsilon-tilde = epsilon - sqrt(ln(1/delta)/(2h)) with calibration size h, singleton bound sigma-tilde = (epsilon-tilde - P(E))/P(S), estimated by (n epsilon-tilde - e)/s — a PAC-type guarantee with two parameters; prior singleton-error formulas (Linusson et al. 2016/2018, Bortolussi et al. 2019) hold only online, not in the offline inductive setting practitioners use; Mondrian (label-conditional) version: sigma_k = (epsilon_k - P(E_k))/P(S_k), estimated (n_k epsilon_k - e_k)/s_k per category.

Conformal-reject demos: full CP Mondrian 1-NN on qsar-biodeg (1055x41) — max singleton proportion ~= 0.4 -> minimum achievable reject rate ~= 0.6, and the same reject rate can arise from different epsilon so always pick the smallest epsilon (lowest error); offline ICP RandomForest on spambase — very low error rates achievable but only at high reject rates; limits: not all reject rates are achievable, sigma-hat is noisy where it matters (large epsilon, few singletons), and exchangeability breaks under distribution shift — the guarantee is weakest precisely when abstention is most needed (novelty); batch offline ICP: sigma-tilde_k = (N_k epsilon-tilde_k - e_k)/s_k per batch, delta_{k+1} = delta_k^{h_{k+1}/h_k}.

Neu & Zhivotovskiy (2020, arXiv:2001.10623) proved that a no-bet option at cost c < 1/2 turns online-prediction regret from growing sqrt(T) into a horizon-independent log N bound: Theorem 1 gives R_T <= log N / eta with eta = 2(1-2c); Corollary 2 tuning eta gives R_T <= (log N)/(2(1-2c)) AND sqrt(T log N / 2), with a matching lower bound of order log N/(1-2c) — tight; the fast rate vs slow rate comparison: log N/(1-2c) vs sqrt(T log N); worked example: N=10 experts, c=0.49 -> regret <= log 10 / 0.04 ~= 57.6 total forever vs ~sqrt(T*2.3) growing with T.

The fast-rates abstention rule: predict the weighted-majority class k*_t with confidence p*_t, abstain with probability alpha_t = 2(1-p*_t); expected loss E[l-hat_t] = alpha_t*c + (1-alpha_t)*1{k*_t != y_t}; Lemma 4's proof step is E[l-hat_t] = r_t - (1-2c)(r_t AND (1-r_t)) where r_t = sum_i q_{t,i} 1{y_{t,i} != y_t}; abstention cost c must be strictly below 1/2 (near-1/2 gives weak constants); extensions cover time-varying costs c_t <= 1/2 (Proposition 5) and a Tsybakov-type margin condition (1/T) sum_t 1{1/2 - c_t < x} <= beta x^{alpha/(1-alpha)} (Definition 6) yielding R_T = O((log N)^{1/(2-alpha)} T^{(1-alpha)/(2-alpha)}) (Corollary 7).

Bianchi & Lanz (2025, arXiv:2503.04470) added skeleton pose (YOLO11-x-pose, COCO 17 keypoints, mAP 69.5% @ 0.5:0.95, 91.1% @ 0.5, 58.8M params) to a Gate-Shift-Fuse RGB action-recognition network for binary athlete fall classification in figure skating (FR-FS dataset: 417 samples — 276 fall, 141 non-fall, 103 frames each, from the FIV dataset + PyeongChang 2018 footage): early-fusion X = [RGB; H(keypoints)] with H = sum_j exp(-||p-k_j||^2/2 sigma^2) (Gaussian heatmap as 4th input channel); late-fusion z = MHA(concat(L2(f_RGB), L2(f_pose))) with a pose MLP 34-dim -> FC64 -> FC128 -> FC128 then FC halve-dim -> BN -> ReLU -> dropout twice (FC1 64, FC2 32) -> FC classifier, cross-entropy loss; design rule from results: early-fusion wins with large backbones, late-fusion wins with light backbones.

Gate-Shift-Pose results (ResNet18/ResNet50, ImageNet init, SGD momentum 0.9, wd 5e-4, LR 0.01 cosine annealing, batch {4,8}, segments {16,32}, 120 epochs): ResNet18 — RGB-only GSF best 67.79% -> early-fusion best 81.25% -> late-fusion best 95.19% (+27.4 pp, ~40% relative per paper); ResNet50 — RGB-only GSF 81.73% -> early-fusion 98.08% (+16.35 pp, ~20% relative) -> late-fusion 87.02%; batch 4 > batch 8 on this small dataset; 32 segments > 16 consistently; but a leakage flag exists — the train/val split protocol is not described (same athletes may appear in both splits) and baselines were likely undertrained, inflating the gain claims.

Sanchez Catalina & Cantwell (arXiv:2512.15269v1) jointly inferred latent player skills s_i AND the unknown monotone win-probability kernel p(s_i - s_j) from pairwise-comparison data via EM + belief propagation instead of assuming a logistic kernel — the only joint skill-plus-kernel method in the tracked corpus (corpus inventories Elo, Glicko, TrueSkill, Bradley-Terry, Plackett-Luce all fixing the kernel a priori); kernel parametrizations: (i) Chebyshev polynomial expansion of the log-odds curve, (ii) neural network with monotonicity constraints; E-step runs belief propagation over the match graph for posterior skill marginals, M-step updates kernel parameters.

On synthetic data (1,024 players x 64 matches each with known ground-truth kernel) the method recovered both skills and kernel (no exact numerics quoted in the ledger); on the ATP tour (fit 2021-2022, predict 2023-2024 from prior-12-month observations, strictly chronological) it gave 'competitive predictions' (no exact numeric quoted); compared against fixed-logistic Bradley-Terry/Elo on skill RMSE (synthetic) and log-loss (ATP prediction); core lesson — learning the kernel per sport captures favorite-longshot asymmetries and diminishing returns to large skill gaps that a fixed sigmoid misses; the ledger's gate: ADAPT iff the learned kernel beats fixed logistic on held-out NFL seasons (lower log-loss on at least two); if the learned kernel collapses to logistic, adaptation adds nothing; code at github.com/gcant/pairwise-comparison-inference.

Hassanzadeh, Davari & Goossens (arXiv:2512.16968v1) built two optimization models for a 32-team NBA: M1 (pure travel minimization, assignment MIP) and M2 (Nash bargaining — displayed as minimizing sum_i log(w_i) where w_i = team i's travel-increase ratio vs baseline; the ledger flags that the text describes product maximization but the displayed form maximizes product(1/w_i), pushing each increase ratio toward 1, so verify intended bargaining semantics before reusing M2 verbatim), constrained by market exposure (metropolitan population proxy) >= gamma = 0.8 of baseline per team, across a {82, 72} games x {2, 4} divisions/conference x 15 expansion pairings grid from six candidate cities (Seattle, Las Vegas, Montreal, Vancouver, Tampa, Mexico City).
equation: Σ_i log(w_i), w_i = team i's travel-increase ratio vs baseline

claim: Current 30-team theory travel ~= 2,583,763 miles; re-optimized current structure: 2,583,209 (M1) vs 2,583,232 (M2) — fairness costs only ~23 miles in 2.58M, essentially nothing in aggregate; Mexico City + Vancouver is the only pairing above 2.8M miles (2,802,722 in the 82-game/4-division scenario); theory distance (opponent distances weighted by expected game frequency from division/conference structure) regressed vs 2004-2018 actual travel gives R^2 ~= 0.34 in-sample — calibration, not validation; authors' limitations: no back-to-back or long-road-trip modeling, distance != fatigue (no sports-science integration), fairness only via Nash bargaining (no max-min/CVaR).

Wheatcroft (arXiv:1908.08980v1) argued against the Ranked Probability Score for football outcome forecasts: ignorance (log) score identifies the true forecasting system faster and more reliably than Brier and RPS — Brier = sum_i(p_i - o_i)^2 (eq. 1); RPS = sum_{i=1}^{r-1} sum_{j=1}^{i}(p_j - o_j)^2 (eq. 2); IGN = -log_2(p(Y)) (eq. 3); all three proper, only ignorance is local, only RPS is distance-sensitive; hierarchy ignorance > Brier > RPS at low imperfection (delta=0.01, 0.025; 95% resampling intervals exclude zero for large n); ignorance still significantly better at delta=0.05, 0.1; mean relative ignorance Delta (bits) <=> 2^Delta = mean increase in probability density placed on the outcome.
equation: IGN = −log₂(p(Y)); 2^Δ = mean increase in probability density placed on the outcome

claim: Experiment 2 imperfection measure: epsilon = (1/3)(|p-tilde_h - p_h| + |p-tilde_d - p_d| + |p-tilde_a - p_a|) (eq. 4), imperfect forecast drawn from {epsilon < delta}; Experiment 1 (perfect vs imperfect forecast pairs over n repeated draws): ignorance identifies the perfect system fastest for almost all n while RPS barely improves with n on match 4; odds -> probabilities (App. B, eq. 5): p_h = (1/O_h)/sum(1/O_i) — margin removed by renormalization, max odds across bookmakers used; data: football-data.co.uk, 39,343 matches, top five English leagues 2005/06 onward (EPL 6,460; Championship/League One/League Two 6,624 each; National League 6,488); ledger gate: adopt ignorance as primary engine-variant selection metric, promote a challenger only if mean relative ignorance >= 0.05 bits (2^0.05 ~= 1.035x mean probability placed on the outcome) on held-out games with 95% resampling interval excluding zero.

Srilakshmi et al. (arXiv:2508.14065v1) proposed WiDIR — a wide-and-deep multi-branch learning-to-rank model for personalized fantasy contest recommendation on Dream11: wide linear branch (memorizes feature interactions) + three deep branches (player tower, contest tower, player-contest interaction tower), embeddings concatenated into a final scoring layer; pairwise hinge loss max(0, 1 - s_i(c) + s_i(c')) where s_i(c) is the score of contest c for user i and c' a lower-ranked contest; offline evaluation precision/recall at 1, 3, 5, 10; online 4-arm A/B (control, Popular, LightGBM ranker, WiDIR), 1M players per cohort, 6 weeks; serving rankings within 10 ms, inference restricted to users active in the previous month.

WiDIR beat Popular and LightGBM offline (P/R@k) and won the online A/B — but the paper reports the win via plots only, exact numeric lifts not stated in text (chart-read only); scale: ~1B training joins, 100k players, 1.5M contests; test ~0.5B joins, 100k players, 0.9M contests; ~12 mo train / 2 mo validation / 6 mo test, time-ordered; 107 player features, 11 contest features, 9 player-contest interaction features; candidate list fixed at 100 contests (50/100/200 evaluated); verdict: no value for the prediction engine itself, only for product — adapt the architecture for personalized pick-feed/notification ranking with a >=5% relative P/R@5 gate over LightGBM before adoption.

Kublashvili (arXiv:2512.01723v1) claimed a 'HistoricalML' neuro-symbolic framework for sparse historical data (WWI naval arms race, Punic Wars) but the ledger verdict was REJECT — no genuine validation: hand-authored data (colonial case N=7; Punic case N=2); circular calibration (model confirms hand-fed structure); arbitrary ground truth; no held-out validation; degenerate '100.0% [100.0%, 100.0%]' claim signals broken machinery; example outputs: Germany projected 18.1% vs historical 8.7% (discrepancy +107.9%), tension factor 36.43, naval-arms correlation 0.79, Cannae 57.3%, Zama 57.8%; the only actionable note is that ledger 1306 ('Kelly Betting as Bayesian Model Evaluation') is its replacement.

Suglia et al. (arXiv:2211.04534v1) 'Going for GOAL' is a video-grounded football commentary dataset with a four-task benchmark: (1) commentary retrieval (video->commentary), (2) frame reordering (order shuffled frames), (3) moment retrieval (commentary->video moment), (4) commentary generation; data: 1,107 English football highlight videos, 2018-2020, 4,387.38 minutes total (mean 3.96, min 1.3, max 11.6) — Serie A 638, Premier League 167, UCL 62, Europa League 61, FA Cup 34, Carabao Cup 18, Championship 77, Euro qualifiers 50; baselines MLP, bi-GRU, bi-LSTM, HERO, VRoBERTa, BART variants; verdict: ADAPT the retrieval task, REJECT the generation task.

GOAL benchmark numbers: commentary retrieval (best config) R@1 63%, MRR 0.79, mean rank 1.58 (main) vs 1.57 (appendix) — discrepancy preserved as read; frame reordering: MLP 10.42%, MLP+position 10.99% (main) vs 10.42% (appendix), bi-GRU 90%, bi-LSTM 91%, HERO 87%; moment retrieval: HERO soft 70.6%, weighted 2.6%; VRoBERTa 32.24%, 2.11%; generation (all weak — uniformly below usable bar): BART BERTScore 0.848, BLEU 0.79%, METEOR 3.80%, ROUGE-L 8.79%; HERO-nt 0.847, 0.60%, 3.7%, 7.2%; Oracle BART KB-target 0.874, 2.28%, 8.21%, 21.2%; manual 100-sample: BART plausible 71% / repetition 9% / incoherent 20%; HERO 77%/0%/23%; HERO+video 43%/0%/57%.

A computer-vision pipeline (YOLOv4 + Kalman tracking + OpenPose) to flag head-injury risk in rugby tackles from broadcast video was REJECTED as a failure case: on 109 front-on one-on-one rugby tackle clips, 45 clips (41%) could not be processed at all even with manual tuning (only 64/109 evaluated — 58 clean + 6 with manual parameter changes); at the 15% risk region: accuracy 62.50% on the 64 successful clips, 36.70% over all 109 clips; F1 = 0.50, Cohen's kappa = 0.28 (fair agreement); the target is a heuristic fixed head-height-threshold label, not actual concussions/injuries — no novel formulas; a cautionary example that CV injury-risk papers without prospective injury outcomes are proofs of concept, not evidence.

Dey et al. (2017, arXiv:1711.05865) predicted a FIFA 2017 footballer's price from 41 game attributes framed as classification over 119 quantized price bands: feedforward MLP [41, 2000, 1500, 500, 119], ReLU hidden layers, softmax over 119 price classes, lr 0.01, decay 0.001, momentum 0.99, L2 0.0005, batch size 20, early stopping patience 10; top-5 accuracy 87.2%, average percentage price error 6.32%; no baselines reported (no linear model, no GBM); the 2000-1500-500 MLP is heavily overparameterized on 10,914 training rows (of 17,240 FIFA 2017 players; 1,926 validation / 2,500 test, random split; goalkeepers excluded) — FIFA prices are subjective game-design valuations, not market transactions.

Bajons & Kook (2025, arXiv:2509.20083) converted observed-minus-expected metrics into player-effect estimates with valid frequentist inference via double machine learning: traditional GAX_p := sum_j (Y_j - h-hat(Z_j)) X_jp (eq. 1); residualized rGAX_p := sum_j (Y_j - h-hat(Z_j)) (X_jp - f-hat_p(Z_j)) (eq. 5), the GCM/double-ML statistic (Shah & Peters 2020; Chernozhukov et al. 2017); implementation: xgboost for h-hat, out-of-bag-tuned ranger RF for propensity f-hat_p, p-values/CIs via the comets R package; Proposition 1 (double robustness): beta = 0 iff E[Cov(Y, X_p | Z)] = 0 — test consistent for direction of player effect even if one nuisance regression is misspecified; product-rate condition: product of nuisance errors must be oP(N^-1).

Residualization survives expectation-model misspecification far better than raw metrics: soccer (StatsBomb top-5 leagues 2015/16; 45,197 shots, 4,308 goals, 728 shooters >=20 shots) robustness slopes (all-data metric on restricted-data metric) rGAX 0.936 (SE 0.005) vs GAX 0.757 (0.005); vs low-frequency model rGAX 0.879 vs GAX 0.612; correlation with raw metrics ~= 1 everywhere (soccer corr(GAX, rGAX) = 0.998; goalkeeping corr(GSAX, rGSAX) = 0.999; NBA corr(qSI, rqSI) = 0.984 binary / 0.964 score value; NFL rCPAE corr(CPAE, rCPAE) = 0.997; injury corr(IAX, rIAX) = 0.98) — so marginal value is the uncertainty quantification (CIs/p-values), not new rankings; all ten top soccer rGAX players had one-sided 95% CIs excluding zero while Messi and Ronaldo were top-60 but NOT statistically significant that season.

NFL application of the rGAX framework: residualized completion percentage above expectation (rCPAE) for the 2022/23 season using nflfastR (QBs >=300 attempts, nflfastR CP model as h-hat); rCPAE ranking order: Geno Smith (CPAE 1 | rCPAE 1), Mahomes (2|2), Burrow (3|3), Herbert (4|4), Cousins (6|5), Hurts (5|6), Prescott (7|7), Dalton (8|8), Murray (11|9), Allen (12|10), Brissett (13|11), Tagovailoa (9|12), Lawrence (10|13), Rodgers (15|14), Stafford (14|15); goalkeeping: top 8 keepers had significant negative effects on scoring likelihood; injury case (Liverpool 2017/18-2018/19, 28 players, 42 player-season rows, 33 events) correctly null on tiny n; authors prescribe Bonferroni-Holm/BH/BY multiplicity correction for decision use (paper figures are not multiplicity-corrected).

Sawarni et al. (2026, arXiv:2510.19672) learned policies that may abstain (defer to a safe default) under uncertainty: abstaining value V^(p)(pi) := E[1{pi(X)!=*} v(pi,X) + 1{pi(X)=*} g_o(*,X)] with g_o(*,x) := E[(Y(1)+Y(0))/2 + p | X=x] (abstention earns random-guess value + bonus p); abstaining regret (eq. 2) Reg_n^(p)(pi) := V(pi*) - V^(p)(pi); Theorem 3.1: Reg_n^(p)(pi-tilde) ~=< (d log(nd) + log(1/delta)) / (p n kappa^2) w.p. >= 1-delta — fast O(1/n) rate where p acts as a 'synthetic margin'; Proposition 4.3: min_{P in P_alpha} V(pi) = V^(alpha/2)(pi) - alpha — abstention bonus p = alpha/2 equals worst-case value under a W1-ball distribution shift of radius alpha.

Algorithm 1 (disagreement-based abstention): learn near-optimal set Pi-hat on D1, project each pi in Pi-hat to abstain exactly where it disagrees with pi-hat, then run EWM with abstention on D2; unknown-propensity variant uses doubly-robust pseudo-outcomes; Algorithm 3 (safe policy improvement): grid bonuses -> abstaining policies on D_train -> impute abstentions with baseline omega -> one-sided LCB test V_n(pi-hat) - V_n(omega) - z_{1-delta/k} sigma-hat/sqrt(n_test) > 0 with Bonferroni correction -> deploy first passing candidate; safe-upgrade simulations: at n <= 500 EWM wins, at n >= 1000 Algorithm 3 dominates (highest improvement rate, largest mean value gain among accepted policies, Type-I error <= 0.05 across >2,000 reps); simulations used X i.i.d. standard normal, clipped logistic propensity [0.1, 0.9], kappa=0.1, delta=0.05; safe-upgrade sims: X ~ U[0,1]^5, tau(X)=2(X1+X2-1), noise variance 0.01-1.0, n in {200,500,1000,2000,5000}, 500 reps per setting; limitations: bonus p is a free parameter (1/p in the rate constant), regret measured against best binary policy so abstention gets credit for the free bonus, binary treatments only, no real-data validation.

Nobre & Fontanari (2020, arXiv:2001.10039) empirically tested Page's diversity prediction theorem with three estimation experiments (STEM students, University of Sao Paulo, Jan 2020): collective error gamma = (<g> - G)^2, individual error epsilon = (1/N) sum(g_i - G)^2, diversity delta = (1/N) sum(g_i - <g>)^2, identity gamma = epsilon - delta (exact algebraic identity, no independence assumption) — but gamma = epsilon - delta does NOT imply raising delta lowers gamma, because epsilon and delta are not independent; raising diversity can raise individual error unpredictably; experiments: (1) candies in a jar N=105 guesses, truth G=636; (2) paper strip length N=139, G=22.4 cm; (3) book page count N=139, G=784; plus 10^4 resampled 'virtual experiments' per task at group sizes 10/20/40/60.

Prediction spread does NOT correlate with collective accuracy: Pearson r(diversity, collective error) — jar: -0.005 (N=10), 0.04 (N=20), 0.06 (N=40), 0.07 (N=60); strip: 0.28 (N=10), 0.11 (N=20), -0.049 (N=40), -0.11 (N=60) — all |r| <= 0.28 at every group size; jar: crowd <g>=531 (error 16.5%, better than 70% of individuals, skewness 0.73, best guess 630); optimal group size N=5 maximizes P(error<5%) at 14%, a single random estimate beats any aggregation with N>=20, P(error<5%) decays as alpha e^{-beta N^2} (alpha=0.12, beta=0.0021); strip: crowd <g>=22.0 cm (error 1.8%, better than 85% of individuals, best 22.5 cm), P(error<5%) increases monotonically with N, a single estimate has 30% chance within 5%; book: crowd <g>=561 (error 28.4%, better than only 63% of individuals, skewness 1.22, best 800, error 2%); when the crowd is systematically biased, adding members converges the mean to the wrong value — crowd accuracy is 'most likely an artifice of selective attention'.

Ren et al. (2023, arXiv:2311.12379) sampled learning rates and combination weights for LSTM forecast ensembles from a Dirichlet process DP(alpha, H) with alpha=1000 on M4 weekly time series (single-model baseline S at fixed lr=0.001; two-LSTM-module + dropout + dense output, lag 7): G ~ DP(alpha,H), H in {EXP(0.001), N(0.001,0.01), Beta(1,1000)}, stick-breaking beta_i, pi_i = beta_i product_{k<i}(1-beta_k); ensemble E(m,alpha,H,p) of p checkpoints from one LSTM run, p in {10,...,100}; metrics MAE/RMSE averaged over the M4 weekly series set — but alpha=1000 degenerates the DP to its base distribution (the DP adds nothing; sampling from EXP/N/Beta needs no DP); the ledger verdict was REJECT — the DP machinery is decorative, headline claims are contradicted by the paper's own tables, and train/test were merged before [0,1] normalization (leakage).

The paper's own tables contradicted its 'substantial improvement' headline: mixed ensemble E' is near-identical to the plain average of the three homogeneous ensembles (at p=50: MAE 0.2368 vs 0.2369; RMSE 0.0765 vs 0.0770); Tables III/IV — simple-average MAE 0.331 (p=10) -> 0.217 (p=100) vs single 0.294; weighted-average MAE 0.137 -> 0.067; simple-average RMSE 0.137 -> 0.067 vs single 0.137; weighted-average RMSE 0.083 -> 0.063; ensemble with p<=10 is WORSE than the single model; p=20-50 gives roughly 50% error reduction vs single model; gains flatten after p~=60; possible table error: Table III's weighted-average MAE row is numerically identical to Table IV's simple-average RMSE row.

A head-to-head of Poisson vs negative binomial vs GEV vs self-affirmation feedback models for per-team goal distributions (arXiv:physics/0606016v1, Bittner et al. 2006) found: Poisson systematically underfits heavy tails; NBD fits well in most domestic leagues; the multiplicative-feedback model handles the heavier-tailed World Cup qualifying data best; GEV competitive in some leagues — so the multiplicative feedback family is the best performer on heavy-tailed (high-variance) competitions; additive feedback: p(n) = p(n-1) + kappa; multiplicative: p(n) = kappa*p(n-1); recurrence P_N(n) = [1-p(n)]*P_{N-1}(n) + p(n-1)*P_{N-1}(n-1); additive-model continuum limit: NBD with r = p_0/kappa, p = 1 - e^{-kappa t} (mechanistic reading of NBD parameters).

Within-match home/away goal correlation is weak negative (~-0.02 to -0.03, barely significant — R = -0.015 +/- 0.011 Oberliga, -0.031 +/- 0.009 Bundesliga): no meaningful in-match goal coupling detected, supporting a marginal-independence assumption; and the authors' own warning — apparent self-affirmation/contagion may be spurious, an artifact of mixing heterogeneous team strengths rather than genuine in-match momentum — binds as methodological discipline: do not cite this as evidence of momentum; caveat: soccer goals, not NFL points (scores come in 3s/7s), so transfer is at the distributional-family level, not parameters; data: ~12,800 Bundesliga (1963/64-2004/05), ~7,700 East German Oberliga, ~1,050 Frauen-Bundesliga, ~3,400 FIFA World Cup qualifiers, no covariates, no train/test split (descriptive model selection).

Bittner et al. (2007, arXiv:0705.2724v1) derived that the self-affirmation feedback model of soccer goal counts subsumes the negative-binomial and GEV fits: Model A (additive) p(n) = p0 + kappa*n, Model B (multiplicative) p(n) = p0*kappa^n, Model C coupled home/away multiplicative feedback; recurrence P_N(n) = [1-p(n)]*P_{N-1}(n) + p(n-1)*P_{N-1}(n-1); NBD limit of Model A: r = p0/kappa, p = 1 - e^{-kappa*N} (N->inf with p0*N, kappa*N fixed) — unifying the phenomenological fits as special cases of the feedback framework.

The self-affirmation follow-up was REJECTED — purely descriptive, zero out-of-sample forecasting, no calibration, no betting test; replaced by ledger 1352: Model B (multiplicative) was generally the best in-sample fit with chi^2/dof (home/away) — Oberliga 0.75/3.35, Bundesliga 1.25/1.96, Frauen-Bundesliga 3.24/0.95, World Cup qualification 0.92/0.80; validation was in-sample chi^2/dof against Poisson, NBD, GEV with no train/test split and no time-ordered validation; era-pooled fits treated 1963-2005 Bundesliga as one distribution despite structural change; the feedback parameter is a league-level constant, not a team trait — it cannot rate or rank teams; the paper never forecasts a match, goal count, or market price.

Nielsen (2013, arXiv:1311.2550v2) derived the Kelly growth-optimal dynamic stake/risk fraction under a periodically reset stop-loss rule: the optimal strategy itself obeys a nonlinear PDE with no value function needed, solved numerically with closed-form asymptotics — main result (eq. 16): d_t alpha = -(sigma^2/2)*alpha^2*d_pi(pi^2 d_pi alpha), or in risk dollars gamma = pi*alpha: d_t gamma = -(sigma^2/2)*gamma^2*d_pi^2 gamma — a nonlinear backward diffusion independent of drift (drift enters via boundary conditions); market GBM dS_t = S_t(mu dt + sigma dW_t), portfolio fraction alpha in risky, d pi_t/pi_t = alpha[(mu - r)dt + sigma dW_t]; recovered known solutions: free Kelly alphaK = (mu - r)/sigma^2, terminal-stop alpha(pi) = alphaK(1 - pi_c/pi) (CPPI with Kelly multiplier), Grossman-Zhou drawdown Kelly alpha = alphaK(1 - lambda m_t/pi_t), multi-asset = u(pi,t)*alphaK.

Stop-loss solution boundary conditions: alpha -> alphaK (pi -> infinity), alpha(pi_c, t) = 0, alpha(pi, T) = alphaK for pi > pi_c; scaled coords z = pi_c/pi, theta = (T-t)/tau, tau = 2 sigma^2/(mu - r)^2, u = alpha/alphaK solving d_theta u = u^2 z^2 d_z^2 u (eq. B5); explicit Euler stable for Delta theta/(Delta z)^2 < 0.5; long-horizon limit u(z, theta) -> 1 - z; Fig. 1(b) (Sharpe s=1.0, monthly reset): with stop 1%/5%/10%/20% below current value, u rises with time-to-reset, and the 1%-below-stop curve stays near 0 for most of the month (deep 'dead zone'), recovering only in the final days; VaR example: 3% daily 95% VaR (~30% annual vol) caps u <= 0.3 at s=1.0; author-acknowledged limitations: continuous-time GBM with no gap risk (stop-losses not truly enforceable at pi_c under jumps), no transaction costs, mu/sigma assumed known (Bayesian uncertainty incorporation recommended); new to corpus — existing Kelly ledgers (0171, 0626, 0813) contain no stop-loss-constrained Kelly.

Hsieh, Gubner & Barmish (2018, arXiv:1807.05265) gave a control-theoretic Kelly-optimal portfolio framework centered on the Dominant Asset Theorem: maximize per-period expected log growth g_n(K) = (1/n)*E[log(1 + K^T X_n)] over the unit simplex (K_i >= 0, sum K_i = 1), X_n = n-step compound return vector; asset j is dominant iff E[(1 + X_i)/(1 + X_j)] <= 1 for every i != j; the Dominant Asset Theorem states that under dominance, K* = e_j and g_n* = g_1* for all n >= 1 — if one asset dominates, the Kelly-optimal portfolio is all-in on it at any rebalancing frequency; empirical demo: Netflix + Facebook adjusted daily closes, 4 years from Jan 24, 2013, rolling 126-day windows; assumptions: known i.i.d. returns, log utility, long-only, no transaction costs.
equation: g_n(K) = (1/n)·E[log(1 + KᵀX_n)]; dominant iff E[(1 + X_i)/(1 + X_j)] ≤ 1 ∀i≠j; K* = e_j

claim: Wei & Xu (2021, arXiv:2112.14451v1) solved dynamic Kelly (growth-optimal) portfolio choice in continuous time with a VaR/ES tail-risk governor on log-returns in closed form via quantile formulation and convex envelopes: objective max_{X_T} lambda*E[R] - rho_Phi(R), R = log(X_T/x), rho_Phi = weighted VaR, lambda >= 0 growth-vs-risk trade-off; optimal quantile H-star(s; lambda, eta) = (1+lambda) eta^{-1} delta'(s; lambda) with convex envelope delta of the integrand; VaR (Dirac at alpha) and ES (phi(z) = (1/alpha)*1_{z<=alpha}) specializations give closed-form policies; lambda = 0 -> minimum-risk, lambda -> infinity -> growth-optimal, interior solutions are lambda/(1+lambda)-mixtures of growth and min-risk wealth.

Frontier findings: the growth-optimal portfolio has the highest expected log-return AND the highest tail risk (stated for both VaR and ES frontiers); min-VaR expected log-return = -inf (degenerate extreme) while min-ES is finite, so only the mean-ES frontier is a finite usable curve; increasing confidence alpha shifts the entire frontier left (lower risk at fixed expected log-return); minimum achievable ES decreases in alpha; mean-VaR terminal payoff is digital-like (pays X^VaR in good states, 0 otherwise) while mean-ES payoff is continuous in the state price density (good states: fraction lambda/(1+lambda) of growth-optimal; intermediate: constant X^ES; bad: multiple (alpha^{-1}+lambda)/(1+lambda)); key contrast with He et al. (2015) — putting mean-WVaR on terminal wealth gives a vertical (improper) frontier, whereas the log-return criterion yields a proper concave frontier; limitations: no empirical validation, complete-market/Black-Scholes assumptions, does not address estimation error in theta (the dominant real-world Kelly risk); illustrations at T=1, r=0.05, theta=0.4.

arXiv:2411.11012v1 builds FanDuel MLB lineups as a binary integer program: maximize sum of projections subject to salary cap, positional constraints, and one-player-per-lineup binary variables, solved in Python/PuLP with the COIN-OR solver.
equation: max Σ p_i x_i s.t. Σ s_i x_i ≤ 35,000, positional constraints, x_i ∈ {0,1}, 9 players

claim: SaberSim MLB projections (June 1–11, 2019, 408 players) were biased low: mean projection 8.41 vs mean actual 9.55 fantasy points, mean salary ~$3,903, minimum actual −15.
In a 30-day analysis the highest-projected FanDuel MLB lineup averaged 144.6 actual points versus 251.9 for the hindsight-optimal lineup — a 107.3-point gap, capturing ~57% of the ex-post optimum.

Methodological critique of arXiv:2411.11012v1: maximizing mean projection is a cash-game objective misapplied to tournaments; tournament optimization needs stacking constraints and 90th-percentile upper-tail projection objectives, plus variance, ownership, and correlation modeling.

Nguyen & Yurko (2025, arXiv:2507.06122) model NFL ball-carrier frame-level turn angles with a Bayesian circular mixed-effects model on NFL Big Data Bowl 2025 tracking data (9 weeks of 2022, 9,480 plays, 136 games, 5,431 rushing attempts, 10 Hz), where frame heading b_t = atan2(y_{t+1}−y_t, x_{t+1}−x_t) and turn angle φ_t = b_t − b_{t−1}; higher von Mises concentration κ means a straighter runner.
equation: φ_ijt ~ vonMises(μ_ijt, κ_ijt); tan(μ_ijt/2) = α₀ + x_ijtᵀβ; log κ_ijt = γ₀ + z_ijtᵀψ + u_j; u_j ~ N(0, σ²_p[j])

claim: Ball-carrier model estimates: speed raises turn-angle concentration (ψ̂_s = 0.709, 95% CI [0.705, 0.713], i.e., faster = straighter); acceleration lowers it (ψ̂_a = −0.094, CI [−0.101, −0.087]); distance covered ψ̂_dis = −0.015; run plays ψ̂_run = 0.044; WR ψ̂_WR = −0.134; TE ψ̂_TE = 0.064 (CI overlaps 0).

Player-level random-effect SD of turn-angle concentration: RB σ̂ = 0.135 [0.111, 0.164], TE 0.300 [0.234, 0.378], WR 0.304 [0.257, 0.355] — WR/TE far more heterogeneous than RB; 95% CIs of top vs bottom players within RB and WR do not overlap, so estimates discriminate reliably.

Eye-test alignment from the turn-angle model: Justice Hill most variable RB, Jonathan Taylor least; DK Metcalf straight-line; George Pickens most variable WR; Kittle, Pitts, Kelce top-5 most variable TEs; correlation with combine 40-yard dash time r = 0.135.
