The turn-angle model was fit in Stan via brms with NUTS: 4 chains × 3,500 iterations (1,500 burn-in), 8,000 posterior draws, weakly informative half-t₃ priors, R̂ ≈ 1; limitations include no train/test predictive split (descriptive only), no year-over-year stability analysis, and 10 Hz sampling possibly aliasing the fastest cuts.

Florez, Guindani & Vannucci (2024, arXiv:2409.17129v1) propose Bayesian bivariate Conway-Maxwell-Poisson regression for correlated sports counts with team-specific dispersion parameters and game-level correlated random effects fit by Exchange-algorithm MCMC.
equation: P(Y=y|μ,ν) = (μ^y/y!)^ν / Z(μ,ν); E(Y) ≈ μ + 1/(2ν) − 1/2; Var(Y) ≈ μ/ν; mode = ⌊μ⌋ (ν<1 over-dispersed, ν>1 under-dispersed, ν=1 Poisson)

claim: In 20-team/380-game simulations at n=1900, CMP regression had the lowest DIC in every dispersion regime (e.g., over-dispersed y_1: CMP 7269.45 vs NB 7314.27 vs Poisson 7470.95); the true home advantage of 0.5 was recovered by CMP while Poisson/NB missed under over-/under-dispersion.

EPL COVID-era home advantage (log scale) measured by bivariate CMP: pre-pandemic 0.238 (26.8% more home goals), during 0.0916 (9.6%), post 0.288 (33.4%); P(HA_during < HA_before) = 0.8525, P(HA_during < HA_after) = 0.9527; home win% moved 45% → 39% → 44% but the ANOVA p = 0.154 is not significant.

CMP model limitations: 1,000 Exchange-algorithm iterations ≈ 30 s vs ~15 s for Poisson/NB; real-data fits used 180K iterations with ESS only 400–500; diffuse priors break convergence (R̂ up to 4–5); all model comparison is in-sample DIC with no out-of-sample forecasting.

Meister (2024, arXiv:2412.14144): the Kelly-optimal fraction for an all-or-nothing binary contract is f = (q−p)/(1−p), where q is subjective belief and p is market price (equivalently f = (Q−P)/(1+Q) with P = p/(1−p), Q = q/(1−q)).

Meister's modified payout for non-binary payoff structure: U_α(q,p,f) = (1−q)·log(1−f) + q·log(1 + f·(p/(1−p))^α), with Chernoff bound F(k,N,p) ≤ exp(−N·D(k/N‖p)) and k_Q(f) = (Q − N·log(1−f))/(log(1+f) − log(1−f)).

Error asymmetry result: misestimating the win probability costs growth linearly in ε, D(k/N‖p+ε) − D(k/N‖p) = ((p − k/N)/(p(1−p)))·ε + O(ε²), while miscalculating the Kelly fraction costs only quadratically, U(p, 2p−1+ε) − U(p, 2p−1) = −ε²/(4p(1−p)) + O(ε³) — so probability accuracy matters more than sizing precision.

Under Kelly-optimal behavior the gap between prediction-market prices and participants' mean beliefs can be enormous: in a toy two-investor case with 0%/100% beliefs, even the minutest capital imbalance drives the price to zero or one while the mean expectation barely moves from 1/2; gap bounds E_− ∈ [0, 1/2] for p < 1/2, [1/2, 1] for p > 1/2, = 1/2 at p = 1/2, and E_+ = p.
equation: Σ_i C_i·f_i(p, q_i) = 0; mean belief = capital-weighted Σ C_i·q_i

claim: Szczecinski (2022, arXiv:2010.11187v3) G-Elo: margin of victory is discretized into J+1 ordinal point-differential categories and fit with an Adjacent Categories model, yielding Elo-identical updates θ_{t+1,i} ← θ_{t,i} + K̃σ(ỹ_t − G(z_t)) with redefined scores; binary Elo and Elo-Davidson are special cases (J=1, J=2).

G-Elo Adjacent Categories model: Pr{Y_t=h|z_t} = 10^{α_h+δ_h z_t/σ} / Σ_l 10^{α_l+δ_l z_t/σ} (Eq. 11) with symmetry α_h = α_{J−h}, δ_h = −δ_{J−h}; NFL J=6 categories {d<−10}, {−10≤d<−5}, {−5≤d<0}, {d=0}, {0<d≤5}, {5<d≤10}, {d>10} with thresholds Δ′=5, Δ″=10.

G-Elo closed-form frequency coefficient estimators: ξ = √(f_0 f_J); η = (1/2)log10(f_H/f_A); α_h = (1/2)log10(f_h f_{J−h}) − log10 ξ; δ_h = (1/(2η))log10(f_h/f_{J−h}); J=2 reduces to Elo-Davidson with κ = 10^{α_1}, α_1 = log10(f_D/√(f_H f_A)) — exposing that plain Elo's implicit κ=2 assumes ~50% draws.

NFL (10 seasons 2009/10–2018/19, first five train / last five test, metrics on second half of test seasons): G-Elo J=6 achieved LS 0.6224, RPS 0.2166, accuracy 0.6656 vs Elo-Davidson LS 0.6304, RPS 0.2200, accuracy 0.6375 — a +2.8pp accuracy gain largely from dropping draw modeling (NFL draw frequency f_D = 0.001).

EPL results for G-Elo J=6: LS 0.9679, RPS 0.1987, accuracy 0.5389 vs Elo-Davidson LS 0.9740, RPS 0.2006, accuracy 0.5442 — small consistent log-score/RPS gains, accuracy flat; closed-form frequency estimators generalized slightly better than ML-optimized coefficients on test data, and the K̃ minimizing training log-loss also minimized test log-loss.

arXiv:2202.13749v1, a 123-page master's thesis running OpenSim/SCONE/Moco musculoskeletal what-if simulations of ACL landing mechanics, was REJECTED in the ledger: no injury-labeled cohort, no validated prediction of actual injury incidence, no ROC/AUC metrics, no epidemiological comparison.

ACL landing simulation outputs: landing height 30→55 cm raised vGRF 1.436→1.797 BW and anterior tibial force 6.300→6.699 (units as reported); sweeping the Moco effort-goal weight 0→1 swung vGRF 1.967→11.479 BW — a ~6× swing from one free modeling parameter, demonstrating that simulation-based injury claims without injury labels are quantitatively fragile.

Beep (arXiv:2307.11780v2, KDD 2023) mines multivariate sequential patterns by minimizing an MDL objective over pattern sets: minimize_P L(S|P) = L(P) + Σ_{s∈S} L(s|P), with pattern-set description length plus encoded sequence length (code table CT / code stream CS).

Beep encoding: pattern code L(code_p(p)) = −log2(usage(p)/Σ usage(p_i)); gap/fill/miss codes as relative shares of gaps+fills+misses; miss codes add L_N(|A|) extra bits for the missing-attribute index; code-table length L(P) = L(ST) + L(CT*) with universal-integer coding L_N(k).
Beep's noise tolerance: empty values match any value; missing values tolerate single-value noise (≤ ||p||/10, at most 1 per event); gap events ≤ |p|−1; interleaving and overlapping patterns allowed.

Beep search: initialize with all singletons; iterate pair-combination candidates at every alignment (conflicts → missing value); add candidates reducing L(S|P); prune patterns whose removal reduces L(S|P); stop at stabilization; greedy Krimp-style covering in order ↓||p||, ↓support, ↑lexicographic, KMP search per pattern, time O(|P|·||s|| + ||P|| + ||s||) per sequence.

Beep acceleration via weighted LSH (Ioffe weighted minhash) on sequence-position sets (segments ≤ 20 events), combining pairs only when weighted Jaccard similarity ≥ threshold; LSH alone cut runtime ~10× (1276→120 s, synthetic row 3) at small ΔL% cost.

Table-tennis case study (716 rallies, 10 matches, avg 5.91 events/rally, 4 categorical attributes): Beep returned |P|=62 patterns at avg frequency 12.94 in 425 s vs Ditto |P|=161 at 4.36 in 1747 s (~4.1× faster, 2.6× fewer patterns, ~3× higher per-pattern frequency).

Beep synthetic evaluation: consistently higher ΔL% than Ditto at lower runtime (row 1: Ditto ΔL%=24.5 in 399 s vs Beep ΔL%=27.2 in 79 s, ~5.1×; row 5: Ditto 175 s vs Beep 18 s, ~9.7×); all algorithms recovered all 5 planted patterns per dataset (manual check); a Beep miss-tolerant pattern spanning single-value deviations surfaced an actual data-recording error confirmed by analysts.

Santosh et al. (2024, arXiv:2409.18645v1): selective classifier h=(f,g) with coverage C(h) = fraction predicted, risk R(h) = error on the predicted subset, selection function g(x)=1[g̃(x)>γ]; summaries AURCC (area under risk–coverage curve, lower better), RPP (reversed pair proportion), and Refinement Rf = Σ 1[g̃(x_i)<g̃(x_j), l_i<l_j] / c(|D|−c).
equation: g(x)=1[g̃(x)>γ]; Rf = Σ 1[g̃(x_i)<g̃(x_j), l_i<l_j] / c(|D|−c), c = #correct

claim: Confidence estimators tested: Softmax Response SR = max_y p(y); MC Dropout (10 runs) variants SMP (sample-mean max prob), PV (probability variance), BALD (mutual information / total uncertainty).

Confident Error Regularizer (CER): LCER = Σ_{i,j} Δ_{i,j} 1[e_i > e_j] with Δ_{i,j} = max{0, max_y p_i(y) − max_y p_j(y)}² — penalizes confidence exceeding that of an easier example; weights ∈ {0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5} tuned on AURCC.
equation: LCER = Σ_{i,j} Δ_{i,j} 1[e_i > e_j], Δ_{i,j} = max{0, max_y p_i(y) − max_y p_j(y)}²

claim: MC Dropout beats softmax confidence on every task/metric (e.g., Task B LexLM-large task-loss: SR AURCC 17.92 vs BALD 14.42; RPP 0.914 vs 0.745; mac-F1 64.31); among MC variants BALD leads slightly, then PV, then SMP (BALD captures total incl. aleatoric uncertainty).

CER improves all selective metrics without harming accuracy (Task B LexLM-base: mac-F1 61.42 → 65.21 with CER; AURCC 16.86 → 16.85 SMP / 15.37 PV); the ECE regularizer hurts both calibration and accuracy (non-differentiable); Gambler's loss gives comparable accuracy but worse selective metrics.

Domain pre-training helps calibration but more in-domain ECtHR corpus in pre-training produces more overconfidence (InCaseLawBERT with no ECtHR had the best selective metrics; LegalBERT worse than LexLM); larger models are more accurate but more overconfident (LexLM-large best Task-B accuracy 64.31–65.82 mac-F1 yet overconfident on harder tasks A|B and A).

LexGLUE ECtHR dataset: 11k case fact descriptions, multi-label over 14 convention articles; chronological split train 2001–2016 (9k), val 2016–2017 (1k), test 2017–2019 (1k); tasks B (alleged articles), A (decided violations), A|B (violations given allegations).

AISTATS 2020 dynamic Bradley-Terry: logit(p_ij(t)) = β_i(t) − β_j(t), Σ_i β_i(t) = 0 (Eq. 2); procedure kernel-smooths pairwise data X̃(t) = Σ_m W_h(t,t_m) X^(m) with a Gaussian kernel and LOOCV bandwidth, then fits static BT on smoothed data: β̂(t) = argmin_{Σβ_i=0} R(β;t) (Eq. 6). Reduces to static BT when all t_m equal.

Dynamic BT oracle bounds: pointwise ‖β̂(t)−β*(t)‖_∞ ≤ 48M*(t)κ_h(t) + C_s·h (Thm 5.2); simplified ≤ 72Kκ_h(t) + C_s·h with K = exp(1/p_min) (Thm 5.4); rates O(max{M*κ_h, (log N/(NT))^{1/3}}), matching the Hölder-1 nonparametric rate (exponent 2/3).

BT-true simulations (N=50 teams, 50 time points): rank displacement 2.29 (dynamic BT) vs 3.75 (win rate) vs 3.75 (static BT); LOO prob error 0.37 (both BTs) vs 0.44; LOO nll 0.55 vs 0.56. Model-agnostic: rank displacement 5.48 vs 10.68/10.70; LOO nll 0.68 vs 0.71.

NFL 2011–2015 (nflWAR package): dynamic BT season-end top-10s matched 6–10 of FiveThirtyEight ELO's top 10 each season using no margin-of-victory information; average rank displacement vs ELO 3.4–5.0 across seasons.

Dynamic BT existence/uniqueness: P(Condition 4.1 holds ∀t) ≥ 1 − 4N²exp(−NTp_min/2) (Thm 5.1); assumptions A5.1 (each pair plays ≥ T̲>0 times, controlled spacing), A5.2 (p_ij(t) Lipschitz, ≥ p_min > 0), A5.3 (symmetric bounded kernel, finite total variation); limitations: targets smoothly changing strengths (can miss abrupt changes), no home-field term, NFL validation is rank-overlap only with no probabilistic forecast skill.

2026 arXiv benchmark of five conformal prediction interval wrappers for multi-horizon time series (>3,000 monthly sales series, AutoARIMA base, horizon 12): split CP interval Γ_α(x_new) = [ŷ_new − q_{1−α}, ŷ_new + q_{1−α}] with q the ⌈(1−α)(n_cal+1)⌉-th order statistic; coverage guarantee P(Y ∈ Γ) ≥ 1−α.

Winkler interval score: WIS_i = (u−ℓ) + 2/α·(miss distance), lower better; in the benchmark, valid at 90% were Global-CP, AcMCP, MSCP, ACI, Parametric-PI, while Nixtla-CP, EnbPI, and SPCI (worst) under-covered.

Winkler CD ranking: MSCP (horizon-specific rolling residual matrix S ∈ R^{T×H}, per-horizon quantile) ranked #1, then Parametric-PI, then ACI; MSCP statistically separated on the larger corpus — confirming horizon-specific split CP as the efficient multi-horizon interval design (ACI as coverage-drift fallback).

Adaptive CP update rule tested in the benchmark: ACI with α_{t+1} = α_t + γ(α − err_t); other methods: EnbPI (ensemble bootstrap LOO residuals), SPCI (quantile regression on lagged residuals), Global-CP (Bonferroni α/H), AcMCP (MA(h−1) nonconformity update).

arXiv paper analyzing the 2023 Wimbledon men's final was REJECTED: no genuine Bayesian inference (no priors/posteriors/MCMC), no code, no named data sources, no proper scoring; claimed accuracy 0.913–0.932 and macro-F1 0.912 are circular (labels derived from the same Bayes computation); momentum–win-rate cosine similarity was only 0.0923, undermining the claimed correlation.

Management Science 2026 angular combining: a one-parameter (θ) continuum between horizontal (quantile) and vertical (linear-opinion-pool) averaging of predictive CDFs, FA,θ((1/k)Σxi(c)) = (1/k)ΣFi(xi(c)) along angled line y = −tanθ(x−c); θ=0° → horizontal, θ=90° → vertical.

Angular combining theorems: Var(horizontal) < Var(angular) < Var(vertical); prediction intervals nest horizontal ⊆ angular ⊆ vertical; CRPS(angular) ≤ average member CRPS (Theorem 3); CRPS(F,z) = ∫(F(x)−1(x>z))²dx.

COVID-19 Forecast Hub (84 origins, 52 series): angular averaging +0.8% MQS skill vs vertical (51.5 vs 52.6), weighted angular +2.7% (49.4 vs 50.5); fixed θ=67.5° best no-optimization choice (+1.4%); angular strongest in tails/95% intervals.

Survey of Professional Forecasters CRPS×100: angular beat vertical on US growth (37.8 vs 38.0) and US inflation (35.8 vs 36.4), lost ECB unemployment 22.8 vs 22.6; Nord Pool electricity (2013–2018): angular avg best of averaging methods in all selections (e.g., 177.7 vs vertical 178.9), DM tests significant in >half of 24 series, significantly worse in none; caveat that gains are small in absolute terms (0.4–2.7%).

CQRA-T (Wang et al. 2018, arXiv:1803.06730): per-quantile ensemble weights fit by minimizing pinball loss under nonnegativity + sum-to-one constraints as a linear program — combination ŷ_{t,q} = Σ_n ω_{n,q} ŷ_{n,t,q} (Eq. 15), weights from min_ω Σ_t pinball_q s.t. Σω_n=1, ω_n≥0 (Eq. 14) via auxiliary variables (Eq. 17); overall score L = mean pinball over test years × quantiles (Eq. 18).
equation: ŷ_{t,q} = Σ_n ω_{n,q} ŷ_{n,t,q}; min_ω Σ_t pinball_q s.t. Σω_n=1, ω_n≥0

claim: Simplex constraints make CQRA a special case of lasso → automatic model pruning; quantile crossing handled by naive rearrangement (Chernozhukov et al. 2010).

ISO New England hourly load (2013–2016, 8 zones + system): CQRA-T had lowest pinball loss on all 9 profiles; average improvement vs best individual 4.39% (SYS: 269.953 vs 288.563; CT: 77.961 vs 81.478; ME: 17.492 vs 18.146); pruning kept 6–9 of 13 models per quantile, models #12/#13 pruned for all quantiles.

Cautionary: CQRA-E (simplex constraints on averaged quantiles) strongly worsened vs QRA-E (e.g., SYS 356.527 vs 276.417) — constraints help only with targeted-quantile regressors; unconstrained QRA variants were worse than the best individual on all 10 CER consumers.

VTCS (Iwashita et al. 2025, arXiv:2508.17611): temporal-counterfactual framework shifting a player's movement-initiation timing (±1 s, ξ ∈ [−15,15] frames) and scoring each counterfactual with wUPPCF = UPPCF_i · w_d · w_s (Eq. 5); V_frame(t) = mean wUPPCF over rendezvous region Ω(t) (Eqs. 6–8); V_scenario(ξ) = max 15-frame moving average of V_frame (Eq. 9); V_timing = V_scenario(0) − max_{ξ≠0} V_scenario(ξ) (Eq. 10).
equation: V_timing = V_scenario(0) − max_{ξ≠0} V_scenario(ξ); wUPPCF = UPPCF_i · w_d · w_s

claim: VTCS data (UltimateTrack, drone footage of Nagoya University scrimmages, 18,075 frames at 15 FPS, 64 possessions, 15 entities): 455 candidate initiation sequences → 310 retained after visual review; XGBoost pass-target predictor RMSE ≈ 0.316, R² ≈ 0.163; V_frame separates actual pass targets from non-targets with KS D = 0.3147 (p = 0); team-relative ranking Mann–Whitney p = 0, Cliff's δ = −0.339.

VTCS skill-group surprise: novices' V_timing concentrated closer to zero than experienced players — attributed to homogeneous movement constraining counterfactual range plus heavier defensive pressure on experts; V_timing captures context-adaptive decision quality, not raw skill. Limitations: no outcome prediction tested, no baseline comparison, all other players frozen (limitation acknowledged), 15 FPS limits timing resolution.

ENS-10 (Ashkboos et al. 2022, arXiv:2206.14786): ECMWF IFS reforecasts (Cy43r1/Cy45r1, 0.5° lat/lon), 10 ensemble members, lead times 0/24/48 h, 1998–2017 (20 years), ~3 TB, CC BY 4.0, ERA5 ground truth; train 1998–2015, test 2016–2017. Differentiable Gaussian closed-form CRPS (Baringhaus–Franz identity): CRPS(F,x) = σ[2ψ((x−μ)/σ) + ((x−μ)/σ)(2φ((x−μ)/σ) − 1) − 1/√π].

ENS-10 extreme-event metric: EECRPS(F,y) := |EFI(i,j)| × CRPS(F,y), where the Extreme Forecast Index EFI ∈ [−1,1] measures ensemble deviation from climatology (|EFI| 0.5–0.8 unusual, >0.8 very unusual).

ENS-10 T2m CRPS (10 members): raw 0.733, EMOS 0.749 (worse), MLP 0.672, LeNet 0.659, U-Net 0.644, Transformer 0.626 (best, ~15% under raw); EECRPS T2m raw 0.25 → Transformer 0.214 best; extreme-event skill tracks average skill (no extreme-event breakthrough); 5-ENS vs 10-ENS: all models degrade with 5 members (T2m Transformer 0.649 vs 0.626) — member count matters.

ENS-10 limitations for sports weather: only three variables baselined (Z500, T850, T2m) — no wind speed, no precipitation; Gaussian outputs can't represent multimodal precipitation or bounded quantities; 48 h global benchmark ≠ stadium-scale nowcasting; model cycle changes (Cy43r1/Cy45r1) mean reforecasts can't be pooled across eras.

Hajishirzi et al. (UAI 2012, arXiv:1210.4854): weakly-supervised pipeline aligning sports commentary sentences to structured game events using only rough temporal alignment — per-pair exemplar-SVM models (PairModel), PageRank-style popularity ranking (PairRank), greedy macro-event discovery; dataset PSC: 8 EPL 2010–2011 games, 935 sentences (avg 16.62 words), 14,845 events, 2,147-word vocabulary, 306 players, 55 event types, 1,404 hand-labeled pairs (evaluation only).

Commentary-alignment results: PSC F1 41.4 (AUC 46.8, Precision 33.9, Recall 54.0) vs Liang et al. 2009 27.6, MIL 11.0, No PairModel 23.3, No PairRank 27.3 (>14 pp gain over SOTA claimed); ablations: replacing PairModel with Euclidean distance costs 16 points, replacing PairRank with voting costs 13; macro-event cardinality F1 rises dramatically up to k=4, no boost beyond.
equation: argmax_{|Ei|≤k} ρ(Si,Ei)  (Eq. 1, greedy submodular marginal-gain merge)

claim: RoboCup commentary benchmark (micro-F1): approach 81.6 vs Chen & Mooney 2008 67.0, Chen et al. 2010 73.5, Liang et al. 2009 75.7, Hajishirzi et al. 2011 77.9; with Bordes et al. 2010 heuristics 84.57 vs their 83.0. Limitations: absolute F1 41.4 modest; only pairs with a matching player name get PairModels (tactical/stat sentences invisible); forces ≥1 event per sentence (wrong for stats/weather/strategy); pairwise design scales quadratically; no code released.

arXiv:2605.00864 measured algorithmic arbitrage in Polymarket NBA markets from 75,088,497 high-frequency limit-order-book snapshots (Feb 4 – Mar 4, 2026, 173 games, 3,042 single markets): long arb condition Ask_A + Ask_B < 1.00; short arb (mint-and-sell) Bid_A + Bid_B > 1.00; combinatorial ML-vs-spread Ask(ML_A) + Ask(Spread_dog) < 1.00 with unified state machine T_U = T_ML ∪ T_S and strict forward-fill.

Polymarket NBA single-market arbitrage: 37 raw episodes → 30 (81.1%) post-game artifacts excluded → 7 valid in-game episodes; markets in arb only 0.0001% of time; median duration 3.614 s; capped profit $210.19 aggregate (one blowout outlier; ex-outlier median yield 11.0%, $11.01/episode); uncapped $4,418.44.

Combinatorial (moneyline vs spread) arb: 523 candidates → 233 post-game excluded → 290 active episodes (279 in-game); median 2.00 episodes/game; median duration 16.0 s; median yield 101.01 bps; capped profit $559.59 vs uncapped $2,032.75; 76.9% of episodes liquidity-constrained, average executable size 14.79 shares.

Polymarket NBA liquidity context: median bid-ask spreads pre-game 392.20 bps, in-game 1030.90 bps, post-game 7532.65 bps; 85.7% of arb episodes could absorb $100; polling constraint 3.6–5.5 s per market means arb frequency is a lower bound and durations are upper bounds; Polymarket NBA volume grew $51M (2024) → $0.89B (2025), ~17.45×.

arXiv:2608.00666 measures executable (not theoretical) arbitrage in Polymarket negative-risk multi-outcome markets via payoff identities: subset identity Σ_{k∈S} N_k ≡ (|S|−1)·1 + Σ_{j∈Q\S} Y_j (Eq. 1); settlement edges Δ^settle_Y(t) = 1 − Σ_i a_t(Y_i) and Δ^settle_N(t) = (|Q|−1) − Σ_i a_t(N_i) (Eq. 2).

Converter edge: Δ^{N→Y}_S(t) = (|S|−1) + Σ_{j∈Q\S} b_t(Y_j) − Σ_{k∈S} a_t(N_k) (Eq. 3); reverse edge Δ^{Y→N}_S(t) = Σ_k b_t(N_k) − Σ_{j∈Q\S} a_t(Y_j) − (|S|−1) (Eq. 4, no protocol path); reverse adapter qΣ_{j∈Q\S}Y_j + (|S|−1)q·1 ≡ qΣ_{i∈S}N_i (Eq. 5). Edges measured depth-aware via joint depth-walking, fee-adjusted with conservative taker assumption.

Polymarket arb findings: ~$1.118M mechanism-linked total profit — $1.086M converter-enabled (97%), $32,283 settlement-based (excludes judged-coordinated $381,748 anomaly cluster, 3 addresses, Dec 12 2025); CLOB violation asymmetry 2,098 positive YES-side episodes vs 36 NO-side — violations concentrate on the unsupported protocol side.

Violation persistence: median exact duration 16.15 s (YES, n=253) vs 7.99 s (NO, n=5); 366/624 (58.7%) episodes window-spanning (≥50 min); FPMM ~40% of episodes persist >50 min, some >1 day; converter profit concentrated: top-10 addresses ≈75% of profit; median profit/conversion decayed $1.00 (through Jul 2024) → $0.20 (late 2024–2025) → $0.08 (early 2026) — intensifying competition.

arXiv:1908.08684 (REJECTED in ledger): nonlinear-programming equity-portfolio optimizer minimizing average or maximum trailing 20-day drawdown (four programs MINAVG, MINMAX, MINMAX-S, MINAVG-S), T=30-day in-sample, rebalance every 10 days, ~180 rebalances, SCIP with max(500, 7N) seconds per rebalance; rejected because it sizes from trailing realized drawdown with no edge/probability input and no usable stake-sizing rule.

Ledger assessment of the drawdown-optimizer paper: the claimed >99%-of-out-of-sample-days cumulative-return dominance for EURO STOXX 50 with zero transaction costs, overlapping 30-day in-sample windows, and 10-day rebalancing is a classic overfit signature (in-sample drawdown minimization fitting recent noise).

EnbPI (Chen Xu, Yao Xie, TPAMI 2021, arXiv:2010.09107): no-data-splitting conformal prediction for time series using a bootstrap ensemble LOO predictor f̂_{-i}^{φ} = φ({f̂^b : i ∉ S_b}) with φ = mean (B = 20–50, 25 used); residuals ε̂_i = Y_i − f̂_{-i}^{φ}(X_i); interval C_t = [f̂(X_t) + q̂_β(ε̂-window), f̂(X_t) + q̂_{1−α+β}(ε̂-window)] with β ∈ [0,α] chosen to minimize width (asymmetric quantile); sliding residual window (batch size s = 1), all data trains AND calibrates; coverage → 1−α asymptotically without exchangeability.

Atlanta hourly solar radiation (2018, α=0.1): at train-ratio 0.10 (scarce data) EnbPI coverage 0.893 (SE 1.8e-3) vs AdaptCI 0.828, J+aB 0.747, QOOB 0.684, ICP 0.646, Weighted ICP 0.608 — the no-splitting design dominates exactly when data is scarce; at 0.19: 0.897 vs 0.891; at 0.28: 0.905 vs 0.909.

EnbPI change-point simulation (T=600, mean/variance change at 60%, residual window T′=100): the sliding window re-covers faster than fixed-window methods after the change; retraining after 60 post-change points restores nominal coverage. Limitations: asymptotic theory only (finite-sample coverage empirical); window length T′ untuned; sliding window discards all old residuals even in stable regimes; B=25 × weekly refits is compute-heavy.

O'Hagan et al. (arXiv:2002.01193, 2020): copula-based multivariate hidden Markov model for football momentum regimes — hidden states S_t ∈ {1..K}; state-dependent joint f(y_t|S_t) = c(F_1(y_1t|θ_1), F_2(y_2t|θ_2); η)·f_1·f_2 with Conway–Maxwell–Poisson marginals and Clayton copula; transitions via multinomial logit P(S_t=j|S_{t-1}=i, x_t) = exp(γ_ij′x_t) / Σ_k exp(γ_ik′x_t) with covariates opponent market value, score diff, home/away, match minute; estimation by numerical ML via nlm() with 50 random starts; model selection by AIC/BIC over K=2..5 and copula families.

Copula-HMM on Borussia Dortmund 2017/18 (34 matches, 3,214 minute-level observations of shots on goal + ball touches): copula model beat conditional-independence baseline by ΔAIC = 48, ΔBIC = 35 (Clayton selected); BIC + interpretability favor K=3 states (3-state BIC 20,979 vs 2-state 21,020 vs 4-state 21,030 vs 5-state 21,098); 3-state means shots 0.226/0.132/0.147, touches 2.032/4.583/9.732 — decoded as low-control/counter-attack, balanced, dominant possession; adding all transition covariates improved fit by ΔAIC = 51.

Copula-HMM trust caveat: all model selection is in-sample on one team's season (no out-of-sample validation), and decoded momentum states confound coaching tactical shifts with momentum — any port must control for scheme/tempo changes or the states will rediscover them.

arXiv:2309.01641 (2023): expectation propagation as approximate-inference backend for dynamic probit smoothing (y_t∈{0,1}, P(y_t=1)=Φ(x_t′θ_t), θ_t random walk) — EP approximates the SUN smoothing distribution p(θ_1:T|y_1:T) by Gaussian q(θ)=N(m,V) with per-t site updates: cavity q_{\t}(θ_t) ∝ q(θ_t)/q̃_t(θ_t), tilted p̂ ∝ q_{\t}·p(y_t|θ_t), moment-match E_p̂[θ_t], Cov_p̂[θ_t]; probit likelihood gives closed-form tilted moments via univariate truncated-normal formulas; state dynamics via Kalman-smoother forward-backward passes per EP sweep.

EP benchmark (CAC40 daily opening direction, n=241, 2023 MacBook Pro): EP 0.43 s vs PFM-VB 0.27 s, MF-VB 0.20 s, exact SUN sampler 36.28 s — EP ~100× faster than exact sampling but ~60% more expensive than PFM-VB for a small accuracy gain (EP slightly more accurate than PFM-VB vs 10,000 exact smoothing draws; MF-VB visibly over-shrinks); EP has no convergence guarantee (damping/double-loop needed in hard cases); fixed W, P_0; no predictive calibration.

arXiv:2406.13749 (2024): theory of forecast pooling when experts communicate over a network before reporting — Attention Centrality αᵢ(A) = Σ_{j∈Nᵢ(A)} 1/dⱼ − 1 (Def. 4); the pooling effect decomposes into zero-mean network bias E_ϵ[𝓑(x)|A] = 0 (Prop. 1) plus topology-driven variance Var[𝓑(x)|A] = (σ²/n)(n⁻¹Σᵢαᵢ² + 2ρn⁻¹Σ_{i<j}αᵢαⱼ).

Network topology corollaries: star topology (n≥3) gives Var = σ²(1−ρ)(n−2)²(n−1)/(4n³) → σ²(1−ρ)/4 as n→∞ — the star is the WORST structure (e.g., every model leaning on one hub input like the consensus line); line topology gives Var = σ²(1−ρ)/(9n²) → 0; d-regular/balanced networks give αᵢ=0 ∀i hence zero network bias and zero network-induced variance (the 'only if' direction is proof-under-review).
equation: Cor. 1 (star): Var = σ²(1−ρ)(n−2)²(n−1)/(4n³); Cor. 2 (line): Var = σ²(1−ρ)/(9n²)

claim: Shared pre-pooling communication adds NO bias in expectation but inflates pooled-forecast variance governed entirely by information topology — averaging more models that read the same hub is not diversification; realized network bias for a fixed network + fixed season can be ±1/3-scale. Lemma 1: under common correlation + common variance, Bayesian pooling collapses to simple average — pooling-rule choice adds nothing.

Janvin, Young, Ryalen & Stensrud (arXiv:2202.08500, 2022): formal causal-inference framework for recurrent events with competing events — estimands: total effect E[Y^{a=1}_k] vs E[Y^{a=0}_k] (Eq. 1); controlled direct effect E[Y^{a=1,d̄=0}_k] vs E[Y^{a=0,d̄=0}_k] (Eq. 3); separable effects via hypothetical treatment components (aY, aD) with isolation conditions (Eq. 4); estimators via a unified stochastic differential equation with Horvitz–Thompson/Hájek IPW integrators; a competing event is censoring for the controlled direct effect but NOT for the total effect.
equation: Total: E[Y^{a=1}_k] vs E[Y^{a=0}_k]; CDE: E[Y^{a=1,d̄=0}_k] vs E[Y^{a=0,d̄=0}_k]

claim: SPRINT trial demonstration (1,312 standard + 1,311 intensive arms, recurrent AKI over 1,000 days): total effect 0.017 [−0.001, 0.037]; controlled direct effect 0.017 [−0.003, 0.037]; separable direct effect (aD=1) 0.011 [−0.005, 0.034] — all 95% bootstrap CIs, weights truncated to [0.2, 5], smoothing b ∈ {100, 200, 500} similar; borderline increased AKI under intensive treatment with no evidence the kidney-specific component explains it; separable effects rest on strong, untestable modified-treatment assumptions.

Raeth & Ludwig (2025, arXiv:2512.14779): decision-calibration framework comparing ECMWF IFS ENS vs ArchesweatherGen on frost, heat, and wind-power decision tasks — Bayes decision rule δ_c(F_x) = argmin_a E_{Y~F_x}[c(a,Y)] (Eq. 1); cost gap C_gap = |C_exp − C_obs| (Eq. 4) between forecast-anticipated and observed decision costs; key structural insight: miscalibration only changes decisions where cost functions cross; elsewhere calibration is irrelevant.

Decision-calibration findings (WeatherBench 50-member ensembles, Europe 2021, 1.5°): frost — CRPS/PIT/SSR similar yet decision rankings change as threshold θ rises; heat — Arches improves over IFS at high θ (tail events) with geographic variation lost in spatial aggregation (better in Mediterranean than central Europe); wind power at 1-day lead — Arches slightly worse on CRPS/SSR but better on decision calibration and lower observed costs ('from an economic perspective, Arches is the better model'); model rankings flip between forecast-level and decision-level evaluation.

arXiv:2202.03034 (2022): two-parameter energy-conservation model of the coefficient of restitution ε of a gas-filled ball vs internal pressure — ε² = (P_in − P_out + λ_1)/(P_in − P_out + λ_2), with λ_1 = fictitious pressure from rubber energy storage, λ_2 = λ + λ_1; temperature extension via P_in = kT → ε(T) with Kelvin constants T_1 = P_out/k, T_2 = (P_out − λ)/k; validated −22°C to 80°C. Ideal gas law gives ~1 psi pressure drop per ~20°F temperature drop (ΔP/P = ΔT/T).
equation: ε² = (P_in − P_out + λ_1)/(P_in − P_out + λ_2); ε² = E_a/E_b = (h_a/h_b); ΔP/P = ΔT/T

claim: Ball restitution measurements: basketball ε 0.407 (deflated) → 0.869 (13 psi gauge) — pressure dominates liveliness; tennis ball ε 0.447 at −22°C → 0.813 at 80°C (temperature swings move ε by ~0.37); χ² fits: basketball χ² = 13.4 (13 dof; 90% threshold 19.8) at λ_1 = 0.80, λ_2 = 4.67; tennis temperature χ² = 3.3 (90% threshold 9.2) at T_1 = 237.3 K, T_2 = 177.3 K.

Ball restitution limitations: test velocity ~6 m/s vs up to 65 m/s in competitive tennis (small-deformation assumption breaks at elite impact speeds); no NFL football tested (prolate spheroid, laces) — basketball→football extrapolation needs empirical validation.

Hu et al. (arXiv:2406.12084v2, 2026): Discounted Cumulative Accuracy for narrative score aggregation — DCA = Σ_{t=0}^{T} p_t(1 − t/T), with p_t = (1/N)Σ_n 1{|s_n − s*_n| = t} — exact accuracy at T=0, linear near-miss discount as T grows (DCG-inspired); tolerances tested T ∈ {0,1,3,5,10}, rankings stable across T.

NBA narrative score aggregation (28,492 ESPN games 2002–2023, 400 human-written quarters): monolithic accuracy Claude-3-Opus 67.20% / DCA 93.56, GPT-4o 45.54% / 86.70, Llama-3-70B 17.45%, Llama-3-8B 4.43%, Gemini-Pro-1.5 4.58%; divide-and-conquer DnC-10 → GPT-4o 88.61% / 98.41 (nearly doubles monolithic), Claude-3-Opus DnC-10 84.16%, Llama-3-70B DnC-3 80.45%; batch-10 optimal for strong models, batch-3 for weaker, batch-1 underperforms everywhere.

SportsGen (Hu et al.): turn-by-turn Markov action graph over 16 actions; team efficiency E ∈ [0,100]; S:NS ratios ∈ {1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5}; per-action Gaussian timestamps; avg game 466 plays / 6,229 tokens; human/GPT-4 preference: SportsGen preferred 39%, tie 7–9%, NBA narratives 52–54%; denser scoring degrades all models and symbolic substitution degrades GPT-4o/Llama-3-70B (Claude-3-Opus most resilient); DnC-10 costs ~10× the calls of monolithic (unquoted price) and score-summation is the easiest aggregation so these accuracies are an upper bound for per-player attribution.

Augenblick, Lazarus & Thaler (2021, arXiv:2109.09871): overinference from weak signals, underinference from strong signals — perceived signal strength Ŝ = k·S^β with fitted k=0.88, β=0.76 (Study 1a); overinference when S < S* = k^{1/(1−β)}, underinference above.

DGP-agnostic Bayesian test (Proposition 2): E[M_{t1,t2}] = E[R_{t1,t2}] for any DGP under Bayesian updating, where M = Σ squared belief changes (movement), R = drop in perceived variance u_t(π) = (1−π_t)π_t (uncertainty reduction); excess movement = M − R, >0 = overinference, <0 = underinference.
equation: E[M_{t1,t2}] = E[R_{t1,t2}]; u_t(π) = (1−π_t)π_t; excess movement = M − R

claim: Betfair 2006–2014 (>5M in-play transactions, five sports, ~260k events): all five sports show movement > uncertainty reduction early and movement below uncertainty reduction late — basketball crosses at end of Q3; four of five sports stay negative after crossing (hockey returns only in the final period); S&P 500 options show positive excess movement until a few weeks before expiry, then reverse within two weeks; lab: robust underinference for strong signals (diagnosticity p ≥ 2/3), overinference for weak signals (novel).

Overinference paper limitations: prices-as-beliefs is a joint test; speculative trading can generate excess movement even if individuals are Bayesian; signal strength proxied by time-to-maturity (monotone proxy, microstructure confounds possible); Betfair 2006–2014 market structure is dated; football included but figures emphasize basketball; no out-of-sample trading test.

Kardaras, Obłój & Platen (2012, arXiv:1206.2305): a drawdown-constrained growth-optimal (numéraire) strategy exists, is unique, and is given explicitly by the Azéma–Yor transform of the unconstrained Kelly fund — operationally, a state-dependent fraction of wealth in the Kelly fund vs cash, set by the acceptable drawdown parameter α, under drawdown constraint X_t ≥ α · max_{s≤t} X_s, α ∈ [0,1).

Numéraire property via expected relative return: X/X̂ is a nonnegative local martingale (Theorem 1.3, under no-arbitrage-of-first-kind (A1) + long-run growth (A2)); the Azéma–Yor transform ^αX̂ is a model-independent pathwise bijection between wealth processes and drawdown-constrained ones with the numéraire property in the constrained class; turnpike theorem (3.6): asymptotically growth-optimal = limit of finite-horizon numéraire strategies.

Ledger's discrete-time reconstruction of the Azéma–Yor rule: risky fraction π = 1 − α/d_t where d_t = B_t/M_t (bankroll / running max), i.e., risk only the cushion above the α floor; suggested start α = 0.7 (never lose >30% from peak); with a savings baseline, X̂ and ^αX̂ share the same instantaneous Sharpe ratio (both on the Markowitz efficient frontier).

Gilbert (2009, arXiv:0911.3100): under the Independent Chip Model, a 'fair bet' (zero-EV gamble, E[Δc_i] = 0, Var(Δc_i) > 0) between two players ALWAYS lowers both participants' tournament EV while raising the EV of all non-participants — Result 1: E[E_i(c+Δc)] < E_i(c) for participants (strict Jensen on concave E_i); Result 2: Σ_{non-participants} E[E_k] increases (prize-pool conservation).
equation: E_i(c) = Σ_k P_i(k|c)·prize_k (concave in chips); fair bet: E[Δc_i] = 0, Var(Δc_i) > 0

claim: ICM equity is concave in chips (diminishing marginal chip value under top-heavy payouts; 2nd/3rd-place probs via Malmuth-Harville recursion) ⇒ any mean-preserving spread in a player's chip distribution lowers expected equity — variance without edge donates equity to the field; results sharp only for two-player bets (3+ player bets can break the concavity argument via correlated eliminations).

NNTD (Neural Network Training Dynamics, arXiv:2205.13532): selective-classification signal scoring each example by its late-weighted prediction disagreement across training checkpoints vs the final model's label — abstain on examples the model 'changed its mind about' late in training; late-weighted average over 25–50 checkpoints of 1[prediction at checkpoint t ≠ final prediction], exponential-style weighting favoring late checkpoints (best k = 0.05); no extra head, no extra training — free if checkpoints are kept.

NNTD results: CIFAR-10 coverage at fixed error — 2% error: NNTD 91.2 vs SAT 90.3, DG 89.1, SN 88.3, SR 85.8, MC-DO 86.1; 1% error: 86.4 (best); 0.5% error: 75.9 (best); SVHN at 2%/1%/0.5%: 98.5/96.3/88.1 (best at all three); CIFAR-10 at 90% coverage: NNTD error 1.83 vs SAT 1.90, DG 2.19, SN 2.29, SR 2.78, MC-DO 2.87.

NNTD limitations: disagreement measured against the final model's own label, not ground truth — confidently-wrong subpopulations are invisible; k = 0.05 tuned on the same benchmarks it wins on; 25–50 checkpoints suffice.

Ehrlich, Boudreaux, Boudreau & Sanders (2021, arXiv:2112.14846): horse-race of Bill James's Pythagorean against a novel difference-form contest-success function on 1,000 simulated 2014 MLB seasons (2.43M games, Strategic Baseball Simulator): (1) original Pythagorean EWP_{i,j} = rs_{i,j}²/(rs_{i,j}² + ra_{i,j}²); (2) general Tullock EWP_{i,j} = rs_{i,j}^α/(rs_{i,j}^α + ra_{i,j}^α); (3) difference-form CSF EWP_{i,j} = 1/(1 + e^{α(ra_{i,j} − rs_{i,j})}); win proportions log-transformed to parameter-linear forms, estimated by OLS with team fixed effects, model selection by AIC.
equation: EWP_{i,j} = 1/(1 + e^{α(ra_{i,j} − rs_{i,j})})  (difference form); EWP_{i,j} = rs_{i,j}^α/(rs_{i,j}^α + ra_{i,j}^α)  (Tullock)

claim: Pythagorean horse-race: Tullock form estimated exponent 1.722 (SE 0.005), R² = 0.826, AIC = −49,671.95, RMSE = 0.106; difference form parameter 0.003 (SE 0.000006), R² = 0.829, AIC = −50,128.41, RMSE = 0.105; AIC ratio P_T/P_D = e^{−228.23} ≈ 7.60×10^{−100} ('exceedingly unlikely' Tullock is the best fit); but practical gap is tiny (ΔR² = 0.003, ΔRMSE = 0.001) — the astronomical AIC ratio is a large-N artifact, statistical significance here is not practical significance (ledger INFERENCE).

Validity anchor for the simulator: fitted Tullock exponent 1.72 matches prior empirical MLB estimates (Dayaratna & Miller 2012), offered as evidence the simulator reproduces the real DGP; fitted on win proportions not binary outcomes; MLB-only (162-game season; NFL's 17-game season far noisier — needs a 4-game rolling-window stress test); all inference is about the SBS DGP, not real baseball.

Moshrefi & Rana (arXiv:2607.18299): APMM, a hierarchical LMSR-style automated market maker for parlays pricing multi-leg parlays correlation-aware via shared low-order interaction parameters — parlay price = LMSR-style gradient of a convex cost function with sufficient statistics θ_S (interaction parameters for leg-subsets S, |S| ≤ K); truncated hierarchy assumes conditional independence of high-order interactions given low-order ones; loss bounds: concentrated low-order informed flow → quadratic operator loss; diffuse bounded flow → linear loss.

APMM historical replay on Kalshi NBA same-game-parlay markets (Apr–Jun 2026: 7,372 markets / 29,257 trades; 2-leg 6,250/27,984; 3+ leg ~1,122/~1,273): trader price ratios APMM ÷ independent LMSR by parlay order: 1-leg 1.000, 2-leg 0.994, 3-leg 0.981, 4-leg 0.971, 5-leg 0.961, 6-leg 0.938, pooled 0.978 — trader pricing edge grows with order (up to ~6% cheaper at order 6); aggregate maker loss near-zero to negative (maker roughly breaks even to slightly profitable), lower than independent LMSRs in most games.

APMM limitations: in-sample replay (parameters estimated on the same tape); non-adversarial flow assumption; fee design future work (results exclude fees); strategic traders could attack the truncation residual; higher-leg data thin (only ~1,273 trades at 3+ legs, so order-5/6 ratios estimated on small samples).

van Arem, Söhl, Bruinsma, Jongbloed (arXiv:2604.21087): Expected Threat (xT) model fixed point x = s + T·x (s = goal-given-shot vector, T = transition matrix); value iteration converges geometrically (Prop. 1: error after m iterations ≤ γᵐ/(1−γ)·‖x⁽⁰⁾−x⁽¹⁾‖∞); concentration bounds ‖ŝ−s‖∞ = O(√(log K/n)), ‖T̂−T‖∞ = O(K√(log K/n)) (Props. 3–4); model error measured in ℓ∞: max_s |x̂(s) − x(s)|.
equation: x = s + T·x; ‖ŝ−s‖∞ = O(√(log K/n)); ‖T̂−T‖∞ = O(K√(log K/n))

claim: Fitted empirical error law from 104,000 resampled xT models: log(error) = c + α·log K + β·log n + ε with OLS c = −2.0916 (SE 0.017), α = 1.0100 (SE 0.002), β = −1.0267 (SE 0.003), R² = 0.864, residual variance 0.1782 — i.e., error ≈ LogNormal(−2.0916 + 1.01·log K − 1.0267·log n, 0.1782), much tighter than worst-case theory.
equation: log(error) = c + α·log K + β·log n + ε; c = −2.0916, α = 1.0100, β = −1.0267

claim: xT quality rules of thumb (StatsBomb open data ~4M events, 6.5 league-seasons): classic Singh (2019) xT (12×8 grid, ~1 PL season) has P(error < 0.0192) = 0.2209 — likely not valid for scouting; with n = 2.4M (4 seasons) select K = 192 (16×12 grid) — most flexible grid with P(error < 0.0192) ≥ 0.90; a 24×18 grid needs n ≈ 3,348,000 (~5.4 seasons); acceptability criterion <10% of players misassigned a quartile (≤1 quartile shift) with 90% probability → maximal acceptable error 0.0192 (1.92 pp per state).

xT error decomposition: goal-probability (ŝ) estimation error dominates transition-matrix (T̂) error — error correlates strongly with ŝ-error, weakly with transition error; Euro 2020: midfielder xT-created/90 ranged 0.055–0.336 (Q4: Havertz, Sabitzer, Damsgaard, Müller); limitations: 'ground truth' models are themselves estimates, ℓ∞ is conservative (single rarely-visited high-xT state dominates), single-expert basis for the 10%/90% criterion.

NeSymReS (Biggio et al., 2021, arXiv:2106.06427): pre-trained Set-Transformer→skeleton-decoder symbolic regression — Set Transformer encoder (11M params, m=50 inducing points, O(nm)) maps (x,y) set → latent z; Transformer decoder (13M params) models P(ē_{k+1} | ē_{1:k}, z), trained with cross-entropy on prefix-notation skeletons (Adam, lr 1e-4, no schedule); test time: encode data → beam-search skeletons → BFGS constant fitting on MSE → select best by in-sample loss + 1e-14 × (skeleton token count).

NeSymReS pre-training: 1.5M steps ≈ 225M distinct procedurally generated equations; 10M skeletons pre-sampled with up to 3 numerical constants each; accuracy increases monotonically with pre-training dataset size (Fig. 2) — claimed as the only method that 'improves with experience'; key caveat: the distribution over equations used during pre-training strongly influences the prior over equations of the final system (generator = prior).

NeSymReS evaluation: outperforms all baselines (GP variants, DSR, Eureqa-style, EQL, GrammarVAE-style) on all 5 test sets in both time and accuracy by a large margin on most compute budgets; test-time budget ~100 s per equation; on Nguyen at ~10³ s, NeSymReS ≈ DSR (DSR was fine-tuned on Nguyen-7/10, NeSymReS was not); limitations: synthetic-benchmark evaluation only, noise robustness unstressed, skeleton/constant decoupling assumes BFGS succeeds, 'improves with experience' shown only within the synthetic family; code released at github.com/SymposiumOrganization/NeuralSymbolicRegressionThatScales.

OpenFE (Zhang et al., ICML 2023, arXiv:2211.12507): production open-source expand-and-reduce automated feature generation using FeatureBoost (GBDT residual fitting for incremental-gain scoring) plus two-stage coarse-to-fine pruning, beating expert Kaggle features on IEEE Fraud and BNP.
equation: max_{S ⊆ A(T)} E(L(D_tr, T+S), D_vld, T+S)  (Eq. 1, E larger-better)

claim: FeatureBoost (Alg. 2): fit f′ only on new features T′ to base-model residuals: minimize L(f′) = Σᵢ l(yᵢ, ŷᵢ + f′(xᵢ[T′])); incremental gain Δ = L(f) − L(f′); LightGBM GBDT (1000 estimators, lr 0.1, 16 leaves). Pruning: Stage I SuccessivePruning — split D into 2^q blocks, score each candidate τ alone with Δ_τ on growing subsets, keep top half, dedupe, drop Δ_τ ≤ 0; Stage II FeatureAttribution — joint FeatureBoost, MDI per-feature importance, keep top-ranked.
equation: minimize L(f′) = Σᵢ l(yᵢ, ŷᵢ + f′(xᵢ[T′])); Δ = L(f) − L(f′)

claim: OpenFE theory: Thm 4.1 — with GroupBy features, test loss → 0 as #groups and group size grow (Rademacher bound); Thm 4.2 — without generation, a Bernoulli-group instance keeps test loss ≥ 1/64 for any predictor regardless of sample size; operators: unary (Freq/Abs/Log/Sqrt/Sigmoid/Round/Residual), binary (min/max/+/-//), GroupBy aggregations (ThenMin/Max/Mean/Median/Std/Rank/Count/NUnique; Combine, CombineThenFreq); complexity O(2^{−q}·q·n·m²).

OpenFE results: 10 benchmarks (LightGBM, 10 repeats) significantly best on all 10 — DI AUC 0.731±0.001 → 0.888±0.002 (largest gain), CA RMSE 0.432→0.421, ME RMSE 1128.4→982.0, BR AUC 0.756→0.786; Kaggle IEEE Fraud: baseline rank 2286/6351 → expert 76/6351 → OpenFE 42/6351 (beats 99.3%); BNP: 31/2920 → 12/2920 (beats 99.6%); CC18: significantly best on 40 of 49 improvable datasets, avg +1.9% accuracy.

OpenFE efficiency and limitations: runtime 3.5 min vs SAFE 4.3, FCTree 24.4, AutoCross 141, AutoFeat 163.3, FETCH 533.3 (avg TE/DI/NO/VE); MI-scoring variant worse than FeatureBoost on all 6 reported sets; TIME SERIES EXPLICITLY UNSUPPORTED ('new features should be computed from the past data; OpenFE cannot handle such constraints'); FeatureBoost scores candidates in-sample-ish (optimism; mitigated by held-out final eval); top DI feature was freq(patient_id) — a base feature useless alone (never splits in XGBoost), evidence against split-based candidate pre-filtering.

Feature-programming framework for multivariate time series: programmable, hyperparameter-free feature generation modeling increments as spin-gas Glauber dynamics with three operators — Difference[s1,s2] (smooth then subtract), Window[s,lookback] (max/min/mean over fixed lookback), Shift[s,Δτ] (arbitrary time displacement) — arranged in a 0th/1st/2nd-order (position/momentum/acceleration) hierarchy; default program K=45 extended features, lookbacks [7,25]; no search, LLM, or training in the loop.
equation: X_{t+Δt} = X_t + c·Σ σ_{t+lδt}; φe(X) = (σi,t, δσi,t/δt, δδσi,t/δtδt)

claim: Feature programming results: one-step-ahead, basic+extended beats basic-only everywhere except electricity-LSTM; R² improvements 1.3–5.85% (Taxi noisiest: +4.3/5.9/3.4% R² for MLP/CNN/LSTM; +2.3/3.4/3.0% Pearson); multi-horizon (predict 20 from length-20): +88+% R² and +27+% Pearson on average — gains widen with horizon; simple models on extended features ≈ SOTA (TCN, TFT, N-BEATS) on raw; weakest base model gains most (TFT on Taxi R² 54.58→61.31, +12.3% relative); generation time negligible vs training (Taxi 24.34 s vs 5,461.75 s MLP).
Feature-programming limitations: no feature selection/pruning mechanism exists; 80/20 random split (not walk-forward) used — noted as a hygiene weakness.

SSWNP (self-supervised waypoint noise prediction): plug-in auxiliary task for trajectory prediction — duplicate each observed trajectory into a clean view and a Gaussian noise-perturbed view, force both to predict the true future (spatial consistency), and train a noise-prediction head on the encoder, with zero inference-time overhead. Views: X̃_i^{≤t_ob} = X_i^{≤t_ob} + Φ_i^{≤t_ob}, Φ = ω·Φ′, Φ′ ∼ N(0,1); ω=0.05 best on NBA validation; L_sup = (1/N) Σ_i [L_tp(Ŷ_i,Y_i) + L_tp(Ŷ̃_i,Y_i)]; L_ss = (1/N) Σ_i [MSE(Φ̂_i,0) + MSE(Φ̃̂_i,Φ_i)]; L_total = L_sup + λ·L_ss with λ=0.01.
equation: X̃_i^{≤t_ob} = X_i^{≤t_ob} + Φ_i^{≤t_ob}, Φ = ω·Φ′, Φ′ ∼ N(0,1); L_total = L_sup + λ·L_ss

claim: SSWNP results (metrics minADE/minFDE, tested drop-in on GroupNet CVAE, AutoBot Transformer, SSAGCN, Graph-TERN): NBA SportVU GroupNet+SSWNP ADE/FDE 1.13/1.69 → 0.903/1.147 (RD 22.33/38.28%); spatial-consistency-only ablation 1.018/1.362 (both modules contribute); TrajNet++ AutoBot+SSWNP 33.8% ADE / 36.4% FDE improvement; ETH-UCY RD 8.60/14.00% vs B1, 16.60/23.20% vs B2; SSWNP resilient under test-time noise injection where baselines degrade significantly.
SSWNP limitations: ω and λ are dataset-specific; NBA SportVU is 25 Hz with known jitter (generalization to 10 Hz NFL RFID untested).

Concept-drift study (deployed at Walmart): no single drift detector wins across metrics — headline empirical finding; prescribes majority-vote ensembles (abrupt: ADWIN+HDDM-A+KSWIN; gradual: HDDM-A+HDDM-W+Page-Hinkley); majority-vote ensemble was top-3 on every metric on the change-risk data ('if not the best, always in the top-3'); production deployment credited with 33% reduction in major incidents and multi-million-dollar savings (Q2 2021, attribution with acknowledged confounders).

New drift-evaluation metrics: TPD = detected-true / actual drifts (optimal 1; fixes TPR inflation from multiple detections inside one ADI); Drift Count = total actual drifts detected; ADI = 4× drift width; ADD = mean instances between true and detected drift; prequential error e_i = (1/i)Σ_k L(y_k, ŷ_k) shown misleading (a constantly-firing bad detector lowers prequential error via constant retraining).
equation: TPD = detected-true / actual drifts; e_i = (1/i)Σ_k L(y_k, ŷ_k)

claim: Sparsity-aware imputation recipe: runs-test on missingness indicator to separate MAR/MNAR, Q-Q distribution fit, mask-complete-rows RMSE bake-off; kNN variants dominate (kNN50 for <30% sparsity, kNN100 above on multivariate normal); imputation always helped — positive effect on all 6 metrics for all 7 detectors on both datasets (Harvard synthetic + proprietary Walmart change-risk ~50K binary-labeled change requests).
Drift-study limitations: drifts are label-flip injections after shuffling (coarse proxy for organic regime change); no significance tests for the ensemble-vs-best-single gap.

NGGP for few-shot regression: per-observation invertible 1-D Continuous Normalizing Flow (FFJORD), conditioned on input features, applied to the GP posterior to model heteroscedastic/skewed/multi-modal noise while keeping closed-form GP conditioning. GP posterior: μ* = K(X*,X)(K(X,X)+σ²I)⁻¹y; K* = K(X*,X*)+σ²I − K(X*,X)(K(X,X)+σ²I)⁻¹K(X,X*); CNF log-probability: log p(y) = log p(f_β⁻¹(y)) − ∫ Tr(∂g_β/∂z(t)) dt.
equation: log p(y) = log p(f_β⁻¹(y)) − ∫ Tr(∂g_β/∂z(t)) dt

claim: Flow-conditioned marginal likelihood: log p(y|X,φ,θ,β) = log p(zʰ|X,φ,θ) − Σ_d ∫ ∂g_β/∂z_d(t) dt, zʰ = f_β⁻¹(y,h_φ(X)); deep kernel: feature extractor h_φ → NN Linear/RBF/Spectral-Mixture kernel; meta-training maximizes flow-augmented marginal log-likelihood (Deep Kernel Transfer paradigm).
equation: log p(y|X,φ,θ,β) = log p(zʰ|X,φ,θ) − Σ_d ∫ ∂g_β/∂z_d(t) dt

claim: NGGP results: mixed-noise sines in-range NLL DKT+Spectral 0.37±0.16 vs NGGP+NN Linear 0.17±0.15 (heteroscedastic noise), out-of-range 1.58±0.40 vs 1.35±0.38; head-pose out-of-range NLL 0.00±0.09 vs NGGP+Spectral −0.62±0.24 (substantial calibration win under domain shift); NASDAQ100 out-of-range NLL DKT+RBF 1.049±2.028 vs NGGP+RBF −2.978±0.571, MSE×100 0.181±0.089 vs 0.016±0.034; wins concentrate in NLL (probabilistic calibration) and out-of-range robustness, not raw MSE.

NGGP costs/limitations: O(n³) GP + per-step FFJORD ODE solves; authors state NGGP harder to train than DKT, only worthwhile when data genuinely non-Gaussian; no calibration diagnostics shown; no tabular/discrete-event sports data tested.

MAML (Finn, Abbeel & Levine, 2017): meta-learns a network initialization θ explicitly optimized so that a few gradient steps on K new-task examples produce good generalization. Meta-objective: min_θ Σ_{T_i∼p(T)} ℒ_{T_i}(f_{θ−α∇_θℒ_{T_i}(f_θ)}) (Eq. 1); inner update θ′_i = θ − α∇_θℒ_{T_i}(f_θ); outer update θ ← θ − β∇_θΣ_{T_i}ℒ_{T_i}(f_{θ′_i}); first-order approximation (drop second derivatives, evaluate meta-gradient at θ′_i): 'nearly the same' accuracy at ~33% compute speedup.
equation: min_θ Σ_{T_i∼p(T)} ℒ_{T_i}(f_{θ−α∇_θℒ_{T_i}(f_θ)}); θ′_i = θ − α∇_θℒ_{T_i}(f_θ)

claim: MAML results: synthetic sine regression adapts 'with only 5 datapoints' where pretrain+fine-tune fails; Omniglot 5-way 98.7±0.4% (1-shot), 99.9±0.1% (5-shot), 20-way 95.8±0.3%/98.9±0.2%; miniImageNet 5-way 48.70±1.84% (1-shot), 63.11±0.92% (5-shot) vs meta-learner LSTM 43.44/60.60, matching nets 43.56/55.31, fine-tune 28.86/49.79; first-order approx 48.07±1.75% / 63.15±0.91% ('nearly the same'); RL cheetah/ant adapt in two or three gradient steps; pretraining 'in some cases worse than random initialization.'

CFCQL (Shao et al. 2023) for offline multi-agent RL: per-agent counterfactual regularization keeps CQL's value lower-bound guarantee while avoiding the exponential-in-agents over-conservatism of naive joint CQL (MACQL). Evaluation (Eq. 4): Q̂_{k+1} ← argmin_Q α[Σ_{i=1}^n λ_i E_{s∼D, a^i∼μ^i, a^{−i}∼β^{−i}}[Q(s,a)] − E_{s∼D, a∼β}[Q(s,a)]] + Bellman error Ê_D(π,Q,k), Σλ_i=1, λ_i≥0 — penalize agent i's OOD actions counterfactually (others' actions held at behavior data), linearly combined.
equation: Q̂_{k+1} ← argmin_Q α[Σ_i λ_i E_{s∼D, a^i∼μ^i, a^{−i}∼β^{−i}}[Q(s,a)] − E_{s∼D, a∼β}[Q(s,a)]] + Bellman error

claim: CFCQL theory: Theorem 4.1 — V̂^π(s)=E_{π(a|s)}[Q̂^π(s,a)] lower-bounds the true policy value from exact evaluation; Theorem 4.2 — CFCQL's conservatism is milder than MACQL's (quantified gap) while still a lower bound; Theorems 4.3/4.4 — better safe-policy-improvement bounds.

CFCQL results (MPE Cooperative Navigation): CFCQL 62.2±8.1 / 52.2±9.6 / 65.0±10.2 / 112±4 (Random/Med-Rep/Medium/Expert) vs MACQL 45.6±8.7 / 25.5±5.9 / 14.3±20.2 / 12.2±31, OMAR 34.4±5.3 / 37.9±12.3 / 47.9±18.9 / 114.9±2.6 — CFCQL best or tied-best on all four; MACQL collapses on Medium/Expert (over-conservatism); Predator-Prey: CFCQL 78.5±15.6 / 71.1±6 / 68.5±21.8 vs MACQL 25.2±11.5 / 11.9±9.2 / 55±43.2; the CFCQL–MACQL gap is largest where data is weakest (Random/Med-Rep).

Decision Diffuser (Ajay et al., ICLR 2023, arXiv:2211.15657): reframes sequential decision-making as conditional generative modeling — a return/constraint-conditioned diffusion model over STATE sequences only, with inverse-dynamics action recovery, sidestepping value-function estimation. Training objective (Eq. 4): max_θ E_{τ~D}[ log p_θ(x_0(τ) | y(τ)) ], with x_k(τ) ≐ (s_t,…,s_{t+H−1})_k (noisy state sequence); classifier-free guidance sampling: ε_θ(x_k,k) + ω(ε_θ(x_k,y,k) − ε_θ(x_k,k)), ω = guidance scale, plus low-temperature sampling; inverse dynamics: a_t ≐ f_φ(s_t, s_{t+1}).
equation: max_θ E_{τ~D}[ log p_θ(x_0(τ) | y(τ)) ]; ε_θ(x_k,k) + ω(ε_θ(x_k,y,k) − ε_θ(x_k,k))

claim: Decision Diffuser results (D4RL Med-Expert): HalfCheetah — BC 55.2, CQL 91.6, IQL 86.7, DT 86.8, TT 95, MOReL 53.3, Diffuser 79.8, DD 90.6±1.3; Hopper — BC 52.5, CQL 105.4, IQL 91.5, DT 107.6, TT 110.0, MOReL 108.7, Diffuser 107.2, DD 111.8±1.8; constraint composition: single-constraint training → combined-constraint satisfaction at test time (qualitative, 2D toy only); limitations: return conditioning cannot invent better-than-dataset play (pricing tail-event ceiling); low-temp sampling trades diversity for return; ω is a sensitive knob; constraint composition unproven at NFL complexity.

Regime-PCMCI (Kretschmer et al., 2020): jointly learns regime assignment and per-regime causal graphs from observational time series by alternating between (a) PCMCI causal discovery on regime subsets and (b) constrained regime learning. Step 1: fix regime weights {Γ(t)}, run PCMCI on {x_t : γ_k(t) ≥ 0.5} (eq. 11) → per-regime parents {P_k}, coefficients {Φ_k} (eq. 13); Step 2: fix graphs, solve for Γ(t) minimizing L(Γ,P) = Σ_t Σ_k γ_k(t)·d(x_t − Ĝ_t(P_k; Φ_k)) (eq. 8), subject to Σ_k γ_k(t)=1, γ_k(t)∈[0,1] (eq. 9) and persistence Σ_t |γ_k(t+1)−γ_k(t)| ≤ N_C (eq. 10); tuning N_C ≈ T/(N_M·N_K); N_K selected via AICc (eq. 18); multiple random restarts N_A × N_Q.
equation: L(Γ,P) = Σ_t Σ_k γ_k(t)·d(x_t − Ĝ_t(P_k; Φ_k)); Σ_t |γ_k(t+1)−γ_k(t)| ≤ N_C

claim: Regime-PCMCI results: sign-change synthetic case — regime reconstruction matches truth 99.6% of time steps (97% averaged over realizations); TPR=0.99, FPR=0.01; per-link coefficient error 0.028 (9%); N_K=3 experiments (N_R=100 each): TPR_all=0.98 vs TPR^ref_all=1.0, FPR_all=0.05 vs FPR^ref_all=0.01, ΔΦ=0.033 vs ΔΦ^ref=0.020; AICc correctly selects N_K in the {2,3} test scenarios; ENSO–AIR real data (N_K=2): top 13 annealing runs all find ENSO→AIR link in one regime only, standardized effect −0.4 (one SD ENSO increase → 0.4 SD AIR decrease), matching documented climatology.

Regime-PCMCI limitations: low-dim N_K=3 experiments took ~45 minutes (hardware unspecified) — scaling pain at d≈30; FPR above known-regime reference (misassignments cause false positives/negatives); backward-looking detection (needs streaming variant); no public code for the regime wrapper (tigramite provides PCMCI).

AutoGluon-Tabular (arXiv:2003.06505): battle-tested open-source tabular AutoML replacing the CASH (algorithm-selection + hyperparameter search) paradigm with a fixed strong model zoo (LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, Random Forest, ExtraTrees, kNN, PyTorch tabular NN with entity embeddings + skip connections, ordered cheap→expensive), multi-layer stacking (layer-2+ stackers reuse base types; skip connections concatenate raw features each layer), and repeated k-fold bagging (OOF predictions become stacker-layer features), plus ensemble selection (Caruana) or weighted average on top.

AutoGluon results: OpenML Benchmark (4h): champion on 23/39 datasets; avg rank 1.8438; avg rescaled loss 0.1385; 1 failure (H2O: champion 2, avg rank 3.1250, rescaled loss 0.2447, 8 failures); Kaggle suite: avg rank 1.7143, avg percentile 0.7041 (~70% of human teams beaten), 0 failures, 7 champions; ablation (avg rescaled loss): full 0.1660 → NoRepeat 0.2199 → NoMultiStack 0.5237 → NoBag 0.7199 → NoNetwork 0.8171 — multi-layer stacking is the single biggest contributor ('Even after 4h, the NoMultiStack variant could usually not outperform the full version trained for only 1h'); headline 'beat 99% of data scientists' claim is 2 cherry-picked Kaggle competitions (honest number: avg percentile 0.7041).

AutoGluon benchmark cross-dataset aggregation metric: per-dataset loss rescaled to [0,1] with champion=0, worst=1, linear interpolation; no temporal validation in the benchmark (cross-sectional) — must wrap with rolling-origin/purged folds for sequential NFL data.

BADGE (arXiv:1906.03671): hyperparameter-free batch active-learning rule blending uncertainty and diversity by running k-means++ seeding over hallucinated last-layer gradient embeddings. Method: seed labeled set with M=100 random examples; per round compute hallucinated label ŷ(x)=argmaxᵢ f(x;θₜ)ᵢ, gradient embedding gₓ = ∂ℓ_CE(f(x;θ),ŷ)/∂θ_out (final layer only), select batch via k-means++ on {gₓ} (favors high magnitude = uncertainty, non-redundant directions = diversity), retrain from scratch each round. Proposition 1: ‖gₓʸ‖² = (Σᵢ pᵢ² + 1 − 2p_y) ‖z(x;V)‖², so ŷ = argmin_y ‖gₓʸ‖ — the hallucinated-gradient norm is a lower bound on the true-label gradient norm.

BADGE results: best overall performance across 231 experiments (7 algorithms × 33 combos); small batch (100, 1000) or MLP: BADGE and Marg best; large batch (10000): Marg degrades, BADGE/ALBL/Coreset best; k-means++ vs k-DPP sampling statistical performance 'nearly perfectly overlaps' with large runtime advantage for k-means++; k-means++ on gradient embeddings yields higher log-det Gram determinant (diversity) AND higher average gradient magnitude (uncertainty) than FF-k-center and even than k-DPP; early rounds favor diversity sampling, later rounds favor uncertainty sampling — BADGE matches whichever is winning ('good choice regardless of labeling budget').

BADGE comparison statistic: pairwise t-statistic t = √5 μ̂/σ̂; algorithm i beats j iff t > 2.776 (two-sided, p=0.05); aggregation: pairwise penalty matrix + CDF of normalized errors neᵢ = ēᵢ/ē_rand. Caveats: Coreset often performs worse than random on complex non-image data with MLP (diversity on meaningless penultimate representations is deleterious); uncertainty-only methods fail at large batch sizes by selecting near-identical batches; no cost-awareness in the paper (every query costs the same).

AzureML Feature Store architecture paper (arXiv:2305.20077v1): systems-design paper (no experiments, no numbers) distilling production learnings on offline/online stores, point-in-time joins, leakage prevention, merge semantics. Offline keeps every record keyed (event_timestamp + creation_timestamp) per ID; online keeps latest record per ID assuming TTL satisfies max(tuple(event_timestamp, creation_timestamp)); offline insert iff (IDs + event_ts + creation_ts) key absent else no-op; online override iff new event_ts > existing, or equal event_ts with new creation_ts > existing, else no-op.

Feature-store leakage-prevention rule: for an observation event at ts₀, retrieval uses only past-of-ts₀ feature values (nearest past value, accounting for expected source/feature data delay); feature window logic: source_window_start_ts = feature_window_start_ts − source_lookback, compute on source window then filter to feature window; materialization = one-time backfill + scheduled incremental (concurrent overlapping-window jobs forbidden).

Feature-store paper caveats: zero numbers reported; several §3 components explicitly 'aspirational... not formally implemented at publication time'; merge-semantics caveat (§4.5.2): 'assuming that there is no failure of dumping the calculated Feature Set records' — eventual consistency under failure relies entirely on retries with no staleness bound; eventual consistency cannot answer 'what did the online store hold at time T' (file proposes snapshot manifests — content-addressed per-materialization).

StreamShield (arXiv:2602.03189v1), ByteDance's production resiliency solution for Apache Flink (70,000+ concurrent jobs, 11M+ slots): formal SLO framing S = (γ, λ_max, τ_max), γ ∈ {full, partial} completeness, λ_max max end-to-end latency, τ_max max recovery time; design mechanisms such that completeness(J) = γ, latency(J) ≤ λ_max, recovery_time(J, e_i) ≤ τ_max, minimizing overhead; key probability math: p=0.0001 per-task failure per 5-min checkpoint interval ⇒ expect ≥1 failure per interval across tens of thousands of tasks.
equation: S = (γ, λ_max, τ_max); completeness(J) = γ, latency(J) ≤ λ_max, recovery_time(J, e_i) ≤ τ_max

claim: StreamShield results: job startup (Nexmark Q2) — 2048 TMs: 500,889 ms baseline vs 201,234 ms StreamShield (>50% reduction); adaptive shuffle on skewed workload: 32 TMs 34 KQPS baseline vs 580 KQPS (+1600%); region checkpointing (12h, 5% slow-HDFS-upload injection): success rate 53.9% (1253/2326) without vs 93.5% (2099/2244) with; single-task recovery (TM killed at T+15): baseline throughput dropped to zero for minutes, StreamShield sustained near-steady throughput ('reduces recovery latency by orders of magnitude'); HotUpdate: restart latency reduced to 20 s.

StreamShield limitations: ByteDance-internal (no external replication, no confidence intervals, test cluster much smaller than production); Flink v1.11 is old (2020), several mechanisms now overlap upstream; WeakHash loss-gating criteria are qualitative; no cost accounting.

Cui et al. (2021, arXiv:2103.16196): AutoML-Zero-style evolutionary framework discovering quantitative 'alphas' (programs over scalar/vector/matrix operands), tractable via redundancy-pruning + fingerprint-caching and mined into weakly-correlated sets with a 15% Pearson-correlation cutoff protocol; portfolio long top-50 / short bottom-50 predicted returns; return R = (P_t − P_{t−1})/P_{t−1}; SR = (R̄_p − R_r)/σ_p with R_r = 0, annualized over 252 days; weak-correlation gate |Pearson(portfolio returns)| ≤ 15% (hedge-fund standard per Kakushadze 2016).

Redundancy pruning: represent alpha as a graph (operators=edges, operands=nodes; prediction s_1 = root); recursively mark nodes redundant unless a leaf is the input feature matrix m_0; prune ops with redundant output operands (overwritten assignments, dead branches, alphas never reading m_0); fingerprint = hash of pruned op-string; cache hit reuses stored fitness. Search: population 100, tournament 10, per-op mutation prob 0.9; 1-epoch fitness evals during evolution; alpha class caps 10 scalar / 16 vector / 4 matrix operands, ops per function capped 21/21/45; 60h time budget per round, keep best-SR alpha per round.

AlphaEvolve results (NASDAQ 5-year daily 2013–2017, 1,026 stocks): Round 0 evolved domain-initialized alpha SR 21.323797, IC 0.067358, correlation with existing set 0.030301 vs GA alpha_G_0 SR 13.034052, IC 0.048853, starting domain alpha SR 4.111784, IC 0.013159; weak-correlation rounds: AlphaEvolve stays positive every round (SR 13.58/15.07/9.50 rounds 1–4, ICs 0.028–0.067) while GA collapses (alpha_G_2 SR −1.936161, IC 0.000779; alpha_G_3 SR −1.971355); all four initializations reach competitive alphas (round-0 SRs 10.7–21.3): low initialization sensitivity.

AlphaEvolve limitations: validation set double-dipped (fitness AND 15% cutoff); SR 21.3 annualized from ~5 months of validation data; no transaction costs; 1-epoch fitness rank-preservation unvalidated.

CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019, NeurIPS, arXiv:1907.00503): conditional tabular GAN with mode-specific normalization and training-by-sampling with log-frequency weighting for imbalanced categorical columns. Mode-specific normalization: P(c_i) = Σ_k μ_k N(c_i; η_k, φ_k) (VGM); value assigned to mode with prob ρ_k = μ_k N(c_{i,j}; η_k, φ_k); represented as (one-hot mode indicator β_{i,j}, within-mode scalar α_{i,j} = (c_{i,j} − η_k)/(4φ_k)).

CTGAN conditional generator: P(row) = Σ_k P_G(row|D_{i*}=k) P(D_{i*}=k); condition mask m_i^{(k)} = 1 iff i=i*, k=k*; generator loss adds cross-entropy between mask m_{i*} and generated one-hot d̂_{i*}; training-by-sampling: pick discrete column uniformly, then value with PMF ∝ log-frequency (upweights rare categories).

CTGAN benchmark results (SDGym: 7 simulated + 8 real): beats Bayesian-network baselines on 7/8 real datasets vs CLBN and 8/8 vs PrivBN; real-data ML-efficacy (avg clf F1 / reg R²): Identity 0.743/0.14, CTGAN 0.469/−0.43 (63% of Identity F1), TVAE 0.519/−0.20; ablations (absolute): GMM5 −4.1%, GMM10 −8.6%, min-max −25.7% vs VGM; w/o training-by-sampling −17.8% (0% F1 on the imbalanced credit dataset — load-bearing); w/o conditional generator −36.5%; motivation: 57/123 continuous columns multimodal, 636/1048 categorical columns have a >90% majority class.

CTGAN privacy note: the generator never sees real data during training, so differential-privacy integration is easier than TVAE; networks: generator 2 hidden layers 256-wide, BN+ReLU, skip concatenations, tanh (α̂), Gumbel-softmax τ=0.2; critic PacGAN pac=10, WGAN-GP loss, Adam lr 2e-4; batch 500, 300 epochs.

Karst et al. (WITS 2024, arXiv:2412.14730): five-category evaluation framework for tabular synthetic-data generators — fidelity: column-wise KS statistic (higher = more similar), row-wise Pearson correlation between column pairs; synthesis: fraction of generated records NOT replicating originals within a 1% margin; efficiency: mean training seconds over 30 hyperparameter runs; privacy: 5th percentile of DCR (median Euclidean distance synthetic→original) and NNDR (nearest/second-nearest distance ratio), higher = lower re-identification risk; graph structure: NetSimile score (higher = more similar networks).

Synthetic-transaction benchmark (5.2M real bank transactions + 4.2M IBM-simulated): FinDiff column fidelity 0.95429 / row fidelity 0.98524 (beats TVAE by 6.41%/1.18%, CTGAN 0.87787/0.95258); synthesis 0.84101 (diffusion copies more; DGAN/WGAN 1.0); DCR 0.00033 (worst privacy) but NNDR 0.98781; efficiency 625 s; DGAN: DCR 1.81121 (best privacy), synthesis 1.0, column fidelity 0.47808 (worst); CTGAN: fidelity 0.878/0.953, synthesis 0.99998, DCR 0.01968, slowest 2267 s (65.3% slower than non-GANs); WGAN: fastest GAN 538 s, worst column fidelity 0.24064, graph collapsed to single cluster (NetSimile = NaN on real data).

Benchmark verdicts and caveats: DGAN for privacy-first sharing, FinDiff/TVAE for augmentation fidelity, CTGAN for balanced general use; all models fail graph replication (real-graph self-similarity 8.026 vs synthetic ~30); 'FinDiff wins fidelity' partially circular (framework adapted from FinDiff's own paper); ~16% of FinDiff records within 1% of a real record; no downstream task utility metric (no TSTR); PRISMA review finding: GANs are 70% of proposed architectures but only 50% of post-2023 top performers — field shifting toward diffusion/VAE.

BioDisco (Ke et al., 2025, arXiv:2508.01285): multi-agent hypothesis-generation pipeline grounding hypotheses in dual-mode evidence (knowledge graphs + literature retrieval), refining through Scientist → Critic → Reviewer agents with a decision-module score threshold; validation via temporal 'future discovery' evaluation (generate using only pre-cutoff data/literature, test whether hypotheses imply relationships discovered after the cutoff) plus Bradley–Terry paired comparisons with ties as half-wins (Davidson 1970 tie-explicit extension fitted separately, similar results); packaged as pip tool pypi.org/project/biodisco.

BioDisco limitations: KG/literature snapshots must be strictly pre-cutoff or the temporal test is void; Critic scores are LLM-judged with no human-score correlation reported; biomedical-to-sports transfer is analogical; the file recommends the Critic be a deterministic backtest gate, not an LLM judge.

PAMFN (Zeng & Zheng 2024, arXiv:2402.09444): progressive adaptive multimodal fusion network for action quality assessment learning per-segment fusion policies (PolicyNet choosing among ranked FusionNets) over RGB, optical flow, and audio branches. Decoder: Q=W^q f^m, K=W^k f^{ms}, V=W^v f^{ms}; f̄^{ms}=softmax(−QKᵀ/√d)V (negative-sign attention extracting dissimilar/neglected info); FusionNet: f̄^cs_{i,t,k} = α^v f^v_{i−1,t} + α^f f^f_{i−1,t} + α^a f^a_{i−1,t}; PolicyNet outputs a_{i,t}=c meaning 'enable the top-c ranked FusionNets.'
equation: f̄^{ms}=softmax(−QKᵀ/√d)V; f̄^cs_{i,t,k} = α^v f^v_{i−1,t} + α^f f^f_{i−1,t} + α^a f^a_{i−1,t}

claim: PAMFN evaluation metric: Spearman's ρ = Σ(x_i−x̄)(y_i−ȳ)/√[Σ(x_i−x̄)²Σ(y_i−ȳ)²], Fisher z-averaged across actions; datasets Rhythmic Gymnastics (1,000 videos, 4 apparatuses, ~1m35s @ 25fps; referee scores) and Fis-V (500 figure-skating videos, ~2m50s; TES/PCS).

PAMFN results: RG avg Spearman 0.819 (Ball 0.757, Clubs 0.825, Hoop 0.836, Ribbon 0.846) vs GDLT 0.765 (+0.054); Fis-V avg 0.822 (TES 0.754, PCS 0.872) vs GDLT 0.761 (+0.061); prior RGB-only ACTION-NET 0.728/0.744; weighted late fusion of all three modalities scored 0.703/0.798 — WORSE than PAMFN and sometimes worse than unimodal ('most multimodal methods using Weighted Fusion achieve worse results than unimodality methods on RG'); audio-only unimodal 0.317 RG avg but 0.575 on Fis-V (music correlates with skating scores); inference 33 ms, 18.06M params (excludes feature-extraction cost).

Moirai (Woo et al. 2024, arXiv:2402.02592v2): masked-encoder transformer time-series foundation model pretrained on LOTSA (27B+ observations, 9 domains) with multi-scale patching and any-variate attention, emitting mixture-distribution forecasts trained by NLL. Any-variate flattening: X ∈ ℝ^{T×V} → patches with variate-index attention bias, attention over (time × variate) tokens; O((T·V)²); multi-scale patches at sizes {p_1,…,p_k}, embeddings concatenated; output p(y) = Σ_m π_m · Dist(y; θ_m) (mixture of Student-t/Gaussian), trained with −log p(y_future).
equation: p(y) = Σ_m π_m · Dist(y; θ_m), trained with −log p(y_future)

claim: Moirai Electricity benchmark CRPS (lower better): Moirai-Large 0.050, Moirai-Base 0.055, Moirai-Small 0.072 vs TiDE 0.048, PatchTST 0.052, TFT 0.050, DeepAR 0.065, AutoARIMA 0.327, SeasonalNaive 0.070 — Moirai-Large matches the best supervised models; scaling helps monotonically; Small lags; zero-shot competitive across Monash with fine-tuning closing remaining gaps.

Moirai limitations: mixture-of-t output cannot express discrete key-number mass (margins landing exactly 3/7); any-variate attention is O((T·V)²), exploding for joint team+player modeling; LOTSA is generic — sports zero-shot transfer is speculative.

Qian, Wang & Wen (2015, arXiv:1501.01126): Composite Risk Measure framework unifying stochastic programming, robust optimization, DRO, and worst-case VaR in one two-layer framework — inner risk over outcomes given a distribution F, outer risk over the Bayesian posterior of F's parameters. CRM objective: min_{x∈X} μ(g_F(H(x,ξ))), F∼P_1 (posterior), ξ∼F.

Composite risk measures: VaR-Expectation (21): min_x VaR_δ(E_{ξ∼F}[H(x,ξ)]) — provably less conservative than DRO: γ*_VaR ≤ γ*_DR at same δ; non-convex (ADM); CVaR-Expectation (33): min_x CVaR_δ(E_{ξ∼F}[H(x,ξ)]) — convex, LP-solvable via SAA; CVaR-CVaR (32): min_{x,α} α + 1/(1−δ) E[(CVaR_ε(H(x,ξ_F))−α)^+] — nested CVaR over both layers with SAA sample complexity M ≥ C_1(H,F)/γ² [C_2(H,F) n + C_3(H,F) log(1/ε)] (36).
Coherence representation (Thm 3.5): ρ(X)=sup_{Q∈Q} E_Q[X]; posterior for normal returns with Jeffreys prior f(μ,Σ)=N(μ|μ_0,t^{−1}Σ)·W^{−1}(Σ|tΣ_0,t−1) (40).

CRM results (359 S&P-500 stocks 2010–2011, rolling 30-day lookback over 300 days, MOSEK/Matlab): VaR-Expectation strictly less conservative than DRO in all 1000 bootstrap experiments, avg 0.070% higher optimal value at δ=0.95 with same probabilistic guarantee; tractability at N=100,000 SAA samples, n=4: VaR-Exp 9.26 s, CVaR-Exp 1.65 s, CVaR-CVaR 17.64 s; real 300-day trading avg daily return: VaR-Exp 0.096%, CVaR-Exp 0.096%, CVaR-CVaR 0.087%, DRO 0.088%, worst-case VaR 0.087%, single-stock 0.078%; CVaR-CVaR volatility lowest at 1.17×10^{−2}; results are bps-level ('robust performance,' not dominance).

Anderson & Zachary (2022, arXiv:2203.01420): rigorous critique of minimax-regret rules — scenario-choice sensitivity, IIA violation, gameability via decoy alternatives — with constructive fix (minimax median regret). Regret R_i(x) = C_i(x) − min_x C_i(x); minimax regret: min_x max_i R_i(x); minimax median regret: min_x median_i R_i(x).
equation: R_i(x) = C_i(x) − min_x C_i(x); minimax regret: min_x max_i R_i(x); minimax median regret: min_x median_i R_i(x)

claim: Minimax-regret critique results: (a) minimax-regret decisions are typically determined by 1–2 binding scenarios — adding/removing one scenario can flip the decision; (b) Lemma 1 (gaming): a decoy decision z with extreme cost M in all-but-one scenario can flip the minimax-regret choice (irrelevant alternative changes the decision); (c) minimax median regret resists the decoy construction; (d) Lemma 2 (IIA characterization): any decision rule minimizing a continuous non-decreasing function of the regret vector that also satisfies IIA is equivalent to minimizing expected cost under some probability distribution — regret-based robustness and IIA cannot coexist.

StruSR (arXiv:2510.06635): guides genetic-programming symbolic regression with local Taylor expansions extracted from a trained PINN via autodiff — PINN Taylor prior T_PINN(x;x₀) = Σ_{k=0}^K u^(k)(x₀)/k!·(x−x₀)^k (default K=5); structure loss L_Taylor(f;x₀) = Σ_{k=0}^K (f^(k)(x₀)/k! − u^(k)(x₀)/k!)²; hybrid fitness F(f) = L_phys(f) + λ·L_Taylor(f) with L_phys = (1/N)Σ(N[f](x_i))² (PDE residual).
equation: L_Taylor(f;x₀) = Σ_{k=0}^K (f^(k)(x₀)/k! − u^(k)(x₀)/k!)²; F(f) = L_phys(f) + λ·L_Taylor(f)

claim: StruSR subtree attribution (masking-based, protects important subexpressions during crossover/mutation): Δ^struct_j = L_Taylor(f_{−s_j}) − L_Taylor(f); Δ^res_j = MSE(N[f_{−s_j}]) − MSE(N[f]); Δ^total_j = β·Δ^res_j + (1−β)·Δ^struct_j; softmax over Δ^total biases evolution toward low-sensitivity subtrees.

StruSR results (8 PDE benchmarks, 75/25 train/test, 10 runs): test MAE — Advection 1.21×10⁻¹³, Diffusion 6.38×10⁻⁶, Poisson2D 7.32×10⁻⁵, Poisson3D 5.62×10⁻³, Heat2D 1.53×10⁻⁶, Heat3D 1.09×10⁻⁴, Wave2D 4.33×10⁻⁵, Wave3D 7.09×10⁻⁶; baselines orders of magnitude worse (Poisson2D: NetGP 5.69×10⁻¹, HD-TLGP 1.87×10⁻², PhySO 7.13); ablation: structure-loss decreases monotonically for StruSR, vanilla GP barely improves structurally, physics-informed GP stalls early, K=5 optimal; recovered forms match ground truth up to algebraic variants (Wave3D: exp(−0.5001t + 1.000x₁² + 0.999x₃²)·sin(x₂)).

tsflex benchmark (5-channel float32 DataFrame, 1 hour at 1000 Hz, 20 runs, Intel Xeon E5-2650 v2): peak memory sequential (MB) — tsflex 1.3±0.1, TSFEL 3.5±0.3, seglearn 435.3±1.5, tsfresh 3540±13.9; runtime sequential (s) — tsflex 4.3±0.1, TSFEL 16.4±0.8, seglearn 9.2±0.1, tsfresh 169.8±1.6; multiprocessing — tsflex 0.7, TSFEL 2.1, tsfresh 98.5; paper claims ~3× faster and ~2.5× less peak memory than closest competitor TSFEL; limitations: benchmark on synthetic regular data, gap handling is the feature function's job (naive function on gapped data silently computes garbage without make_robust), pandas-based not distributed.

Rollout factorization: p_θ(X_{0:T−1}^{1:K}|I_0,C) = ∏_p p_θ(X_p^{1:K}|I_0,X_{<p}^{1:K},C_{≤p}^{1:K}); evidence split into committed base context B_p^v and peer context P_p^v; retrieval score s(q,m)=½(O_{m→q}+O_{q→m}) + λ·ReLU(d_qᵀ d_m) with frustum overlap O_{a→b}=(1/|F_a|)Σ 1[z_b(x)>0 ∧ π_b(x)∈Ω_b] (no estimated depth needed); visibility gate G_i=(1−C_i)P_i, final attention a_i = a_i^base + G_i(a_i^full − a_i^base) — peer influence only where committed history is insufficient.

ConsistWorld results (3,400 Unreal Engine MultiCamVideo scenes + 1,000 Infinigen scenes): Region LPIPS ↓ — Self-Revisit 0.1181, Sync Sharing 0.1179, Async Handoff 0.0700; ablation full 0.1176 vs w/o retrieval 0.3374 vs w/o gating 0.1983 vs neither 0.3818 (retrieval is the dominant component); vs full-history baseline PSNR 18.5583 vs 17.6799, GT-LPIPS 0.4206 vs 0.5203 — selective retrieval beats keeping all history (avoids drift from redundant/conflicting observations); long-horizon (16/24/32 chunks) 0.1046/0.1088/0.1267 vs baseline 0.3820/0.4170/0.4503; agent counts K=2/4/5: 0.1079/0.1221/0.1107 (generalizes to unseen K=5).
